title: The distroless security gap: Why bottom-up containers are the next evolution in OCI images
text:
The distroless security gap: Why bottom-up containers are the next evolution in OCI images
Ever tried to shrink your container images to reduce their attack surface? If you have, you’ve likely discovered a frustrating paradox: shrinking a container often blinds your vulnerability scanners to what’s inside.
We’re facing an industry-wide tension between reducing container attack surfaces and maintaining the security visibility you need. To understand how we got here, and how we can solve it, we have to look at how we historically built containers, and why the current approaches fall short for Day 2 operations.
The anatomy of container bloat
For a long time, full container images were the industry standard. The workflow was simple: developers pulled a base image that included a complete operating system, bundled their application code on top, and shipped it to production.
KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is taking place in Salt Lake City from November 9 to 12. Register Now!
While convenient, this posed a massive security problem. These images included a shell, a package manager, and countless tools and utilities the application never used at runtime. Every piece of unused software in that container represented a potential vulnerability and an unnecessarily large attack surface. If a malicious actor breached the application, they suddenly had a full toolkit to download additional utilities and escalate the attack.
The distroless security gap
To address these security concerns, the “distroless” movement emerged. The idea made sense: while full container images had a larger attack surface because of countless unnecessary components, the distroless approach sought to strip the container down to the bare-minimum dependencies needed for the application to run. No shell, no package manager, no extra utilities.
This certainly reduced the attack surface, but it came at a steep operational cost. Creating a distroless image is complex, fragile, and error-prone. In the effort to cherry-pick and aggressively trim the image, the package metadata — the manifest of what’s installed — often gets stripped out completely.
The unintended consequence is what we now call the “distroless security gap.”
This isn’t just a theoretical problem; it’s a well-documented industry blind spot. Scanners like Trivy will actively throw warning flags when OS package metadata is missing, and a 2022 Rezilion vulnerability report by Yotam Perkal revealed that container scanners suffer from significant false negatives — failing to detect active vulnerabilities simply because they lack the necessary context.
“You might have built an incredibly small container, but if your security team can’t scan it and mathematically prove it is safe, it becomes a massive compliance liability.”
Organizations like Chainguard have similarly noted that if a scanner can’t collect complete package metadata, the scan results won’t accurately reflect the image’s true contents. You might have built an incredibly small container, but if your security team can’t scan it and mathematically prove it is safe, it becomes a massive compliance liability.
Between full and distroless container images, we are left with an imperfect choice: bloated containers with a large attack surface, or minimal containers we cannot audit.
Face-off: Imperative trimming vs bottom-up assembly
Fortunately, there is a third way. Instead of taking a large image and trimming it down, risking the removal of crucial metadata needed for accurate security scans, what if we built containers from the bottom up?
The premise is simple: build your own minimal container image from scratch, including only the exact elements you need. Because you build it from the bottom up rather than stripping it down, you can rest assured that the metadata remains intact. In the open source ecosystem, one example of this new generation of minimal, auditable OCI images is commonly referred to as “rocks.”
A bottom-up container build operates like a conveyor belt with three distinct stations: Slice, Build, and Run.
Station 1: Precision slicing
In a bottom-up build, your container starts as literally an empty image. Using an open-source tool like Chisel, you slice standard, trusted Linux packages (such as those from the Ubuntu archives) into smaller, granular pieces.
Instead of pulling an entire package, you pick only the exact “slices” your application actually needs. Because these slices come straight from curated archives, you maintain a trusted software supply chain with surgical precision. Crucially, the metadata for these slices is preserved, so your security scanners stay fully operational.
Station 2: Declarative builds
Traditionally, containers are assembled with imperative Dockerfiles, where the order of every command matters, and layer caching often creates bloat and fragility.
“It shifts the developer experience from ‘scripting a build’ to ‘declaring a state.'”
Bottom-up builds replace this with a declarative approach. Using an open-source build tool like Rockcraft, developers write a simple YAML file (e.g., rockcraft.yaml) that describes the app and its needs. The tool takes that definition, fetches the source, pulls in the specific package slices requested, compiles everything, and outputs a standard, OCI-compliant container image. It shifts the developer experience from “scripting a build” to “declaring a state.”
name: chiseled-python
base: bare
build-base: ubuntu@26.04-lts
version: "3.14"
summary: Chiseled Python3.14 rock
description: Chiseled Python rock
license: Python-2.0
platforms: { amd64: }
run-user: _daemon_
parts:
    install-python:
        plugin: nil
        stage-packages:
          - base-files_release-info
          - python3_core
Station 3: Taming PID 1 at runtime
The final operational hurdle for minimal containers is what happens when they run. In a standard operating system, the OS handles process management automatically. But inside a container, if your application spawns child processes and those processes die, they leave behind “zombies” — dead processes that still occupy system resources.
Without a proper init system, zombies pile up until your container crashes, causing cascading failures at scale. Traditional base images include process managers, but distroless images often strip them out to save space. To keep minimal containers stable without reintroducing bloat, bottom-up containers use tools like Pebble, a tiny, lightweight service manager that runs as PID 1, serves as the container’s entry point, and safely reaps zombie processes.
What’s next
For too long, the cloud-native ecosystem has treated security visibility and container minimalism as a zero-sum game. The distroless movement was a necessary step in highlighting the dangers of bloated images, but the resulting blind spots in vulnerability scanning are no longer acceptable for enterprise production environments.
“For too long, the cloud-native ecosystem has treated security visibility and container minimalism as a zero-sum game.”
By shifting from an imperative, top-down trimming approach to a declarative, bottom-up assembly process, engineering teams can achieve the best of both worlds. We can build security-maintained, minimal containers that are auditable and operationally stable. Container security shouldn’t come at the expense of developer experience or Day 2 visibility.

title: AI Is Redefining the Concept of a Programming Language's Popularity
text:
Since 2013, we’ve been metaphorically peering over the shoulders of programmers to create our annual interactive rankings of the most popular programming languages. But fundamental shifts in how people are coding may not just make it harder to measure popularity, it could even make the concept itself irrelevant. And then things might get really weird. To see why, let’s start with this year’s rankings and a quick refresher of how we put this thing together.
In the “Spectrum” default ranking, which is weighted with the interests of IEEE members in mind, we see that once again Python has the top spot, with the biggest change in the top five being JavaScript’s drop from third place last year to sixth place this year. As JavaScript is often used to create web pages, and vibe coding is often used to create websites, this drop in the apparent popularity may be due to the effects of AI that we’ll dig into in a moment. But first to finish up with this year’s scores, in the “Jobs” ranking, which looks exclusively at what skills employers are looking for, we see that Python has also taken first place, up from second place last year, though SQL expertise remains an incredibly valuable skill to have on your resume.
Because we can’t literally look over the shoulders of everyone who codes, including kids hacking on Minecraft servers or academic researchers developing new architectures, we rely on proxies to measure popularity. We detail our methodology here, but the upshot is that we merge metrics from multiple sources to create our rankings. The metrics we choose publicly signal interest across a wide range of languages—Google search traffic, questions asked on Stack Exchange, mentions in research papers, activity on the GitHub open source code repository, and so on.
For the first time ever, IEEE Spectrum is hosting an emergency interactive session to discuss whether AI is signaling the end of distinct programming languages as we know it.
We’re bringing our expert team together with an audience of tech enthusiasts, developers, and industry leaders to discuss:
- How AI is rapidly changing the landscape of programming languages
- Why knowing the best languages might not be necessary in your career
- What skills you’ll need instead
But programmers are turning away from many of these public expressions of interest. Rather than page through a book or search a website like Stack Exchange for answers to their questions, they’ll chat with an LLM like Claude or ChatGPT in a private conversation. And with an AI assistant like Cursor helping to write code, the need to pose questions in the first place is significantly decreased. For example, across the total set of languages evaluated in the TPL, the number of questions we saw posted per week on Stack Exchange in 2025 was just 22 percent of what it was in 2024.
With less signal in publicly available metrics, it becomes harder to track popularity across a broad range of languages. This existential problem for our rankings can be tackled by searching for new metrics, or trying to survey programmers—in all their variety—directly. However, an even more fundamental problem is looming in the wings.
Whether it’s a seasoned coder using an AI to handle the grunt work, or a neophyte vibe coding a complete Web app, AI assistance means that programmers can concern themselves less and less with the particulars of any language. First details of syntax, then flow control and functions, and so on up the levels of how a program is put together—more and more is being left to the AI.
Although code-writing LLMs are still very much a work in progress, as they take over an increasing share of the work, programmers inevitably shift from being the kind of people willing to fight religious wars over whether source code should be indented by typing tabs or spaces to people who care less and less about what language is used.
After all, the whole reason different computer languages exist is because given a particular challenge, it’s easier to express a solution in one language versus another. You wouldn’t control a washing machine using the R programming language, or conversely do a statistical analysis on large datasets using C.
But it is technically possible to do both. A human might tear their hair out doing it, but LLMs have about as much hair as they do sentience. As long as there’s enough training data, they’ll generate code for a given prompt in any language you want. In practical terms, this means using one—any one—of today’s most popular general purpose programming languages. In the same way most developers today don’t pay much attention to the instruction sets and other hardware idiosyncrasies of the CPUs that their code runs on, which language a program is vibe coded in ultimately becomes a minor detail.
Sure, there will always be some people who care, just as today there are nerds like me willing to debate the merits of writing for the Z80 versus the 6502 8-bit CPUs. But overall, the popularity of different computer languages could become as obscure a topic as the relative popularity of railway track gauges.
One obvious long-term consequence to this is that it will become harder for new languages to emerge. Previously, new languages could emerge from individuals or small teams evangelizing their approach to potential contributors and users. Presentations, papers, demos, sample code, and tutorials seeded new developer ecosystems. A single well-written book, like Leo Brodie’s Starting Forth or Brian Kernighan and Dennis Ritchie’s The C Programming Language, could make an enormous difference to a language’s popularity.
But while a few samples and a tutorial can be enough material to jump-start adoption among programmers familiar with the ins and outs of hands-on coding, it’s not enough for today’s AIs. Humans build mental models that can extrapolate from relatively small amounts of data. LLMs rely on statistical probabilities, so the more data they can crunch, they better they are. Consequently, programmers have noted that AIs give noticeably poorer results when trying to code in less-used languages.
There are research efforts to make LLMs more universal coders, but that doesn’t really help new languages get off the ground. Fundamentally, new languages grow because they are scratching some itch a programmer has. That itch can be as small as being annoyed at semicolons having to be placed after every statement, or as large as a philosophical argument about the purpose of computation.
But if an AI is soothing our irritations with today’s languages, will any new ones ever reach the kind of critical mass needed to make an impact? Will the popularity of today’s languages remain frozen in time?
What’s the future of programming languages?
Before speculating further about the future, let’s touch base again where we are today. Modern high-level computer languages are really designed to do two things: create an abstraction layer that makes it easier to process data in a suitable fashion, and stop programmers from shooting themselves in the foot.
The first objective has been around since the days of Fortran and Cobol, aimed at processing scientific and business data, respectively. The second objective emerged later, spurred in no small part by Edgar Dijkstra’s 1968 paper “Go To Statement Considered Harmful.” In this he argued for eliminating the ability for a programmer to make jumps to arbitrary points in their code. This restriction was to prevent so-called spaghetti code that makes it hard for a programmer to understand how a computer actually executes a given program. Instead, Dijkstra demanded that programmers bend to structural rules imposed by the language. Dijkstra’s argument ultimately won the day, and most modern languages do indeed minimize or eliminate Go Tos altogether in favor of structures like functions and other programmatic blocks.
These structures don’t exist at the level of the CPU. If you look at the instruction sets for Arm, x86, or RISC-V processors, the flow of a program is controlled by just three types of machine code instructions. These are conditional jumps, unconditional jumps, and jumps with a trace stored (so you can call a subroutine and return to where you started). In other words, it’s Go Tos all the way down. Similarly, strict data types designed to label and protect data from incorrect use dissolve into anonymous bits flowing in and out of memory.
So how much abstraction and anti-foot-shooting structure will a sufficiently advanced coding AI really need? A hint comes from recent research in AI-assisted hardware design, such as Dall-EM, a generative AI developed at Princeton University used to create RF and electromagnetic filters. Designing these filters has always been something of a black art, involving the wrangling of complex electromagnetic fields as they swirl around little strips of metal. But Dall-EM can take in the desired inputs and outputs and spit out something that looks like a QR code. The results are something no human would ever design—but it works.
Similarly, could we get our AIs to go straight from prompt to an intermediate language that could be fed into the interpreter or compiler of our choice? Do we need high-level languages at all in that future? True, this would turn programs into inscrutable black boxes, but they could still be divided into modular testable units for sanity and quality checks. And instead of trying to read or maintain source code, programmers would just tweak their prompts and generate software afresh.
What’s the role of the programmer in a future without source code? Architecture design and algorithm selection would remain vital skills—for example, should a pathfinding program use a classic approach like the A* algorithm, or instead should it try to implement a new method? How should a piece of software be interfaced with a larger system? How should new hardware be exploited? In this scenario, computer science degrees, with their emphasis on fundamentals over the details of programming languages, rise in value over coding boot camps.
Will there be a Top Programming Language in 2026? Right now, programming is going through the biggest transformation since compilers broke onto the scene in the early 1950s. Even if the predictions that much of AI is a bubble about to burst come true, the thing about tech bubbles is that there’s always some residual technology that survives. It’s likely that using LLMs to write and assist with code is something that’s going to stick. So we’re going to be spending the next 12 months figuring out what popularity means in this new age, and what metrics might be useful to measure. What do you think popularity should mean? What metrics do you think we should consider? Let us know in the comments below.
Stephen Cass is the special projects editor at IEEE Spectrum. He currently helms Spectrum's Hands On column, and is also responsible for interactive projects such as the Top Programming Languages app. He has a bachelor's degree in experimental physics from Trinity College Dublin.

title: Scale isn't one number: three ways a Kubernetes control plane runs out of room
text:
Scale isn’t one number: three ways a Kubernetes control plane runs out of room
Three clusters in trouble, and they look nothing alike.
The first is a training fleet. It sat at a few thousand nodes for months, then a new run landed, and it’s at fifteen thousand. Kube-apiserver starts eating memory. Etcd starts complaining.
The second never passes a few thousand nodes and is having a much worse day. It’s an agent platform, and its objects are alive: sessions created, suspended, resumed, and destroyed thousands of times a minute, every transition a write.
The third is neither big nor fast: a platform cluster with two hundred operators installed and tens of thousands of objects that mostly just sit there, and every apiserver holds a copy of all of them.
Two of those are AI workloads, and one isn’t, which is the least interesting part. They’re running out of room in three different directions, and fixing one does nothing for the others.
KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is taking place in Salt Lake City from November 9 to 12. Register now!
Go looking for guidance, and you find… not much. There’s plenty of advice for getting to 5,000 nodes. Past that, or sideways from it, the internet shrugs.
So you add more apiservers. It’s a documented option in kOps and the standard answer you’ll get from most people. It makes your problem worse, because every apiserver you add replicates the entire watch cache. You bought request capacity and paid for it in memory you didn’t have.
None of these is a research project. Clusters well past 5,000 nodes run in production today on stock upstream components. Nobody got there with a magic fork; they got there by being deliberate about what each store holds.
The scale isn’t the hard part. The assembly instructions are missing.
Three kinds of scale
Ask how big a control plane needs to be and the answer comes back in nodes. That’s how the second and third clusters end up tuned for a problem they don’t have.
“The scale isn’t the hard part. The assembly instructions are missing.”
Node-bound. Training and RL fleets: large, homogeneous, and the pressure is every kubelet reporting in. At 100,000 nodes with a 10-second heartbeat, liveness alone generates about 10,000 writes per second, and in our measurements lease renewals were roughly 70% of write QPS. Most of what that control plane does is nodes politely saying “still here,” forever.
Churn-bound. Agent platforms: modest size, very intense day. Systems that pack many agent sessions onto a smaller pool of worker pods express each actor’s lifecycle as a custom resource, so the busiest and shortest-lived objects are CRDs, and the write rate has nothing to do with how many machines you own.
State-bound. Platform clusters: many kinds, many objects, most of them asleep. The cost isn’t writes; it’s resident bytes multiplied by every apiserver holding them. This is the axis where the add-an-apiserver reflex actively hurts.
They’re independent: you can max any one with the other two on the floor. A recipe that only knows node count will happily tune the wrong thing.
Seams and recipes
Seams are the places where you can take Kubernetes apart: a contract between two components, usually at a network boundary, and substitutable, so you can replace what’s behind it without patching upstream.
Think of them the way a tailor thinks about seams in a jacket: take it in at the waist, let out the shoulders, still the same jacket. Cut somewhere that isn’t a seam, and you’ve made a very expensive rag.
“Think of them the way a tailor thinks about seams in a jacket. Cut somewhere that isn’t a seam, and you’ve made a very expensive rag.”
Recipes are scale-tested configurations built around those seams: executable configs that pass their scale test or fail it, with CI telling you the day they stop being true.
The four seams
Seam 1: the storage contract. Which store holds which resource types. Relieves churn. Not all of your cluster state deserves the same durability guarantees. Events and node leases are ephemeral, leader-election leases are ephemeral and chatty, and none need the same durable, Raft-replicated store as your Deployments. KEP-4743 defines the storage-interface boundary, and –etcd-servers-overrides routes resource types to different backends today. etcd isn’t the problem, and none of this argues for replacing it; a general-purpose consistent store shouldn’t absorb traffic when no business is durable.
The gap: –etcd-servers-overrides only knows about built-in resources, so a churn-bound platform can’t route the very custom resources generating its write storm. Watch for an enhancement in a future release.
Seam 2: the node liveness contract. How liveness reaches the control plane. Relieves node count. Two fixes for that heartbeat load, and they compose. Absorb it: a node-facing tier in front of the control plane handles renewals and propagates only real state transitions. Make it cheaper: route renewals through etcd’s in-memory lease refresh instead of a full Raft commit. That one lands in etcd itself, so it helps every cluster, down to the three-node one.
Seam 3: the shard axis. The field that controllers, caches, and stores agree to shard on. Relieves all three. Horizontal scaling means every layer agrees on how objects are divided. Pick the wrong axis and your controller spends its life reaching for objects in someone else’s shard. KEP-5866 introduces hash-range filtering for API traffic, the foundation. Coordination, resharding, and sharding the controller manager are out of scope, and all three need work.
Seam 4: cache residency. What an apiserver actually keeps in memory. Relieves state. Remember the apiserver that replicates the whole watch cache? That’s this seam, and the state-bound cluster’s entire problem. One that only ever talks to the scheduler doesn’t need every object resident, and a two-shard prototype cuts heap by roughly half per shard. There’s a floor: with every disableable cache off, an apiserver still carries about 0.9 KB per RBAC object, because the authorizer’s informers hold them regardless.
The gap: residency doesn’t exist upstream yet. KEP-5866 filters egress, so the cache still stores everything. Prototype branches and a draft KEP update are up for review.
The recipe ladder
| Recipe | Scale | Composition | Seams | Evidence | 
| Classic HA | up to 5k nodes | 2 to 3 identical control planes | none | measured | 
| Role-Split | 5k to 20k | separate machine pools for API serving, scheduler, KCM, etcd | 4 | shipped, benefit not yet measured | 
| Node Plane | 20k to 65k | Role-Split plus a node-facing tier that absorbs the leases | 1, 2 | measured, n=1 | 
| Partitioned Store | ~100k | Node Plane plus resource types split across independent stores | 1 on top of 2 | externally demonstrated | 
| Sharded Slice | beyond | K shard units, each a controller plus apiserver pinned to a hash range | 3, 4 | doesn’t exist yet | 
That last row is on the ladder on purpose: publishing the rung nobody has built is how it stays useful. The bigger gap is the index. You pick a rung by node count, the one axis of three with measurements behind it. No one, us included, has published a scale-tested recipe for a churn-bound or state-bound cluster.
None of this is a distribution: stock upstream binaries, shipped as CI-tested configuration, so a release that changes the calculus shows up as a test failure first.
Where you can push
- Per-CRD storage configuration, for Seam 1. No KEP yet so that the use cases will shape it. If your hot objects are custom resources, bring your write rates to SIG API Machinery. Numbers off a real churn-bound cluster are the most useful thing anyone could contribute.
- KEP-5866 and the residency extension, for Seams 3 and 4. Prototype branches are up for review, and the design is not settled.
- Recipes nobody has published. Above 20,000 nodes, or serious churn, or a cluster that’s simply heavy: you know something the rest of us don’t.
We’ll be at KubeCon NA. Bring your worst control-plane graph and tell us which seam we got wrong.
Training fleets, agent platforms, and the unglamorous platform cluster are running out of room in three different directions, and all three should get there with stock upstream components. Most of the pieces are already on the workbench. Let’s put them together!

title: Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill
text:
When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.
“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”
What’s Your Ask?
Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:
- Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.
- Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.
- Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.
- Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.
- Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.
- Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.
Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”
For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits.
Mapping Your Way Into Washington
Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.
On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”
Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”
For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.
A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.
“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology
The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?
During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls.
Shortcuts to Influence
Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.
“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.
It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.
And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”
Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”
