Organizations need to stay current where they can and have a deliberate security strategy for the systems they can’t upgrade immediately. The faster vulnerabilities are discovered, the more important this will become.
What happens now?
For PHP users, the immediate priority is straightforward: move to a fixed release or obtain appropriate security fixes for an otherwise unsupported version. But let’s talk more long-term.
It can be tempting to use PHP2Shell as evidence that PHP is suddenly less secure, but that couldn’t be further from the truth. The combined community and vendor effort this week proves that. Instead, we need to change our outlook on security, because vulnerabilities like these will only become more common.
“Yes, our capacity to find difficult security problems has improved. But our ability to respond needs to keep pace.”
AI is changing which security investigations are practical and how quickly they can happen. That’s valuable when researchers are working with projects and the wider ecosystem to resolve vulnerabilities. But it also puts more pressure on organizations to know what they’re running, stay on supported releases when possible, establish clear vulnerability-response processes, and have a plan for applications that cannot be upgraded immediately.
Yes, our capacity to find difficult security problems has improved. But our ability to respond needs to keep pace.

title: OpenAI donates Open Responses, its spec for a common LLM API, to the Agentic AI Foundation
text:
OpenAI donates Open Responses, its spec for a common LLM API, to the Agentic AI Foundation
OpenAI on Thursday announced that it is donating the Open Responses API specification to the open source Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF).
In addition to Open Responses, OpenSandbox, Anthropic’s Agent Skills, and HuggingFace’s OpenEv framework for agent environments are also joining the AAIF.
The join other AAIF projects like the MCP and A2A protocols, AGENTS.md (also from OpenAI), the open source AI agent goose, agentgateway, and Agent Router. The foundation, which is part of the Linux Foundation, launched in December 2025, with MCP, goose, and AGENTS.md as its first projects.
As for Open Responses, the core idea here is to provide developers with a set of core API calls that should work across LLM providers. When OpenAI first announced the specification in January, the team behind the project noted that virtually all LLM providers now offer the same building blocks (messages, tool calls, function calling, etc.), but that they also all represent them differently in their APIs.
Open Responses aims to create a spec that standardizes these primitives so that developers don’t have to translate between each vendor’s idiosyncratic API when they switch between models.
“When we co-founded AAIF, we contributed AGENTS.md, a way to give coding agents project-specific instructions,” an OpenAI spokesperson told The New Stack. “Open Responses addresses another part of building agents by giving developers a shared format for working with models across endpoints that support it, so they have fewer provider-specific integrations to maintain. Vercel AI Gateway and Databricks Model Serving already implement it, and AAIF will provide a neutral home for developers and providers to continue developing the specification together.”
Why a neutral home matters
It’s this neutral home that is generally the reason why companies donate projects to a foundation. The AAIF is part of the Linux Foundation, which has become somewhat of the de facto standard for providing vendor-neutral homes for popular open source projects, with a technical steering committee, which will initially be made up of project maintainers, handling the technical discussions.
Who already supports it — and who doesn’t
There is already wide support for the spec, with the likes of AWS (in Bedrock), Databricks, LM Studio, Ollama, Hugging Face, Nvidia, OpenRouter, Red Hat, Vercel, and open source projects like vLLM and OGC (previously Llama Stack) supporting it.
Among the names that are missing from this list is OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, which defines its own Messages API for giving developers access to its models. Anthropic is a member of the AAIF, so maybe we’ll see the company adopt this spec at some point in the future.
With the Interactions API, Google, too, has its default for letting developers work with its models.
Open Responses doesn’t hide its lineage. The project’s own contributor guide notes that its core schema files are copied from OpenAI’s API. And while OpenAI’s earlier Chat Completions API became an early standard that others used to model their offerings after, Anthropic’s Messages API has now also left a clear mark (in large part thanks to the success of Claude Code), with the likes of DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.ai, MiniMax, and others exposing Anthropic-compatible endpoints, too.
That split is exactly the kind of fragmentation a vendor-neutral spec like this is meant to fix, of course.

title: AI found a critical PHP flaw. The bigger failure began in 2024.
text:
AI found a critical PHP flaw. The bigger failure began in 2024.
Did one of your favorite websites go dark on Wednesday? Some did, as operators took services offline while they waited for fixes to two critical flaws in PHP, the language behind much of the web.
The precaution didn’t mean those sites were hacked. The holes themselves were bad news with a capital B. But the bigger long-term concern might be how the embargo on the patches was handled.
PHP powers roughly 70% of websites, but that figure describes PHP’s reach, not the number of vulnerable or compromised sites.
WordPress told site owners to update PHP; these flaws don’t require a WordPress update.
The flaws are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The PHP project’s fixed releases are 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12; users of older PHP branches need a supported upgrade or a distributor’s backport.
The PHP security emergency, aka PHP2Shell, exposed more than dangerous bugs in a widely used language. The release also set off a dispute over coordinated disclosure and underscored the pressure on open-source maintainers as AI-assisted researchers find and develop exploits faster.
The road to this emergency ran through OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative. Working in that program, security firm Calif used GPT-5.6 Sol to find a route to remote code execution and reported it to PHP on August 11. OpenAI independently reported the same underlying issue that day; Wiz reported its findings on August 24. PHP’s maintainers led the fixes. They had spotted signs of the underlying out-of-memory problem in 2024, but its full impact became clear only this August.
“This is about as broad as a critical vulnerability gets.”
“This is about as broad as a critical vulnerability gets,” Moshe Siman Tov Bustan of OX Security said in a statement. “If you have a publicly accessible PHP instance and haven’t patched it, start from the assumption that you’re exposed. If you find evidence of exploitation, assume compromise, not just exposure.”
OX Security CEO Neatsun Ziv added: “This is what an internet-scale vulnerability looks like. When a flaw hits technology this ubiquitous, the blast radius isn’t one product or one industry. It’s the web itself.”
Behind those warnings, open-source leaders are debating how the industry should respond when discovery outpaces remediation. The New Stack has reported on the flood of AI-generated vulnerability reports facing maintainers; PHP’s case adds a dispute over whether an embargo still protected users once details began to leak.
A disclosure dispute and an admission of failure
Before the patches were released, details of PHP2Shell began to leak. The PHP Foundation says two CVE IDs circulated on October 20, followed by an accidentally published proof-of-concept video.
Chainguard CEO and co-founder Dan Lorenc then released patched container images more than six hours before the October 21 coordinated release. He says he believed reports of active exploitation justified the decision to break the embargo.
The speed concern is real: After WordPress released version 7.1.2 on September 22 to fix CVE-2026-87902, Patchstack observed probes against WordPress sites that same day and attempts to write files the next day.
That, by the way, is bad enough. But the WordPress episode doesn’t establish whether attackers successfully exploited these PHP flaws when Chainguard published its images.
Why Lorenc jumped the clock
In an email to The New Stack, later reflected in his LinkedIn post, Lorenc said Chainguard independently discovered the same issue with its testing harness and a frontier AI model prompted to “find bad vulnerabilities in PHP.”
Lorenc said Chainguard first heard on Friday, October 16, that a PHP issue was coming. It independently found the issue that night, received a full briefing on Saturday, October 17, and helped test fixes.
He said news began leaking Monday, October 19, and discussion intensified Tuesday night, when several vendors reported what they believed were exploits in the wild.
Lorenc wites that, after a video call with other researchers, he decided to ship the fixes and immediately notified the disclosure group. He said he believed the coordinated disclosure guidelines allowed early release when there was evidence of exploitation in the wild.
Lorenc said three considerations drove the decision. These were how easily Chainguard had independently discovered the vulnerability and built an exploit, how much information was already circulating about the vulnerabilities and fixes, and the evidence shared about active exploitation.
Chainguard made its patched images publicly accessible, rather than restricting them to customers. Lorenc acknowledged that the PHP Foundation disagreed with his decision.
They certainly didn’t agree. The PHP Foundation’s account was blunter: “Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix.” It said Chainguard had received the patch early so customers could update at the agreed disclosure time.
In the foundation’s view, publishing the built images gave attackers a chance to study the fix while other PHP users were still waiting for patches.
“We’re not always going to get it right, and not everyone is going to agree with our decisions.”
Lorenc wrote that he was sorry his decision added stress for PHP’s maintainers. “We’re not always going to get it right, and not everyone is going to agree with our decisions,” he said, adding that Chainguard’s goal was to protect the most people.
What counts as an exploit?
The disagreement centered on what counted as evidence of active exploitation. Lorenc said other vendors had seen exploits in the wild. The PHP Foundation said its security team had not identified a functional exploit among the circulating proofs of concept at the time of release.
Amazon Threat Intelligence later reported an apparent exploit attempt against one of its honeypots on October 17 and more attempts early on October 21. Still, it said it was unclear whether those attempts would have succeeded on real systems.
The competing risks are clear. Yes, holding an embargo gives distributors time to prepare updates together. And, true, releasing a fix early may protect users who can obtain it. But it also gives attackers clues while other PHP users are still waiting for patches.
The capital-B problem underneath
The PHP Foundation also acknowledged a separate failure in its response. Developers noticed signs of the out-of-memory problem behind one CVE during a 2024 audit, but had not found a concrete route to remote code execution.
The foundation said competing fixes carried difficult compatibility and security trade-offs, and work repeatedly stalled. It called the delay “a structural failure” caused by its decision process and lack of resources.
The New Stack has previously reported on the link between paid maintenance and security practices. The foundation is now seeking more support from companies, hosts and governments that depend on PHP.
Canonical, Ubuntu Linux‘s parent company, offers a less critical assessment of the overall response. In an e-mail, Luci Stanescu, Canonical’s security engineering manager, says, “Canonical supports and recommends coordinated vulnerability disclosure according to best practices. The early embargo leak by a third-party was unfortunate, but we believe the disclosure process worked well.”
That assessment differs in emphasis from the PHP Foundation’s criticism: a leak can undermine part of the process without necessarily invalidating the broader coordination effort.
For CIQ Chief Technology Officer Peter Nelson, whose company is Rocky Linux’s founding sponsor, the PHP episode fits a broader change already underway in Linux security.
“We have seen AI used in exploiting vulnerabilities in the kernel space for the past six months,” Nelson says. “This represents more research going into other widely used software programs like PHP. We expect to see more of it as open-source projects continue to use AI and other means to harden the code and provide a greater defense against vulnerabilities like this.”
“Today, such vulnerability exploitation requires a frontier model. Tomorrow that won’t be the case.”
Nelson expects that pressure to continue as advanced vulnerability-research capabilities become more accessible. “Today, such vulnerability exploitation requires a frontier model. Tomorrow that won’t be the case.”
Lorenc also frames the challenge as an industry-wide problem rather than one confined to PHP. “This is unfortunately the new normal for the industry, and we’re going to need to work together as one team to have a chance at securing our critical infrastructure fast enough to stop attackers from causing real harm.”
Patching cannot wait for the usual maintenance window.
For enterprise users, the immediate consequences are operational. Gunnar Hellekson, Red Hat’s vice president and general manager for Lightwell, a joint Red Hat–IBM effort to address vulnerable open-source dependencies, tells The New Stack in an email that the PHP flaws illustrate the risk in dependable software that organizations may rarely think about.
Hellekson said that stable production software can be easy to overlook even as AI-driven discovery increases the volume and speed of vulnerability findings. The PHP issues, he said, remind us how deeply open source is woven into the systems that run businesses.
He emphasized getting tested updates from trusted suppliers, especially when vulnerabilities affect vital programs like PHP. “Given the potential impact of these vulnerabilities, Red Hat recommends that customers deploy validated, tested patches as soon as they are available from trusted sources including Red Hat, even outside of normal patching windows.”
“Software that supports millions of websites cannot depend on a handful of maintainers to manage increasingly sophisticated threats alone.”
Beyond that, we need more resources, in general, for open-source software maintenance and security. As Kara Sprague, CEO of HackerOne, says in a statement sent to the media, “The PHP discoveries are also a reminder that open-source security is everyone’s responsibility. Software that supports millions of websites cannot depend on a handful of maintainers to manage increasingly sophisticated threats alone.”
No, no it can’t.
For organizations running affected PHP systems, the “patch it right now!” problem remains: deploy a fixed build and review systems for signs of attempted exploitation, including activity dating back to October 17.
This is where the competing assessments converge. Better-funded maintainers, more resilient disclosure procedures, and broader access to defensive tools could address the longer-term problem. And that’s the capital-B problem underneath this week’s patch.

title: PHP’s security scramble is just a preview: AI is digging up flaws faster than maintainers can fix them
text:
PHP’s security scramble is just a preview: AI is digging up flaws faster than maintainers can fix them
One of the biggest security scares to hit the web is causing widespread disruption, prompting businesses, hospitals, schools, and government agencies to temporarily shut down websites and online services as they scramble to protect themselves against two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language underpinning much of the internet.
The vulnerabilities, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute malicious code on affected servers. Major technology companies have been racing to protect users, with Cloudflare deploying firewall protections and Automattic confirming that websites hosted across its platforms, including WordPress.com, WordPress VIP and Tumblr, have been secured. The Wikimedia Foundation, meanwhile, took several supporting services offline until they can be patched.
The PHP project released emergency fixes on Wednesday for versions 8.2 through 8.5. Older versions are no longer officially supported, although some distributions and vendors provide legacy fixes, and PHP has published limited patches for versions 7.4 through 8.1.
But while the PHP vulnerabilities are a major deal in their own right, the circumstances surrounding their discovery, remediation, and disclosure offer a revealing glimpse into the growing pressures facing the open-source community, as AI makes it easier to uncover serious security flaws.
“Find bad vulnerabilities in PHP”: Prompt discovery
News of the impending patches emerged on Tuesday, after details leaked ahead of their scheduled disclosure. The following day, OpenAI revealed that security firm Calif had discovered one of the flaws using its GPT-5.6 Sol model, while Google-owned Wiz had independently identified both vulnerabilities. OpenAI said it spent two months coordinating a response involving PHP maintainers, the security researchers, Cloudflare, and government cybersecurity agencies, as part of its Patch the Planet initiative.
The effort was disrupted when software supply-chain security company Chainguard released patched PHP container images more than six hours before the agreed time. CEO Dan Lorenc acknowledged on LinkedIn that he made the call, noting that Chainguard had independently rediscovered the flaw using a frontier AI model and the simple prompt “find bad vulnerabilities in PHP“.
Lorenc defended the decision by pointing to reports of attacks and the ease of reproducing the vulnerability. The PHP Foundation, for its part, argued that the early release could help attackers while other vendors were still preparing their patches.
“This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure,” the Foundation notes.
Nils Adermann, a PHP Foundation board member and creator and co-maintainer of Composer, says that “there were no confirmed exploits,” adding that any identified activity was merely people attempting exploits.
“The decision you took unilaterally without any communication with the PHP team was both irresponsible and unprofessional.”
“There was a clear embargo until the time of disclosure and public release, that was discussed and evaluated repeatedly as information arrived, weighing the risk of exploitation vs protection from publishing patches without complete updates,” Adermann writes in response to Lorenc’s post. “The decision you took unilaterally without any communication with the PHP team was both irresponsible and unprofessional. The proper thing to do here is apologize, not to justify your clear misbehavior.”
The new normal
The PHP pandemonium highlights a larger concern, however: AI is making it easier to find security flaws, faster than the people responsible for fixing them can respond. And as Lorenc himself put it: “This is unfortunately the new normal for the industry.”
Just a day before OpenAI’s disclosure, Anthropic published research showing that Claude had identified 493 security issues across 25 open-source projects encompassing more than five million lines of code. One configuration flaw had gone unnoticed for 21 years, and had the potential to disable an authentication requirement, allowing unauthorised clients to reach a supposedly restricted server.
While not all of Anthropic’s findings were exploitable vulnerabilities, they underline a growing problem: AI can uncover security weaknesses at scale, but assessing them and developing reliable fixes still takes time and expertise.
Christopher Robinson, CTO of Akrites and CTO / chief security architect at the Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF), says the PHP emergency is also a reminder of the importance of being ready to respond when serious vulnerabilities do emerge.
“The best way to minimize the impact of events like PHP2Shell is to prepare and plan for these things to happen.”
“The best way to minimize the impact of events like PHP2Shell is to prepare and plan for these things to happen,” Robinson tells The New Stack. “Having a vulnerability management process and understanding who can assist when issues become too complex are the best things that both open source projects and commercial entities can do.”
When finding bugs becomes easier than fixing them
For Michelle Tilley, software engineer and CTO of Atuin, an open-source developer tool with more than 32,000 GitHub stars, the kind of emergency response mounted for PHP would be difficult to replicate for smaller open-source projects.
“The response here looked like a vendor emergency, with a coalition, government agencies, and WAF (web application firewall) rules,” Tilley tells The New Stack. “This works for a project like PHP, but no one is going to assemble a coalition for an obscure 3-maintainer library that turns out to be used in software all around the world.”
“This works for a project like PHP, but no one is going to assemble a coalition for an obscure 3-maintainer library that turns out to be used in software all around the world.”
Atuin itself is already receiving more AI-generated bug reports and pull requests, Tilley says. While her company has enough engineering resources to handle them, many smaller projects depend on unpaid maintainers working in their spare time, who can become overwhelmed and walk away.
“These developers can, and do, burn out,” Tilley continues. “Sometimes they arrange for someone else to take over the project; often, they simply stop working on it, and downstream consumers never know. That’s how projects end up with vulnerabilities that will never be patched.”
Ultimately, she wants more responsibility to fall on researchers and businesses that rely on the code.
“There’s no single fix, but the direction is clear,” Tilley says. “The cost of remediation has to move toward the people finding the bugs and the companies depending on the code.”
That pressure extends to larger projects, too. Madelyn Olson, an AWS principal engineer and maintainer of the Valkey database, says that it too is finding and fixing far more security bugs this year than before.
“The hardest part has shifted from finding bugs to fixing them,” Olson tells The New Stack. “PHP is a good example.”
A PHP developer first identified the underlying problem behind one of this week’s vulnerabilities while fixing an issue uncovered during a 2024 security audit, which was organised by the Open Source Technology Improvement Fund (OSTIF). However, attempts to resolve it stalled because proposed fixes risked breaking compatibility, affecting performance or disrupting third-party extensions. Few engineers had the expertise to resolve those trade-offs, according to the PHP Foundation.
“AI is getting very good at finding bugs,” Olson says. “Making the right fix still takes experienced maintainers, and that’s where support from companies matters most.”
“AI is getting very good at finding bugs. Making the right fix still takes experienced maintainers, and that’s where support from companies matters most.”
To manage the influx, Valkey is narrowing its definition of a security vulnerability, using AI to inspect its own code, and making backports and releases easier to produce.
The Chainguard brouhaha also raises the question of whether disclosure timelines need to change. Olson recalls three researchers independently reporting the same Valkey bug in one week, each using LLMs. Valkey is now working toward shorter embargoes — although that is a different matter from breaking an agreed release date.
“If you found a bug with an LLM, it’s safe to say someone else can find it too,” Olson says. “That argues for shorter embargoes and faster releases, and Valkey is working toward shorter embargoes now, which is a trend we’re seeing across most large projects.”
A growing security backlog
Derek Zimmer, executive director of OSTIF, said the volume of both legitimate discoveries and poor-quality reports is creating backlogs, with maintainers spending scarce engineering time just establishing which issues are real.
“Maintainers are drowning in a sea of vulnerability reports from the public which is both slop reports and legitimate reports which are nearly impossible to separate without spending a lot of time to triage.”
“The reality in 2026 is that finding serious bugs is easier than ever, and maintainers are drowning in a sea of vulnerability reports from the public which is both slop reports and legitimate reports which are nearly impossible to separate without spending a lot of time to triage,” Zimmer tells The New Stack.
To help, OSTIF is trialling initiatives such as Project V-LAT, which embeds engineers in projects to review findings and develop fixes, while helping maintainers improve how reports are processed.
Robinson also emphasises the need for shared security expertise and dedicated engineers who can support upstream projects. He rejects the suggestion that exposing more flaws necessarily makes open source less secure, pointing to the opportunity for companies that depend on the code to contribute fixes. Yet, many projects have neither the money nor the expertise to respond independently.
“Most upstream maintainers are also acting as volunteers within the projects, with little to no budget, infrastructure, or supporting tools,” Robinson says. “There will be no ‘one size fits all’ approach here, we’ll need to approach this situation using multiple, parallel approaches to get the broadest chance for successful outcomes.”

title: AI found flaws in the code behind 70% of the web. The fix took two months.
text:
AI found flaws in the code behind 70% of the web. The fix took two months.
PHP powers roughly 70% of the world’s websites, according to Wiz Research, so a flaw in its core engine affects much more than any single application. On Wednesday, researchers disclosed two critical vulnerabilities discovered with help from frontier AI models. OpenAI also proposed a new framework for handling the growing number of security flaws AI is helping uncover.
The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively called PHP2Shell, score 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 severity scale. Researchers at Calif.io found one using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol, while Wiz independently found both using its Wiz Atlas tool alongside Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol. Cloudflare also lists Quarkslab among the parties that disclosed the bugs.
A Decade of Dormant Defects
The problem starts with how PHP handles errors. When a request runs out of memory or crashes, PHP can leave behind references to memory that has already been freed. The next request handled by the same worker process may still treat those references as valid. Wiz found that attackers could exploit this behavior to access sensitive data or run malicious code.
These are memory-safety bugs, including use-after-free and type confusion, that developers have spent years trying to prevent by moving critical C code to languages like Rust. PHP’s engine is written in C, and Wiz showed that attackers could exploit the flaws to run code on WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla without logging in. Researchers also demonstrated attacks that exposed server memory without executing code.
At least one of the flaws affects every PHP release from the past decade, with some vulnerable code dating back to PHP 5.4. The bugs went unnoticed for so long because exploiting them required combining several weaknesses in ways that were difficult to uncover.
That’s where AI made the difference. Wiz says a single researcher using frontier models accomplished in about a week what might once have taken a team of experts months. The company calls the findings “an AI inflection point,” arguing that the vulnerabilities had always been there, but AI had made it easier to turn them into working exploits.
Raluca Ada Popa, head of Gemini Security at Google DeepMind, calls frontier AI “a game-changer for cyber defense” in a statement published by Wiz. Security teams are already putting similar tools to work. Cursor recently released the blueprints for a fleet of AI agents that search its codebase for vulnerabilities and block them in pull requests, reflecting a growing concern that attackers can use the same technology to find weaknesses first.
Two Months to a Patch
Wiz says it found the first flaw on August 19 and confirmed unauthenticated code execution against Drupal the following day. It demonstrated the same against WordPress on August 21 and reported the bugs to PHP’s security team on August 24. The team acknowledged the reports on September 21 and began building a coordinated fix, and the patched releases arrived on Wednesday, the same day the details became public.
Wiz credits partners including Cloudflare, Google Cloud, AWS, Microsoft, and Akamai with helping coordinate protections and guidance.
Part of the challenge was making sure the fix covered every version of the flaw. Wiz says its researchers found several variations of the same underlying problem in how PHP handles memory. Hosting providers, cloud platforms, security vendors, and Linux distributors also needed time to prepare before the details became public. Wiz credits partners including Cloudflare, Google Cloud, AWS, Microsoft, and Akamai with helping coordinate protections and guidance.
Nine Hours of Warning
The details leaked before the planned disclosure date. Cloudflare says it began protecting its customers by default at 3:02 a.m. UTC on Wednesday, roughly nine hours ahead of the public announcement, and it observed attack traffic aimed at those customers while it watched attackers modify their payloads to slip past the rules. Request data alone does not always show whether an exploit succeeded, the company says, so its new protections also examine the server’s response.
“Customers should patch their PHP repos.”
Cloudflare was direct about what a firewall can and cannot do. “Customers should patch their PHP repos,” the company writes, describing its rules as an added layer of defense during the update window rather than a substitute for the fix. Those rules can block exploit attempts, but they do not remove the underlying flaws from the software running on a server.
Rethinking the Rulebook
OpenAI led a coalition effort on PHP over the past two months as part of its Patch the Planet initiative. The company says PHP’s maintainers led the fixes and release, while OpenAI and its partners contributed research, technical support, and coordination, and it then used the moment to propose a framework for responding to the critical vulnerabilities that frontier AI uncovers, asking the security community to help refine it.
Running in five stages, maintainers, researchers, and essential technical partners first confirm and fix the flaw, then test the patch with frontier models to look for bypasses. Affected organizations next receive advance information based on their ability to act, so distributors can backport fixes, hosting providers can test mitigations, and security vendors can write detection rules, with government agencies coming after that to help guidance reach operators of critical infrastructure.
Once the fix and disclosure plans are stable, distributors and service providers prepare updates across their products while public guidance helps operators confirm the updates are running. OpenAI says its work on PHP involved CISA, the Office of the National Cyber Director, the White House’s Super Intelligence Force, and international partners.
“the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.”
OpenAI also addressed the other side of its own technology, writing that “the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits,” and it calls the PHP bugs “one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”
The company has committed $1 billion in subsidized access through Daybreak for Frontline Defenders, aimed at organizations with limited security resources that protect essential services, and it is backing maintainers through Codex for OSS subscriptions and direct sponsorship of projects.
Funding and access to AI models can help, but they won’t solve the growing workload facing open source maintainers. The same tools that uncover vulnerabilities are also generating AI-written code that maintainers have to review, adding to an already demanding job. OpenAI acknowledges that each project has its own priorities, meaning the support may not reach everyone who needs it.
Patch First, Protect Always
The PHP security advisory lists four patched versions released on October 21: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and, 8.2.35. Teams using a Linux distribution or managed hosting provider should check with their vendor, since fixes can be backported without changing the PHP version number.
OpenAI has also released a PHP version checker with two Codex skills for checking local servers and websites. The tool can flag vulnerable versions but cannot confirm whether a patch has been applied, particularly when vendors backport fixes.

title: Why your KubeVirt VMs can’t move between clusters — and how EVPN fixes it
text:
Why your KubeVirt VMs can’t move between clusters — and how EVPN fixes it
Your team has moved VMs to Kubernetes with KubeVirt. The workloads are running. The team is gaining confidence. Then someone asks: can we live-migrate a VM to the other cluster?
Disaster recovery, cluster upgrades, capacity rebalancing – the reasons pile up fast. And KubeVirt’s answer appears straightforward: decentralized live migration, which landed in v1.6, should handle this.
But your network team’s answer is more complicated. The VM likely needs to keep its IP and MAC address on the destination cluster. That means a stretched Layer 2 domain between sites. In traditional infrastructure, you’re looking at new VLANs, switch configurations, and possibly even new hardware. A change window. A ticket. Weeks.
“In traditional infrastructure, you’re looking at new VLANs, switch configurations, and possibly even new hardware. A change window. A ticket. Weeks.”
The migration technology isn’t the problem. What gets in the way, more often than not, is the network.
Why the network is the hard part
Cross-cluster live migration has two network requirements that standard Kubernetes networking doesn’t address.
First, a stretched L2 domain. The VM must land on the destination cluster with the same MAC and IP, on the same broadcast domain. Without this, every migration means IP reassignment, DNS updates, and broken connections. Stateful applications — think PostgreSQL clusters using synchronous replication, or message queues with persistent TCP sessions — can’t tolerate IP changes without manual intervention.
Second, a dedicated migration path. Migration transfers gigabytes of memory state in real time. Pushing that through the same network carrying application traffic creates congestion, unpredictable latency, and no way to independently monitor either traffic class.
In traditional virtualization platforms, these are solved with dedicated migration VLANs and proprietary virtual switch constructs: hardware-coupled, vendor-specific, and often licensed per socket. The open source equivalent needs to work as an overlay, managed declaratively, without touching the physical network.
EVPN/VXLAN provides exactly this. OpenPERouter makes it a Kubernetes-native resource.
EVPN as Kubernetes CRDs
OpenPERouter manages EVPN configuration through three Custom Resource Definitions. An Underlay CR establishes BGP peering between each Kubernetes cluster and its top-of-rack switch. An L2VNI CR creates a Layer 2 overlay network, implemented by a VXLAN segment identified by a VNI number and scoped to a VRF. Finally, the L3VNI CR enables IP routing between different subnets and connects your cluster to external networks.
The application network uses VNI 110 in VRF “red”:
apiVersion: openpe.openperouter.github.io/v1alpha1
kind: L2VNI
metadata:
  name: application-net
  namespace: openperouter-system
spec:
  vni: 110
  vrf: red
  hostmaster:
    type: linux-bridge
    linuxBridge:
      autoCreate: true
  l2gatewayips: ["192.170.10.1/24"]
Both clusters get an identical L2VNI resource, and VMs on either cluster share L2 adjacency on the 192.170.1.0/24 subnet. A VM on cluster A at 192.170.1.3 can reach a VM on cluster B at 192.170.1.30 as if they were on the same switch.
The migration network is a second L2VNI. It uses the exact same pattern but a different VNI:
apiVersion: openpe.openperouter.github.io/v1alpha1
kind: L2VNI
metadata:
  name: migration-net
  namespace: openperouter-system
spec:
  vni: 666
  vrf: rouge
  hostmaster:
    type: linux-bridge
    linuxBridge:
      autoCreate: true
  l2gatewayips: ["192.170.10.1/24"]
All the migration network needs is a unique VNI and VRF in the L2VNI CR — in this example, 666 and rouge —  and the migration traffic is isolated from the application network. This overlay rides on the existing IP connectivity between sites. The VXLAN tunnel endpoints don’t even need to be on the same network segment. As long as there’s IP reachability between sites (which can traverse any number of routed hops), the overlay converges.
“Two CRDs define what used to require a network team and a change window.”
Two CRDs define what used to require a network team and a change window.
Operating the migration
With the network fabric in place, here’s what an operator actually does on Day 2 when a VM needs to move.
IP management across clusters needs an IPAM strategy that prevents conflicts without central coordination. The examples use Whereabouts with complementary exclude ranges, which means that each cluster’s Network Attachment Definition covers the same 192.170.10.0/24 subnet but excludes the other cluster’s half. Cluster A allocates from the lower range, cluster B from the upper. But Whereabouts is a design choice, not a requirement; any IPAM provider that can partition ranges across clusters works here.
The migration itself is three resources:
The target VM must be provisioned by the user on cluster B with runStrategy: WaitAsReceiver – same MAC address, same IP configuration, sitting idle until it receives the incoming migration.
Afterward, a VirtualMachineInstanceMigration receiver on cluster B declares readiness:
apiVersion: kubevirt.io/v1
kind: VirtualMachineInstanceMigration
metadata:
  name: vmim-target
spec:
  receive:
    migrationID: cross-cluster-demo
  vmiName: vm-1
A matching sender on cluster A points to the receiver’s migration IP (obtained from the receiver’s .status.synchronizationAddresses) and initiates the transfer.
apiVersion: kubevirt.io/v1
kind: VirtualMachineInstanceMigration
metadata:
  name: migration-source
spec:
  sendTo:
    connectURL: "<receiver VMI migration .status.synchronizationAddresses[0]>:9185"
    migrationID: cross-cluster-demo
  vmiName: vm-1
EOF
Under the hood, migration traffic flows over VNI 666, isolated from VNI 110. The VM is copied to cluster B with its identity intact. EVPN updates MAC/IP advertisements across the fabric – traffic to the VM starts arriving at the new cluster. No DNS changes, no IP reassignment, no connection resets.
Who owns what
The real shift here is operational, not just technical. The configuration for the BGP EVPN — that is, the overlay networks, VRFs, and VNIs — moves from the network team’s domain into the Kubernetes admin’s hands.
“The operational model shifts from ‘request physical network changes and wait’ to ‘apply a CR and the overlay converges.'”
The network team still owns the underlay: IP addressing for router endpoints and links, physical connectivity, and routing between sites. That doesn’t change. But once the underlay is in place, everything above it — stretched L2 domains, dedicated migration networks, VRF isolation — is declared through Kubernetes CRDs by the same platform team managing the clusters. No tickets to the network team to add a VLAN. No change windows to stretch a broadcast domain to a new site.
The following table highlights the shift in operational responsibilities compared to traditional virtualization stacks:
|  | Network Admin Role | Kubernetes Admin Role | 
|---|---|---|
| Traditional Virtualization | Manages physical switches, VLANs, and hardware configurations for every VM movement. | Dependent on the network team for tickets and manual change windows. | 
| KubeVirt + OpenPERouter | Sets up foundational IP connectivity, router endpoints, and links. | Manages the overlay network, BGP/EVPN configurations, and VM mobility declaratively via K8s CRDs. | 
The operational model shifts from “request physical network changes and wait” to “apply a CR and the overlay converges.” Platform teams manage VM mobility the same way they manage everything else in Kubernetes: declaratively, version-controlled, reviewable.
Getting started
The network shouldn’t be the reason VMs can’t move between clusters. EVPN overlays — managed through Kubernetes CRDs — give multi-cluster KubeVirt deployments the same VM mobility that traditional platforms offered, without the physical network dependency or the licensing model.
For step-by-step walkthroughs, see Stretched Layer 2 Network between Clusters and Dedicated Migration Network for Cross-Cluster Live Migration. Ready-to-use configuration files are in the OpenPERouter examples.
Note: KubeVirt is a CNCF Incubating project, accepted in September 2019 and moved to Incubating maturity in April 2022. The decentralized live migration feature referenced here has been available since v1.6 (July 2025) and remains stable in v1.8 (March 2026).

title: From intent to enforcement: Lessons from operating Kubernetes controllers at scale
text:
From intent to enforcement: Lessons from operating Kubernetes controllers at scale
Kubernetes controllers are what make the platform’s declarative model real. They observe the state, reconcile toward the intent, and keep doing so as the system changes beneath them. At larger scales, though, the hardest problems are no longer about writing the reconcile loop. They are about preserving correctness while caches lag, objects churn, and enforcement depends on a complete view of the world. This post distills what we learned from operating two critical controllers in Amazon EKS at scale.
Kubernetes provides pods with connectivity, but it leaves fine-grained traffic enforcement to the underlying platform. Inside the cluster, intent such as who should be allowed to talk to whom still has to be translated into rules the datapath can enforce. For a small experiment, openness is convenient. For production traffic, it becomes a problem you need to solve, and you want to express that intent once and have it hold as pods are created and destroyed all day long.
In Amazon EKS, two controllers close that gap. The Network Policy Controller governs traffic inside the cluster, deciding which pods may talk to which. The VPC Resource Controller governs how selected pods access AWS resources outside the cluster by assigning them their own AWS security groups, the same stateful firewall that AWS already uses for EC2 instances.
Normally, a pod has no security group of its own and inherits the node’s security group. That means an RDS database that wants to allow one pod must allow inbound from the node’s security group, which implicitly allows every other pod on that node as well. A pod with its own security group can be named directly, so the RDS inbound rule allows only that single workload.
Both are ordinary Kubernetes controllers. They watch the cluster, hold state in memory, and reconcile what they observe with what was declared. That reconciliation is what lets you declare intent once and trust it to hold as pods come and go. EKS runs these controllers across clusters that range from a few pods to a hundred thousand nodes, and that range is where this post comes from. At small scales, a controller’s memory footprint, reconciliation correctness, and component interactions are easy to miss. With thousands of nodes and pods, they become binding constraints: the difference between intent that holds and intent that quietly lapses.
“At small scales, a controller’s memory footprint, reconciliation correctness, and component interactions are easy to miss. With thousands of nodes, they become binding constraints.”
This post looks at how these controllers work, what changes as they scale, and the patterns that emerged from operating them.
Two controller design choices that matter at scale
Network Policy Controller: How do you go from label selectors to packet-level enforcement?
A NetworkPolicy is a declaration of intent written in labels. For example, pods labeled app=web may receive traffic only from pods labeled app=api. Labels are what make the rule durable, since they keep meaning the same thing as pods come and go, but labels are not what the datapath enforces. The eBPF program on each node matches on concrete pod IPs, so something has to resolve app=api into the current set of IPs and keep that set correct as pods churn.
The question is where that resolution happens. It could run on every node, with each node watching all Pods, Namespaces, and NetworkPolicies and computing its own answer, and some network-policy implementations do exactly that — EKS does the join once, centrally. A reconciler in the Network Policy Controller monitors the NetworkPolicy objects, along with the Pods, Namespaces, and Services they reference, resolves selectors to IPs, and writes the resolved answer into a resource it owns, called a PolicyEndpoint.
When a policy matches many pods, or pods are constantly created and destroyed, the controller splits the result across several PolicyEndpoints rather than letting a single object grow too large or be rewritten too often. Each node’s agent then acts only on the PolicyEndpoints for its own pods, rather than every node independently re-resolving the entire cluster. That is what keeps API server load manageable as the cluster grows.
From there, the work moves down to the worker nodes. The VPC CNI runs on each node inside the aws-node DaemonSet, and the same add-on runs a network policy agent beside it. The agent never writes back, which keeps the control plane and data plane cleanly separated. The controller decides, and the node enforces. Enforcement happens in the Linux kernel using eBPF rather than long chains of iptables rules. The agent programs the allowed addresses into the kernel as eBPF rules, and from then on, every packet entering or leaving the pod triggers a map lookup and is allowed or dropped right in the datapath.
VPC Resource Controller: How do you give a pod its own firewall identity?
To give a pod its own security group, you create a SecurityGroupPolicy that specifies that pods matching certain labels should receive this security group. For the controller to honor that, the pod needs its own network interface, since a security group can only attach to an interface.
Each node has a limit on the number of pod network interfaces, and the limit depends on its instance type. An m5.large, for example, supports nine. The controller advertises that limit on each node. So, when you create a pod that matches the policy, the controller mutates the pod to add a request for one interface, and the scheduler treats it like any other resource it has to find room for, just as it looks for CPU or memory. The pod only lands on a node with a free network interface, and every pod that gets its own security group uses one up.
Once the pod is scheduled, the controller calls the EC2 API to assign it a network interface on the node, separate from the one the node uses for everything else. It applies the pod’s security groups to that interface. Now, a rule on an RDS, ElastiCache, or OpenSearch resource can allow exactly that workload and nothing else to run on the same node.
What changes with thousands of nodes and pods
The cost of holding state
A controller’s informer holds a local copy of every object it watches, so reconciliation never has to round-trip to the API server. By default, that copy is the full object: the entire pod spec, all containers, environment variables, annotations, and metadata. A single cached pod can be tens of kilobytes, and at tens of thousands of pods, that becomes hundreds of megabytes of fields the controller never reads. The VPC Resource Controller needs only certain fields such as the pod’s node name, namespace, UID, and its own annotations. The Network Policy Controller needs only labels, pod IPs, container ports, and phase.
The VPC Resource Controller addressed this early by building a custom informer that strips each pod down to the fields it needs before caching it. The Network Policy Controller does the same thing in a different way, using a built-in Kubernetes hook that runs on every object as it arrives and keeps only the fields we need. It also filters out terminated and unscheduled pods on the server side, so they never reach the controller. On a large cluster, this cut memory from several hundred megabytes to under a hundred.
“Define the fields your logic actually reads, strip everything else, and test that reconciliation still works on the stripped-down objects.”
The pattern for your own controllers is simple. Define the fields your logic actually reads, strip everything else before it reaches the cache, and test that reconciliation still works on the stripped-down objects. Keep that trimming to field selection only, since it runs on every object one at a time, and an extra millisecond per object adds up fast on a large cluster.
When stale state can’t self-correct
Kubernetes controllers are level-triggered and forgiving. Acting on a slightly stale view is usually safe, because the next reconcile corrects it. The exceptions are actions that cannot be undone, such as deleting a cloud resource, removing a network interface, or programming a rule to drop packets. For these, a stale view is not self-correcting, because there is no object left to reconcile against.
Before it acts, the controller must be certain its cache reflects reality across every object type the action depends on, not just some of them. The VPC Resource Controller periodically scans for interfaces that are no longer associated with any running pod and reclaims them. That decision compares two things: the existing interfaces and the pods currently running. In steady state, this is safe, since any interface it finds was provisioned by the controller itself, so the owning pod is already in its cache.
The hazard appears at startup. When the controller restarts or a new leader takes over, the interfaces created by the previous instance remain on the nodes, but the new instance starts with an empty cache. If its cleanup scan runs before the pod cache has finished loading, a pod that is genuinely running simply has not appeared yet, so the controller assumes it was deleted and reclaims an interface that live traffic is using.
The Network Policy Controller faces the same problem from the other direction. It enforces policies whose resolved addresses are split across several PolicyEndpoint objects, and it must hold enforcement until the complete set has arrived, because acting on a partial set can open traffic the policy was written to block. In both cases, the fix is the same. The controller waits until all its caches have finished loading from the API server before it runs the irreversible action.
When an irreversible action depends on the state of several caches, wait until all caches have finished loading before acting, and guard the action so it cannot fire on a partial state. The cost of getting this right is a few seconds at boot. The cost of skipping it is deleting infrastructure that is still in use.
When an optimization shifts the constraint
The VPC Resource Controller’s pod interfaces carry a second-order effect that only surfaces at scale. Every pod with its own security group draws a single IP address from the subnet, and that address lands wherever a free slot happens to be in the provided subnet. On a busy cluster, these scattered addresses accumulate alongside ordinary secondary IPs that regular pods take and release as they churn, and over time, the subnet’s free space grows fragmented. None of this matters until you enable an optimization that depends on contiguity.
That optimization was prefix delegation for regular pods. EKS normally hands each pod one secondary IP from the ENIs on the node, and because every address costs an EC2 API call, a node tends to exhaust its pod budget long before it runs out of CPU or memory. Prefix delegation changes the unit of request so the node asks for a /28 block of sixteen addresses at once, which lifts density to 110 pods on the same instance and cuts API traffic to a fraction of what it was.
The catch is that a /28 needs sixteen contiguous addresses. A fragmented subnet can report thousands of free IPs while still failing every prefix allocation with an InsufficientCidrBlocks error, because no sixteen of them sit next to each other. Pods stop scheduling even as every dashboard insists the subnet is healthy, because the monitoring built for the per-IP model counts free addresses, and a free-address count says nothing about whether those addresses are contiguous. The fix is to give prefixes their own contiguous space to draw from, either through VPC subnet CIDR reservations or a dedicated subnet.
The lesson generalizes. An optimization may not actually remove a constraint. It moves it somewhere new, and the metric that looked healthy under the old design can stay green long after the real limit has moved. When you make a change for density or throughput, look for where the pressure went, and make sure something you watch would catch it.
“An optimization may not actually remove a constraint. It moves it somewhere new, and the metric that looked healthy under the old design can stay green long after the real limit has moved.”
The controllers that turn network policy into eBPF rules and attach per-pod security groups are ordinary Kubernetes controllers. What lets them hold up at scale is not special infrastructure but deliberate design: cache only the state you actually read, wait for the state to be complete before taking irreversible action, and ensure your monitoring reflects the system’s real constraints. Those lessons extend well beyond EKS. Any controller that translates high-level intent into concrete enforcement has to solve the same problems of state, timing, and scale.
To use these capabilities on your EKS cluster, read our AWS docs on Network Policy and Security group for pods.

title: What happens when your VPN meets 200 AI agents
text:
What happens when your VPN meets 200 AI agents
Providing secure access for your human staff is no simple task. For one, traditional VPNs often grant unnecessarily broad access, so you may have replaced that aging technology with a newer zero-trust network access (ZTNA) solution. And you may have hammered your human-centered privileged access management (PAM) tools into working order, so your engineers are just as happy as your security auditors.
But what happens when you add dozens or hundreds of AI agents to the equation? We know that today’s enterprise is racing to become agentic.
Or what if you want to run continuous integration (CI) and continuous deployment (CD) jobs? After all, you want a modern DevOps stack! You’ll learn quickly that the tools you built and tuned for human access come up short.
Checking identity upfront isn’t enough to securely control access. You need to be able to tailor access based on need, not merely identity. And you’ll need to be able to revoke access when work is completed and provide an audit trail to boot. Even more, you don’t want to run separate access architecture for humans and agents.
To support both human and agentic network access, companies need a unified architecture that can handle all access requests without compromise or delay. That means one consistent policy regardless of who requests access or what they need.
Join us on July 22
Today, there are frameworks and tools you can use to harmonize network access control, intelligent PAM, and agentic control into a single access layer that can handle any request from any source at any time.
On July 28, 2026, Tailscale Solutions Engineer Kartik Bharath and Tailscale Product Manager XingLu Wang will join The New Stack to dig into the difficulties that human-first access policies face in the agentic era and how to address them.
We’ll walk you through what a unified access architecture actually covers today: human developers, contractors, pipelines, and AI agents, under one consistent policy model, without adding IT overhead or slowing down engineering teams.
How to join this free, live event
You have successfully registered for the webinar.
What you’ll learn:
- A clear model for extending your existing access controls to non-human identities without needing a separate tool for each identity type
- Architectural guidance on where identity-based networking, PAM, and AI agent policy fit together
- A practical starting point for teams that need to move fast without creating new security debt

title: Cloudflare wants to build the economic layer of the AI web
text:
Cloudflare wants to build the economic layer of the AI web
AI has changed the web right before our eyes. With Google’s AI Overviews doing the heavy lifting, publications that once owned the first page of search results are being replaced by summaries. Readers get their answer without ever clicking through. Much of the traffic has simply stopped.
Cloudflare on Wednesday announced a slew of updates for publishers who are facing this new reality. From new crawler classifications and analytics dashboards to Answer Engine Optimization tools and an expansion of its Pay Per Crawl program, it’s clear the company is trying to become the economic pipes of the AI web.
The shift from ‘keep out’ to ‘let’s make a deal’
A year ago, Cloudflare’s pitch was practically defensive, asserting that website owners should be able to block AI crawlers. And while that still holds true, the company has pivoted to discussing building “rails” for an “agentic economy.” And it makes sense. If AI agents are already browsing the web, collecting content, and in some cases buying things, someone needs to handle the business end of how the sites they visit are compensated. Cloudflare thinks that someone should be Cloudflare.
Paying for value, not visits
Roughly a year ago, Cloudflare launched Pay Per Crawl, which let publishers set a price for AI companies to pay when they fetched a page. Now the company is pushing toward Pay Per Use, which means publishers get paid when their content actually appears in an AI-generated answer.
To backtrack, under the old model, an AI crawler pays to visit your site, whether or not it does anything useful with what it finds. Cloudflare says it’s already testing this with Ceramic.ai and You.com, each running slightly different versions of the concept.
Instead of charging for access — which is basically a toll booth — publishers are charging for value.
The economics here flip. Instead of charging for access — which is basically a toll booth — publishers are charging for value. That’s closer to how affiliate marketing or licensing deals work, and it’s a much harder problem to solve. It requires knowing which content contributed to which answer, which means an attribution infrastructure that doesn’t really exist at scale yet.
Crawlers need clearer labels
But here’s where things get more technical — and a bit political.
Cloudflare wants AI companies to stop lumping all their crawlers together. Right now, a single bot from a major AI company might be fetching pages for search indexing, model training, and agent tasks all at once. That makes it impossible for site owners to say yes to one use and no to another.
Starting September 15, Cloudflare plans to change the defaults for new and free-tier sites. AI search crawling stays on, but training and agent access get blocked on ad-supported pages unless the site owner opts in. Mixed-use crawlers that refuse to separate their traffic get blocked entirely.
The company is clearly taking a shot at Google here, noting that Google’s bundled approach gives it access to roughly twice as much content as AI-native competitors. Separating crawlers’ intent has become a prerequisite for any kind of functioning market between publishers and AI companies. Because if site owners can’t distinguish between “index my page for search” and “train your model on my writing,” they’ll increasingly just block everything.
Separating crawlers’ intent has become a prerequisite for any kind of functioning market between publishers and AI companies.
Optimizing for AI answers
Cloudflare is also rolling out a dashboard designed for business teams, called Attribution Business Insights. Think of it as the AI equivalent of knowing your Google Search Console numbers, except the “search engine” is now ChatGPT or Perplexity or whatever agent your reader happened to ask.
On top of that, Cloudflare is introducing Answer Engine Optimization (AEO). The idea is that ranking in Google is no longer enough; for publishers to succeed, they also need to understand how and where their content gets cited in AI-generated responses. That’s a different optimization problem than SEO, and right now almost nobody has good tooling for it.
Infrastructure as competitive advantage
Cloudflare already sits between websites and the internet. It sees the traffic and knows what changed on a page and what didn’t. It can tell a crawler to come back later because nothing’s new, which, by the way, it says would eliminate over 50% of current AI crawl traffic.
That puts Cloudflare in a unique position. It’s already part of the path between AI companies and the web. Now it wants to become the layer that manages access, attribution, and eventually payments between them. If AI agents become the primary way people find information online, Cloudflare is betting the next battle won’t be over who builds the smartest model but instead over who builds the infrastructure everyone else relies on.
