Nwokah explains that Grep (the command-line tool that searches plain text for line matches on a specific keyword or pattern) returns matches, and the agent goes on to read whole files. Further, he notes that a vector database will return a handful of chunks, and then the agent asks again with additional queries. Additionally, a data warehouse returns rows, and the agent combines them itself.
“Infino is a retrieval layer designed for this data reader dynamic. It gives the agent one interface directly over object storage that combines structured and unstructured queries: ranked searches, exact counts, joins, filters and aggregates at low cost and large scale,” Nwokah clarifies.
During the good old years of data search, query patterns were comparatively predictable. When humans or applications queried, search ran on a search database. Analytics ran in a warehouse. Vector databases enabled approximate queries and unlocked a new class of use cases, but they didn’t fundamentally change those query patterns. Each query ran on its own system, with its own copy of the data, its own ingestion pipeline, and its own team to run it.
Today, those operations can still span a database plus a search engine, a vector database, and a data warehouse. The agent has to call each one and then spend additional model turns combining the results. Infino’s answer is to embed retrieval functions directly in SQL, so the whole question can be expressed in one query.
Fewer data tasks, less glue code, centralized policy management
“For developers and data teams, it removes entire pipelines and the time it takes to manage them,” Nwokah enthuses. “That means fewer systems, fewer ingest paths, fewer ETL jobs, fewer schemas to keep aligned, fewer clients in the agent’s tool list, and less glue code to combine their results. It also means one place to govern agents.”
He underlines his organization’s method here and says that when an agent’s data lives in a single copy, developers “can enforce hard policies centrally”, so that means governance over who can read what, which rows and columns an agent can see, and what gets logged.
“Compare that with managing agent permissions across MCP gateways and SaaS tools,” urges Nwokah.
“For developers and data teams, it removes entire pipelines and the time it takes to manage them.”
A developer can enter a single natural-language English question, and it becomes one query that completes in milliseconds, according to Infino. Infino has clarified that the important part isn’t SQL itself; it’s that keyword search, semantic search, filtering, aggregation, and grouping can happen together instead of forcing the agent to orchestrate several systems and reason over a pile of intermediate results.
As an additional challenge uncovered during the platform’s development, Infino noted that even when retrieval is fast, it found that agents spend a lot of time in retrieval loops, i.e., working to formulate a query, search, decide whether the results are good enough, try something else, validate the answer, and repeat. Infino says it integrates targeted inference models with the retrieval engine so these simpler tasks run faster and more cheaply than with frontier models.
The data storage challenge: Apache Parquet
The other challenge Infino tackled is how it stores the data. Instead of maintaining separate copies for search, vectors, and analytics, Infino keeps a single copy in Apache Parquet (a column-oriented storage format) on object storage.
“The core engine is open source, Apache-2.0, on GitHub, and we store all data as valid Parquet files with the search indexes embedded beside the Parquet footer, so any tool that reads Parquet can read the data with or without Infino. Infino Cloud, our hosted service, has some additional proprietary features, like being able to point at your existing Parquet data and make it searchable without building any infrastructure yourself,” adds Nwokah.
Infino stores indexes inside the Parquet files to speed retrieval, while the underlying data remains Parquet. Iceberg and Hudi can manage the same table, and Spark, DuckDB, warehouses, and other Parquet readers can still read it. One copy of the data can therefore serve the different ways an agent needs to query it.
Infino also wanted the path from data to query to be simpler than with traditional data stores. Setting up clusters, nodes, shards, and headcount is a lot of complexity just to query data, the company argues. With Infino, developers can point at Parquet or JSON, ingest the data, then point their agent at Infino and start querying.
Who benefits from this technology?
Nwokah lists four major software engineering practitioner groups who he promises can benefit from the approach outlined here:
- Platform or data engineers looking to get their arms around the proliferation of agents, with a far simpler and far less expensive stack to manage. There is no data lock-in (claims Nwokah), as their data stays in their bucket and is readable by any Parquet reader. Agents can combine both structured and unstructured data through one interface.
- Security engineers looking to put a proper governance layer around their agents. With a single copy of data, the auth policies an agent runs under are enforced centrally and deterministically rather than across a set of MCP gateways and SaaS connectors.
- ML and data science teams doing feature exploration. Infino searches, filters, joins and aggregates over both structured and unstructured data, cutting the time between messy data and clean features.
- Software developers building agent workflows across code, logs, CI output, issues and other engineering data. Instead of giving the agent a different retrieval system for each corpus, they can give it one query interface across all of them.
With its current architecture, Nwokah claims that Infino is designed to be roughly 10× cheaper than traditional search or analytics infrastructures. Infino’s own published comparison puts it at about 10.5× cheaper than Elasticsearch and 23× cheaper than OpenSearch for the workload it tested.
Multi-billion-document use cases
Nwokah confirms that the company is already supporting multi-billion-document use cases in people search, document processing, product analytics, and security.
“We are particularly optimized for teams with agent use cases that are already on Parquet or considering migrating to Parquet, or alternatively who are looking to replace their search tool with something easier to manage and more scalable,” he concludes.
One of the organization’s customers, which Infino did not name, is putting petabytes of data from across their entire company on Infino, according to the company. The Parquet sits in their bucket and is still read by existing tools across different teams. Meanwhile, the product and engineering teams get the scalable agent infrastructure they need to launch AI-native solutions for their customers. Developers can then control their agents from a single interface.
Infino CEO Nwokah formed the company alongside co-founder and head of engineering Vinay Kakade, co-founder Asif Makhani, and chief architect Murali Krishna.
The group spent years building and operating ML and search systems across Amazon, Google, and LinkedIn, including AWS OpenSearch. The changing nature of agentic data querying is their rationale for building Infino: to enable any agent to query data at scale, in one query, over one copy of the data.

title: SAP acquires TechWolf to feed more context into its HR agents
text:
SAP acquires TechWolf to feed more context into its HR agents
SAP on Tuesday announced that it has agreed to acquire TechWolf, a Belgian AI company that maps what employees work on and which skills they use, to feed that data to the HR agents in SAP SuccessFactors.
SAP announced the deal at its Connect conference in Las Vegas. The two companies didn’t disclose terms, and SAP expects the acquisition to close in the fourth quarter, pending regulatory approval.
It’s worth noting that TechWolf already had a long-running partnership with SAP.
Under SAP’s current plans, TechWolf will keep running on its own, with co-founder Andreas De Neve staying on as CEO.
TechWolf’s customers include the likes of Booking.com, HSBC, MetLife, PayPal, AMD, Ericsson, and GSK.
As Manoj Swaminathan, president and chief product officer for SAP Autonomous Suite, notes in the announcement, “TechWolf’s proprietary context graph for skills and work provides an excellent grounding layer for agent queries regarding work and skills planning and talent management.”
He adds that the graph “makes token usage more efficient” to help cut the cost of running HR agents. This will make Joule better at tasks like skills-based hiring and role redesign.
Atlassian, of course, made a similar case for its Teamwork Graph in May, saying agents with access to its context used 48 percent fewer tokens. Other companies are making similar arguments about token efficiency.
The deal also fits the argument SAP made at Sapphire in May that enterprise AI is largely a context problem. SAP expects TechWolf to become a central part of the SuccessFactors portfolio, feeding its data into tools for mapping employee skills, planning headcount, and restructuring teams.
At Connect this week, the company also introduced a Workforce Planning Assistant, which it’s bringing to early adopters this quarter.
How TechWolf works
De Neve, Jeroen Van Hautte, and Mikaël Wornoo founded TechWolf in Ghent in 2018. Its platform plugs into the HR software and other business applications a company already uses and infers skills from people’s actual work, rather than from self-assessments.
TechWolf calls the result a “context graph for work.” The graph covers three layers that range from the individual tasks that make up each job to the skills employees put to use and the outside labor market, then lines that up with where the business is headed.
TechWolf: an existing SAP partner
SAP was among the investors in TechWolf’s $42.75 million Series B in 2024. That round, led by Felix Capital, also included ServiceNow and Workday, two companies that compete with SAP for HR software budgets.
TechWolf’s platform already writes its inferred skills back into SuccessFactors modules like the Talent Intelligence Hub, Recruiting, and Learning, and SAP says joint customers are seeing results from that integration.
For developers, TechWolf may be more familiar for the open models it publishes. Its JobBERT models on Hugging Face map job titles and descriptions into a shared vector space for matching, and the latest version handles English, Spanish, German, and Chinese.
De Neve says in the announcement, “Organizations everywhere are trying to figure out how AI is reshaping work, and what their workforce needs to look like because of it.”
With Reltio, which SAP bought earlier this year, Joule’s agents get one consistent view of a company’s customers, suppliers, and products. TechWolf could give them the same kind of view of its workforce.

title: Runway wants to generate software as you use it. Solaris is its first step.
text:
Runway wants to generate software as you use it. Solaris is its first step.
Runway introduced Solaris on Monday, the first model of a new class of AI systems it calls Interface World Models, which aims to do away with the traditional process of translating designs into code and make the visual interface the application itself.
Solaris is a real-time interactive model that generates an interface frame by frame, learning from users’ clicks, drags, and other interactions to determine what to render next. In it, Runway sees an early step towards a new kind of operating layer in which interfaces are generated in real time.
The image is the application now
Runway argues that conventional visual interfaces require designers and developers to translate designs into code and define interactions in advance. With Solaris, Runway promises to bypass this step entirely.
The Interface World Model handles both rendering and interactions, generating every frame and every response to user input so, as Runway describes it, “the entire frame becomes the interface.” In this way, the interface is no longer a sequence of pages but a continuously generated, interactive experience in which “users interact directly with the scene itself.”
To illustrate its vision, Runway offers several examples of what becomes possible with a generative interface: dragging and dropping a shirt from a rack onto an image of yourself; moving furniture around a room; watching a salad bowl change as you drag and drop ingredients from a pile.
Learning, reasoning, and rendering in real time
Solaris is built on Runway’s Gen-4.5 video generation model and follows the path of GWM-1, its general world model. It observes a user’s clicks, drags, and other interactions as signals to generate the next frame. In doing so, it learns what should happen visually each time a user takes an action so it can respond without requiring each interaction to be explicitly programmed.
Runway says it cut the number of denoising steps, taught the model to generate frames autoregressively, and trained it on its own outputs to maintain visual quality over long sessions.
By doing away with the implementation step where visual designs are translated into code, the image users see quite literally is the application.
It also pairs Solaris with a language model to separate reasoning and rendering. Working together, the language model interprets user requests, decides what the application should do next, and creates prompts to guide rendering. Solaris, meanwhile, generates that behavior in real time.
Runway argues that agents trained on conventional, coded interfaces can struggle to generalize when layouts change. It says that Solaris can eanble agents can train on ever-changing interfaces and never-before-seen layouts.
Altogether, Runway’s approach boils down to three new software capabilities: interfaces can be visual, “alive,” and open-ended, continuously responding to user actions. By doing away with the implementation step in which visual designs are translated into code, the image users see is literally the application.
What you stand to gain when you lose the translation step
Runway conducted two evaluations examining coded and generated interfaces.
First, several state-of-the-art multimodal language models, including Claude Fable 5, were tasked with recreating website interfaces from a single screenshot.
Across 30 interfaces, as visuals became more complex, reconstruction quality consistently fell, which Runway points to as evidence that translating an interface through an intermediate representation loses information. But because Solaris operates directly on the visual interface, the company claims it can preserve the interface’s complete visual and semantic state from the first frame onward.
Next, it tested whether a coded interface can recreate “the same sense of a living, responsive environment” as an Interface World Model can.
Runway stacked Solaris against the state-of-the-art language model Claude Opus 5, giving both models the same starting image and interaction requests. Per Runway, across almost 7,500 pairwise judgments and 30 interaction examples, the 250 participants in its user study preferred Solaris for better adherence to the given instructions and for behaving more naturally within the scene in 61% and 71% of comparisons, respectively.
Runway says the evaluation results point to a fundamental difference between coded interfaces and Interface World Models: the former treats each user interaction as an isolated update to the environment, whereas the latter generates interactions that remain coherent within the scene.
The advent of a new operating layer?
Runway says it expects interface generation to follow the development of image and video generation, with successive models improving speed, coherence, and controllability.
For starters, it says that keeping text stable and legible is a top challenge, along with maintaining coherence over long sessions, grounding generation in richer, verified context, and integrating generated interfaces with the rest of the software stack.
Looking ahead, it envisions a new operating layer that can generate useful interfaces to suit nearly any user need. Personalized storefronts and tutorials are just some of the possibilities Runway puts forth, even going so far as to question whether apps will remain the basic unit of interaction.
Runway says it’s working with partners to launch Solaris publicly and is accepting requests for early access.

title: Astro's GitHub issue backlog is heading to zero for the first time in 5 years. Now Cloudflare is open-sourcing the tool that did it.
text:
Astro’s GitHub issue backlog is heading to zero for the first time in 5 years. Now Cloudflare is open-sourcing the tool that did it.
Most open source maintainers will know the feeling of opening GitHub to a growing pile of issues that can’t feasibly be maintained by a small team. AI coding tools have made things worse: a low-effort bug report, an unreviewed patch, or a speculative vulnerability write-up can all be generated in seconds now, but working out whether any of it holds up still takes a person just as long as it always did.
However, the team behind one popular open source project has reported that it’s on track to clear its issue backlog entirely, by handing the grunt work to a team of agents.
Astro, the JavaScript framework used to build fast, content-heavy websites, is down to around 20 open GitHub issues at the time of writing, from more than 200 at the start of this year — and the team expects to hit zero within the next month, which would be a first in the project’s five-year history. It’s getting there using a team of AI subagents built by its own team, and Cloudflare, which acquired that team in January, announced on Tuesday that it’s open-sourcing the systems for other maintainers to use.
Astro finds its fix
The tool, called triagebot-action, runs as a GitHub Action. When someone opens an issue, it kicks off a four-stage pipeline: reproduce the bug in a sandbox, diagnose the root cause, verify it’s an actual bug, and attempt a fix. Each stage is handled by a separate AI agent, and the whole process is driven by a state machine encoded in GitHub labels, so anyone can see exactly where a given issue sits and why.
“‘Fix’ is always the hardest because the bar is so high.”
Fred Schott, Astro’s co-founder and now a senior engineering manager at Cloudflare, says the “fix” step is the least essential part of the system — triaging an issue and handing the report to a human maintainer is, in his words, “still a pretty great outcome” even without it. But the fix is the hardest part to get right.
“Fix is always the hardest because the bar is so high,” Schott tells The New Stack. “Where all of the other tasks are just ‘can you complete your phase — reproduce the bug, diagnose the cause, etc‘. ‘Fix’ is the one where it has to write code that is of high enough quality that it can be merged.”
That gap is exactly why triage, not fixing, came first. Schott traces it back to watching where agents kept proving reliable and where they didn’t.
“I think [it was] just the gradual realization that issue triage is something agents got very good at, without falling into some of the traps of what they were bad at re: code quality,” he says. “And issue triage is also very time-consuming for us as maintainers, so the realization that automating it, without requiring a maintainer to manually trigger it, would save us a ton of time.”
“Issue triage is also very time-consuming for us as maintainers.”
Astro’s home turf
By way of a brief recap, Astro launched as an open source project back in 2021, and Schott spun up The Astro Technology Company the following year with $7 million in seed funding from a roster of backers that included Lightspeed Venture Partners and Google’s Gradient Ventures.
Cloudflare announced it had acquired that company in January, absorbing the team behind a framework that had come to be used by companies like IKEA, Unilever, and Visa. Astro ships pages as plain HTML by default and only loads JavaScript for the parts of a page that actually need it, unlike React-based frameworks, which tend to send a much larger JavaScript bundle for the whole page. This approach, ultimately, aligns with Cloudflare’s own business of making the web faster.
At the time, The New Stack pondered what the deal meant for Astro’s future, pointing to a pattern of platform companies buying up frontend framework teams — some of which, like Netlify’s 2023 purchase of Gatsby, ended with the acquired framework slowly starved of support once its creators moved on. The question was whether Cloudflare would keep investing in Astro or let it drift into the same kind of neglect.
Six months on, Schott says little has changed. Astro still has four full-time engineers, including Schott himself, and everyone who joined through the acquisition remains on the project full time, though volunteer and Open Collective-funded contributors continue to come and go as they always have. Schott says that Astro “still operates distinctly as its own team,” replete with an open roadmap, release cadence, and so on. The team, it’s worth noting, shipped a redesigned development server as part of an Astro 6 beta in January, but triagebot-action is perhaps the clearest sign yet that it has room to build new things.
Adoption of the tool beyond Astro itself is still early. Schott says Cloudflare’s workers-sdk team is prototyping it internally, but “only Astro currently” runs it in production. The underlying agent framework behind it, called Flue, sits under the Astro organization rather than Cloudflare’s, and both projects are built to run on any infrastructure, with no dependency on Cloudflare-specific tooling.
Built for agents
Zooming out, triagebot-action is the second tool in a week that Cloudflare has open-sourced with AI agents as the primary user. At the tail end of July, Cloudflare released pvcli, a command-line debugger for privacy protocols used in products from the likes of Apple and Microsoft. Cloudflare systems engineer Fisher Darling said at the time that pvcli was “explicitly designed for agent-based debugging.”
Triagebot-action tackles a different problem, but the underlying idea is similar: taking work that traditionally required a person at a keyboard and packaging it into software that an AI agent can execute autonomously.
“It’s great when it works, but it’s also always at the discretion of a maintainer for if it is correct and worth accepting, or better to go and write the fix yourself.”
Looking to the future, the next obvious progression for a tool like triagebot-action is the “fix” element itself. Schott says he doesn’t know when the system will get to the point where its fixes can be trusted close to 100% of the time, but that it’s built to evolve toward that gradually — it launched internally with no fix capability at all, then added a suggested fix left on a branch for a reviewer to look at, and only later gained the ability to open a pull request directly from that suggestion. He can picture it going further still: the agent judging its own confidence or the size of a fix, and eventually opening, or even merging, pull requests on its own.
“We are really taking this part seriously, which is why we really focus on the issue triage part first, and then ‘write the code for me to fix this issue‘ part is secondary and nice to have at the end,” Schott says. “It’s great when it works, but it’s also always at the discretion of a maintainer for if it is correct and worth accepting, or better to go and write the fix yourself.”

title: Your social login buttons run on third-party cookies. FedCM doesn't.
text:
Your social login buttons run on third-party cookies. FedCM doesn’t.
“Sign in with Google” and “Continue with Apple” have carried federated login for more than a decade. They strip away onboarding friction, kill password fatigue, and turn anonymous traffic into accounts, which is why they sit on nearly every consumer signup page. The machinery underneath them is the problem.
Those buttons run on third-party cookies. The legacy social login flow relies on the exact cross-domain mechanism that privacy regulators have spent years trying to shut down.
“The legacy social login flow relies on the exact cross-domain mechanism that privacy regulators have spent years trying to shut down.”
Safari has blocked third-party cookies by default since 2020 (Intelligent Tracking Prevention) and Firefox since 2019 (Enhanced Tracking Protection), which already puts roughly half the web in a cookieless state.
Chrome is the messier story: Google walked back its forced deprecation in 2024 and moved to a user-choice model instead of flipping a switch, so the “cookie-pocalypse” deadline everyone built roadmaps around never actually arrived. Do not read that as a reprieve. Two major engines are blocked by default; Chrome’s Incognito is blocked by default; ad blockers and consent fatigue keep climbing; and the cookie is eroding by attrition, whether or not anyone announces a death date. Any login flow built on it is on borrowed time.
FedCM (Federated Credential Management) is the standard built to keep federated login working once that mechanism is gone. The W3C and the major browser engines developed it as a browser-native API that runs federated identity flows without cross-site tracking.
How it actually works
The shift is architectural. In a legacy flow, clicking a social button fires hidden iframes, redirects, or pop-ups so the identity provider can read its own cookies and confirm who you are. That same channel lets the IdP track you across the web. FedCM puts the browser in the middle as a trusted mediator.
The site asks for an identity token through one explicit API call, navigator.credentials.get(), and the browser runs the rest:
- The site requests an identity token from the browser.
- The browser fetches account details from a config file hosted by the IdP, kept siloed from the site making the request.
- The browser shows a native sign-in prompt instead of a pop-up.
- On explicit user consent, the browser passes a token back to the site’s backend to create a session.
Authentication and passive tracking get decoupled. (More on the API: the FedCM spec and MDN docs.)
It also fixes the NASCAR problem. Years of bolting on every available social login produced signup pages plastered with competing brand buttons, the registration equivalent of a stock car covered in sponsor decals. That is cognitive load, and cognitive load costs conversions.
“FedCM skips the wall of buttons and surfaces the right account in a single native prompt.”
Because the browser already knows which provider you used last, FedCM skips the wall of buttons and surfaces the right account in a single native prompt.
Legacy flow vs. FedCM
|  | Legacy federated flow | FedCM | 
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Hidden iframes, redirects, pop-ups | One browser-mediated API call | 
| Privacy model | Depends on third-party cookies | No third-party cookies; explicit per-sign-in consent | 
| User experience | Redirect chains, blocked pop-ups, the NASCAR button wall | One-tap native browser prompt | 
| Security | Phishable redirect surfaces | Browser-isolated prompt the page can’t spoof | 
The practical payoff is conversion. Every extra click and every interrupted redirect sheds a percentage of the people trying to sign up, and mobile browsers frequently block the secondary windows legacy flows depend on. A single native prompt removes that drop-off.
“Every extra click and every interrupted redirect sheds a percentage of the people trying to sign up, and mobile browsers frequently block the secondary windows legacy flows depend on.”
There is a maintenance angle, too: a standardized browser UI means your team stops building and babysitting bespoke login components, and the flow upgrades through browser releases rather than refactors.
What this looks like in production
Axel Springer runs FedCM on Ory across hundreds of millions of users. Thomas Bergemann, its General Director of Product & Revenue, put the result plainly: “We see an over 15x increase in registrations.” (Read the case study.)
Google’s own testing on browser-mediated sign-in shows the same shape of result: dropping the jarring secondary-window step, the one mobile devices routinely block, cuts user drop-off.
Shopify moved onto browser-mediated identity ahead of the cookie changes and held checkout conversion stable on strict, privacy-centric mobile browsers, the exact environments where legacy flows quietly fail.
Getting started with Ory
Step 1: Put the backend behind a CIAM platform. Don’t hand-roll this. Ory Kratos processes the backend side of FedCM natively, turning browser-side identity assertions into secure user sessions. (See the Ory FedCM deployment docs.)
Step 2: Configure your social sign-in providers. In the Ory Console, open the Social Sign-In panel, select your IdP, and enter its FedCM Config URL. Back-channel trust verification is handled for you.
Step 3: Embed the JavaScript trigger. Drop a lightweight snippet on your login page to detect support and fall back cleanly when it isn’t there:
if ('IdentityCredential' in window) {
  navigator.credentials.get({
    identity: {
      providers: [{
        configURL: 'https://auth.your-business.com/self-service/methods/oidc/fedcm/google',
        clientId: 'YOUR_CLIENT_ID',
      }]
    }
  }).then((credential) => {
    return fetch('/self-service/methods/oidc/fedcm/login', {
      method: 'POST',
      body: JSON.stringify({ token: credential.token })
    });
  }).catch((err) => {
    console.error('FedCM flow interrupted, fallback to traditional OIDC:', err);
  });
}
If the browser doesn’t support FedCM, the flow falls back to a standard OpenID Connect redirect, so nobody gets locked out mid-migration. Want to test before you wire up a real IdP? There’s a free MockFedCM site for that.
Where this leaves you
Federated login is moving into the browser, and the privacy model is moving with it. Safari and Firefox already block by default; Chrome is leaking the cookie out the side rather than killing it outright. Neither path leaves your social logins where they were.
The teams auditing their auth stack now are the ones who won’t be debugging broken login loops on someone else’s timeline later. Better to make this move on your own schedule than on the browser’s.

title: Anthropic overhauled Claude Design to fix the handoff. A designer and an engineer disagree on whether it worked.
text:
Anthropic overhauled Claude Design to fix the handoff. A designer and an engineer disagree on whether it worked.
Anthropic this week announced a major overhaul of Claude Design, the design tool it launched in April as a research preview. The update is intended to simplify the handoff between design and engineering teams through a new bidirectional Design-Code integration and make it easier for users to create designs that adhere to brand guidelines.
Plus, Anthropic says it listened to user feedback and made changes to address token inefficiencies that irked early users, and it also added a new editor and more connectors for easy sharing with tools like Adobe, Base44, Canva, Gamma, Lovable, Miro, Replit, Vercel, and Wix.
But Alfie Martin, lead AI product designer at ABM Industries, tells The New Stack she doesn’t think Claude Design has meaningfully reduced the back-and-forth between departments.
Though she acknowledges the tool could make prototyping easier, she warns that token efficiency may still be a problem — and that asking Claude to make every design update itself isn’t, by default, the most efficient way to get work done.
“Token usage is expensive, and Claude Design uses a lot,” Martin says. “Many times, it takes longer than designing a component or changing that detail yourself.”
Claude Design and Claude Code get closer
The AI company says the new iteration of Claude Design now works more closely with Claude Code, enabling users to jump back and forth between design and coding while keeping work synced.
Going one way, developers can run the /design-sync command in Claude Code to pull design systems directly from local codebases into Claude Design so designers can work off of existing components. When it’s time to ship, designers can easily pass it on to Claude Code, maintaining a continuous line of work. 
Going the other way, developers can run the /design command to create, edit, and sync design projects directly in Claude Code, without leaving the terminal. 
When asked how the Claude Design upgrade could impact workflows, Roman Martynenko, a full-stack software engineer at Henry AI, tells The New Stack he’s a bit more optimistic about the Design-Code integration, saying he’d likely opt for terminal-based work but values the web interface for designers, project managers, and reviews:
“My ideal workflow is: design exploration in the web UI, then engineering-grade handoff in Claude Code with the actual repo context.”
Staying on brand is easier now
A main draw in the Claude Design update is that it “now sticks to your design system across projects,” per Anthropic. In other words, it makes brand consistency the default.
Users can import one or several design systems from a GitHub repo, design files, or raw uploads. This way, for every new project Claude Design creates, it automatically inherits brand assets (e.g., typography, color, spacing) and validates its outputs against those guidelines before revealing the final results.
For companies with strict branding rules, the new feature could make a real difference in maintaining consistency, something the April iteration struggled with, Nate Parrott, a designer at Anthropic, told Fast Company.
It’s likely a welcome control for design leads who want to rein in off-brand work. As Claude Design Admin, a user can set a standard design system and bar others from making edits.
The update also brings a new editor that allows for more fine-tuning with layout controls that let users “drag, resize, and align elements.”
No more separate usage limits
In April, The New Stack took Claude Design for a spin and quickly ran into token trouble. Just building a design system and a news website prototype (plus some tweaks and an explainer video) was enough to burn through over 50% of our weekly allotment.
Anthropic says it heard similar stories and listened.
The tool update ditches separate usage limits and brings Claude Design into a shared pool with Claude Code, chat, and Cowork. Should you exhaust your usage limits, Claude Design will be unavailable — until either your usage resets or you shell out for usage credits.
The shared pool may make it easier to manage token usage, but the jury’s still out on whether it makes a difference in burn rates.
Anthropic may be trying to put Claude Design everywhere, but it won’t change everything
By adding new connectors and deepening Design-Code integration, it seems Anthropic is intent on making Claude a bigger part of how people work. But while the June update is a decidedly more useful version of Claude Design, it won’t do everything.
Theoretically, connecting Claude Design to more tools designers and developers already use should reduce friction between teams, particularly when final implementations don’t match initial designs. As Martin points out, though, the designer-dev back-and-forth is still very much there, and token costs mean Claude-made isn’t always more efficient than human-made.
At the end of the day, speedier, on-brand designs and faster handoffs may encourage more experimentation, but “let[ting] Claude build the whole thing from start to finish,” as Anthropic suggests, isn’t the future, per Martin. Instead, she expects a hybrid model to emerge, where tools like Claude help with early concept validation, but humans still ultimately lead the charge.

title: Google wants to make the web agent-ready
text:
Google wants to make the web agent-ready
At its I/O developer conference on Tuesday, Google announced a number of new features and specs for how it plans to bring its Chrome browser and the web in general into this new era of agentic AI.
As Google developer advocate Paul Kinlan notes in the announcement, “agents are transforming development everywhere, and nowhere is that transformation happening faster than on the web. It’s redefining what we build, how we build, and who builds. As we enter the era of the agentic web, we see a shift that bridges the gap between complex developer workflows, underlying platform capabilities, and everyday user experiences.”
Google argues that the web needs to adapt to AI agents’ needs, making it easier for them to interact with websites, while the browser needs to become more of a proactive assistant for users. Developers, meanwhile, will look for tools that help them get the most out of the web platform, with AI assisting them as needed.
WebMCP in Chrome
At the core of how Google plans to give agents access to websites and the tools they provide is WebMCP, the emerging open standard for exposing JavaScript functions and HTML forms, for example, to agents.
“The whole point about WebMCP is that we want web experiences to be first-class citizens in agentic workflows, and WebMCP allows the web page to expose like individual functions and capabilities to those agents at this time,” Kinlan said in a press briefing ahead of the announcement.
Ideally, WebMCP allows agents to interact with a site, using the tools the website developer enabled for them. That’s much easier on the agent than trying to browse a site using screenshots or by traversing the DOM — and significantly faster, too.
Unsurprisingly, quite a few brands are interested in this as well, including Booking.com, Expedia, Instacart, Intuit, Shopify, and Redfin.
The plan is for Chrome to support WebMCP APIs soon. Google is starting with a WebMCP origin trial in Chrome 149, which is currently in beta.
Automated debugging in Chrome DevTools
For developers, Google is now letting them bring their agents to the Chrome DevTools. Agents can now access DevTool capabilities like console logs, network traffic, and accessibility trees directly. Gone are the days of you telling the agent what you saw in the console. They can now see what is happening directly and react accordingly.
This capability has been around for a little while, but Google now considers it a 1.0 release and ready for day-to-day usage. It’s available in Google’s own Antigravity app and for more than 20 coding agents. The tool uses either a built-in MCP server in Chrome or the Chrome DevTools CLI (because CLIs are sexy again now).
A blueprint for coding agents building web apps
As AI tools speed up coding, the web will also change at a faster clip than before. With the Web Platform Baseline, Google and other browser vendors have defined a set of core capabilities that any web developer can expect to find in modern browsers. Google is now taking this a step further with its new Modern Web Guidance.
Available in early preview, this is essentially a set of skills for AI coding agents to teach them about the capabilities of a given Baseline target.
“We want developers to be confident that their coding agents are using features that the majority of their users will be able to use,” says Kinlan. “In the cases where they might have some browser support matrices that are outside of the baseline requirements — maybe they’re a little bit ahead of it — we’ll also have fallback strategies for when a user has a browser that doesn’t support some of the capabilities that another browser does as well.”
For developers who want to know which Baseline target they should focus on, Google is making it easy to connect to the Google Analytics API to see which browsers their users are on and which modern web features they support.
A richer UI for the web
One major update Google is announcing at I/O is less about agents but is very much about next-gen feature: the HTML-in-Canvas API (combined with element-scoped view transitions. If your eyes glazed over reading that, you’re probably not alone, but as it turns out, this is all about eye candy.
The HTML-in-Canvas API will, as Google puts it, allow developers to “integrate real DOM elements directly into a canvas with WebGL and WebGPU to build an immersive 3D experience that is searchable, accessible, natively translatable, and interacts seamlessly with your built-in browser features.”
This is all about enabling rich graphical user interfaces that weren’t previously possible on the web. The <canvas> element has been around for quite a while and allows web developers to draw graphics on a page using JavaScript. But inside of a <canvas> element, the browser layout engine isn’t available, meaning there’s no text wrapping, focus management, <input> fields, or support for copy-paste, for example.
HTML-in-Canvas brings these two worlds together. Live DOM elements from the layout engine can now be rendered inside a <canvas> element and, most importantly, they can be manipulated in that <canvas> area like any other element on a web page.
As of now, HTML-in-Canvas is a proposed standard, and Firefox and Safari haven’t adopted it yet.
“It changes the way the web feels,” Kinlan explains. “It’s going to give us the ability to change individual elements and style them in ways that we’ve never been able to style them before, all the way up to new types of experiences where you have either rich 3D graphics or 3D experiences that combine both the web and HTML.”
It’s the kind of feature you need to see in a demo (see below). It will also likely drive many a crazy experiment in what new UIs could look like on the web — with the usual excesses that come with that. But come back in a year and many web apps will likely look a bit more like a modern mobile experience than a 2005 Web 2.0 app.

title: DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 vs. Claude Haiku 5.5: More accurate at a fraction of the price
text:
DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 vs. Claude Haiku 5.5: More accurate at a fraction of the price
DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash-1017 on October 17 as an update to its Flash model. Its change log says the update cuts task runtime and output length. It lists 11 benchmark scores, including 42.3 on Terminal-Bench 4.0.
Developers can use it through DeepSeek’s API or a service like OpenRouter. Because it’s an open-weight model, they can also download it from Hugging Face and run it on their own servers. I tested it through OpenRouter on DeepSeek’s own servers, at DeepSeek’s prices.
DeepSeek’s model card compares the update with several rivals, but not Haiku 5.5, so I picked it for this hands-on comparison. Anthropic launched Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7 as its fastest model at standard speed, aimed at high-volume tasks such as classification, summarization, and database queries.
Anthropic notes that its Opus models run faster in Fast Mode. Anthropic reports 39.2 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, 3.1 percentage points below DeepSeek’s reported score. These are vendor-reported results, rather than a controlled head-to-head test.
Haiku costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens for prompts up to 100,000 tokens, then $0.50 and $2.50 above that. DeepSeek’s off-peak rates are $0.15 per million uncached input tokens, $0.003 per million cached input tokens, and $0.60 per million output tokens; peak rates are twice those amounts.
Comparing uncached input and output rates, Haiku is cheaper on short prompts, and DeepSeek is cheaper on long ones. Actual charges also depend on tokenization, caching, and the provider route.
I built three tests around what each company says its model does well to see which one performs better in practice.
The tests
I ran both models once per test through OpenRouter, pinned to DeepSeek’s and Anthropic’s own servers, at default settings. I pinned DeepSeek to model ID 1017 and ran everything off-peak. A script graded every answer against keys I built and checked with a second method before either model saw them.
- Agentic bug fix: A Python job-queue library with three interacting bugs and one wrong test. The model reads, edits, and runs tests through tools, with a 25-turn cap.
- Database queries: A fake CI platform database with 20 questions, answered by writing SQL. Traps include soft deletes, mixed casing, retried builds, time zones, and currency conversion. Two questions can’t be answered from the data.
- Triage: 400 developer error reports, each needing a category, a severity, a service, and a team. That’s 1,600 scored fields. The prompt counted as 153,082 input tokens on DeepSeek and 216,811 on Haiku, past Haiku’s 100,000-token price threshold.
Agentic bug fix
DeepSeek started strong, beating Haiku’s accuracy on the first test. DeepSeek scored 6 of 6. Haiku scored 5 of 6. Both found the first bug even though the error pointed at the wrong file, fixed the third, broke no regression tests, and flagged the wrong test without touching it. Haiku missed one of six hidden tests on the second bug, and DeepSeek didn’t.
Haiku finished in eight turns and 21.6 seconds. DeepSeek took 12 turns and 49.6 seconds but still cost less because it automatically cached most of the repeated input. I didn’t turn on Anthropic’s prompt caching, which requires an opt-in. This compares the caching settings used in these runs; enabling Haiku’s caching could change the cost comparison.
The numbers:
- DeepSeek: 12 calls, 190,139 in, 7,877 out, $0.009, 49.6 s.
- Haiku: 8 calls, 100,461 in, 3,255 out, $0.012, 21.6 s.
Database queries
This is the only test where both models tied for accuracy, both scoring 20 out of 20. Both caught every trap and answered “unknown” to both questions the data couldn’t answer rather than hallucinating. Haiku got the answers in fewer calls and less time. DeepSeek cost about half as much.
The numbers:
- DeepSeek: 12 calls, 75,151 in, 4,608 out, $0.004, 34.9 s.
- Haiku 7 calls, 55,304 in, 5,917 out, $0.009, 28.4 s.
Triage
Here’s where the accuracy differences are clearest. DeepSeek got all 1,600 fields right. Haiku got 1,596. Two of its misses were severity ratings. The routing guide rates a report sev4 if it affects fewer than 50 users or has an error rate under 1%. Haiku rated a report with 49 affected customers as sev3, and another with a 0.8% error rate as sev3. Both should have been sev4.
Haiku’s other two misses were routing mistakes. The guide says one service moved to a new team on August 1 and that reports should be routed by the date in their header. Haiku sent two reports filed after August 1 to the old team. Each mentioned an earlier July date in its body, but the outputs alone don’t explain why Haiku chose the old team.
The same prompt was counted as 153,082 tokens on DeepSeek and 216,811 on Haiku. Because the models use different tokenizers, identical text can produce different token counts. That puts Haiku at a higher long-prompt rate. It costs $0.28, compared with DeepSeek’s $0.06.
The numbers:
- DeepSeek: 153,082 in, 58,923 out, $0.058, 188.3 s.
- Haiku 216,811 in, 69,354 out, $0.282, 228.9 s.
Results
| Test | DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 | Claude Haiku 5.5 | 
| Agentic bug fix | 6 of 6 | 5 of 6 | 
| Database queries | 20 of 20 | 20 of 20 | 
| Triage fields | 1,600 of 1,600 | 1,596 of 1,600 | 
| Total tokens in / out | 418,372 / 71,408 | 372,576 / 78,526 | 
| Total cost | $0.07 | $0.30 | 
| Total model time | 272.8 s | 278.9 s | 
DeepSeek and Haiku came out close on accuracy. DeepSeek edged ahead on the bug fix and the triage job, and they tied on the database queries. Speed was close too: Haiku was faster on the tool-based tests, and DeepSeek was faster on the big triage prompt. Cost was the real difference. DeepSeek came in at $0.07 to Haiku’s $0.30, and most of that gap came from the one long prompt that pushed Haiku onto its higher rate.
What do I think?
For these three runs, I’d pick DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017: it earned full marks on my scoring keys and cost less with the settings I used. Haiku was faster on both tool-based tests, while DeepSeek was faster on triage and slightly faster across the three runs combined. I ran each model only once per test, so these results don’t establish a general accuracy or speed advantage, or show how either model performs at scale. I’d test both on my own workload before making a production choice.

title: Gemini 4 Argon vs. Claude Opus 5.5: Half the price and about half as accurate
text:
Gemini 4 Argon vs. Claude Opus 5.5: Half the price and about half as accurate
When Google announced Gemini 4 Argon to a small group of testers on September 30, it came with a benchmark table that put Argon ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 on 14 of 18 tests. Those include DeepSWE (77.9% vs. 74.2%) and GraphWalks at 256K to 1 million tokens (84.2% vs. 66.8%). Two weeks later, on October 13, Google opened Argon to paid Gemini API developers.
To its credit, Google also showed where Opus 5.5 wins. Opus leads on the other four benchmarks, including Terminal-bench 4.0 (66.4% vs. 57.4%), which tests agentic work in a command line.
Google is also undercutting Anthropic on price, at least for now. Through November 30, Argon costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, half the price of Opus 5.5. On December 1, it rises to $4 and $20, matching Opus. That gives developers about six weeks to decide whether Argon is better or just cheaper.
That gives developers about six weeks to decide whether Argon is better or just cheaper.
Benchmarks don’t always match real work, and a half-price window only matters if the model matches the competitor on quality. To see whether Argon is better or just cheaper (for now), I tested both models head-to-head on three hard tasks from categories where Google claims a lead.
The tests
I ran each test once per model through OpenRouter, on Google’s and Anthropic’s own servers, at default reasoning settings. A script graded every answer against keys I built and verified before testing either model. The answer key adds more scoring areas to help ensure the quality and thoroughness of each test.
- Bug hunt – A 3,500-line Python library with 14 planted logic bugs and five decoys. Each model reviewed the code, then fixed what it found.
- Billing spec – A spec for a subscription billing engine, graded by 80 hidden tests on daylight saving, month-end dates, and rounding. A follow-up added two currencies and 20 more tests.
- Long context – A fake wiki of 400 services with scattered dependencies, at three sizes. Each model answered three graph questions with planted traps.
Bug hunt
This one was a tie. Both models found all 14 bugs, including four that only show up when you follow a value across three or more files. Neither flagged a decoy. In the follow-up, both fixed all 14 bugs without breaking any of the 93 existing tests.
Argon was cheaper. Its review cost averaged 1 cent per bug found, compared to Opus’s 2.4 cents, an average I calculated from the per-call total rather than measured per bug. Argon would still come out cheaper at its full Dec. 1 price, because it used fewer tokens.
- The numbers:
  - Review
    - Argon 53,031 in, 3,964 out, $0.15, 43.0 s.
    - Opus 64,572 in, 4,053 out, $0.34, 38.9 s.
  - Fix
    - Argon 54,923 in, 24,292 out, $0.35, 186.6 s.
    - Opus 66,465 in, 34,263 out, $0.95, 219.8 s.
Billing specs
Here’s where accuracy began to differ between the two models. Opus passed all 80 hidden tests, then all 100 after the currency follow-up. Argon passed 11 of 80, then 20 of 100.
Argon didn’t fail the majority of the tests because its logic was bad. It failed because it made a small mistake early on. Its code passed an extra argument to Python’s `datetime.combine()`, which raises an error, and most of the module depends on that helper. When I corrected that one line myself, Argon scored 80/80 and 100/100. I kept the official scores as graded but wanted to explain what happened, not just list the scores, on this one.
Overall, Argon was cheaper, but the difference between Opus and Argon pricing will disappear once the lower-cost period ends, though Argon’s lower token use would still make it cheaper on this test.
- The numbers:
  - Build
    - Argon 3,907 in, 3,727 out, $0.05, 54.1 s.
    - Opus 5,236 in, 7,763 out, $0.18, 63.0 s.
  - Follow-up
    - Argon 8,881 in, 4,673 out, $0.06, 41.5 s.
    - Opus 11,807 in, 7,267 out, $0.19, 51.9 s.
Long context
Each vendor counts tokens differently. My 500K document came to 549,483 tokens on Argon and 784,087 on Opus. My 900K document came to 1.4 million tokens on Claude’s tokenizer, so Anthropic’s API rejected it. I added a third document of about 600K tokens, the largest that both models could fit.
Both models answered two of the three questions perfectly at every size they ran. The split came on the blast radius question, which asks for every service that goes down when one fails. The answer is 33 services.
Opus got all 33 at 500K and 32 at 600K, with no wrong entries. At 500K, Argon got 20 right and 8 wrong; at 600K, 19 right and 16 wrong; and at 900K, 23 right and 2 wrong. At 600K and 900K, it treated a dependency as removed after the wiki reinstated it. Unlike the billing bug, this wasn’t a small slip. Argon got the reasoning wrong at every size. This is a big red flag.
Unlike the billing bug, this wasn’t a small slip. Argon got the reasoning wrong across the entire answer. This is a big red flag.
Another thing I noticed is that Argon raced through this long-context test. Argon answered quickly without showing any step-by-step work, and Opus took longer because it reasoned first. This shows up in token usage. Opus used over 5,000 tokens, most for reasoning, vs. Argon’s 243-425. That likely connects to Argon’s wrong answers, though I can’t prove the cause from one run.
Argon was cheaper here, but it’s not worth using it on a similar task, as it was largely inaccurate and sloppy.
- The numbers:
  - 500k
    - Argon 549,483 in, 264 out, $1.10, 24.2 s.
    - Opus 784,087 in, 5,532 out, $3.25, 68.3 s.
  - 600k
    - Argon 652,492 in, 425 out, $1.31, 32.4 s.
    - Opus 935,332 in, 5,158 out, $3.84, 69.1 s.
  - 900K
    - Argon 982,367 in, 243 out, $1.97, 41.5 s.
    - Opus not run.
Results
| Test | Gemini 4 Argon | Claude Opus 5.5 | 
| Bug hunt review | 14 of 14, 0 false positives | 14 of 14, 0 false positives | 
| Bug hunt fix | 14 of 14, 93 of 93 tests kept | 14 of 14, 93 of 93 tests kept | 
| Billing spec | 11 of 80 | 80 of 80 | 
| Billing follow-up | 20 of 100 | 100 of 100 | 
| Blast radius, 500K | 20 of 33, 8 wrong | 33 of 33 | 
| Blast radius, 600K | 19 of 33, 16 wrong | 32 of 33 | 
| Blast radius, 900K | 23 of 33, 2 wrong | Rejected, over 1M tokens | 
| Total tokens in / out | 2,305,084 / 37,588 | 1,867,499 / 64,036 | 
| Total cost | $4.98 | $8.75 | 
| Total time | 423.3 s | 511.0 s | 
My results didn’t match Google’s benchmarks. Argon tied Opus on code review and fixing at under half the cost. It lost the spec test over one bad line of code, and it missed or invented services on every long-context blast-radius question.
What do I think?
Based on these tests, I wouldn’t use Argon. Yes, it was cheaper and as accurate as Opus on the bug hunt, but after working with it on the other tests, I wouldn’t unquestioningly trust Argon on any task.
I wouldn’t unquestioningly trust Argon on any task.
Opus 5.5 is one of Anthropic’s leading models, and Artificial Analysis’s independent index ranks it at 58, ahead of Argon’s 53.
While Google is working hard to catch up, it hasn’t yet.

title: Muse Wonder vs. Claude Fable 5.1: Meta’s new model came closer than I expected
text:
Muse Wonder vs. Claude Fable 5.1: Meta’s new model came closer than I expected
Meta launched Muse Wonder on October 12, about three months after Muse Spark 1.1 opened Meta’s paid Model API. Meta says the Muse Wonder series is strong at personal and professional agent tasks, tops its internal MemoryBench memory test, and, in the Full version, leads coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE and SWE-Marathon.
Its model card lists Fable 5.1 among the comparison models, and Meta’s launch post publishes Fable 5.1 scores alongside its own. Those are strong claims, since Fable 5.1 is one of Anthropic’s top models.
Muse Wonder comes in two versions. The standard model is available through the Model API and Muse Code, Meta’s coding agent. A higher-capability version, Muse Wonder Full, is only available inside Muse Code on its top subscription plans.
Muse Wonder is available on Meta’s Model API at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.1 in September; it costs $10 and $50 and is available through the API and Claude’s paid plans. That makes Muse Wonder 60% cheaper per token. Cached input narrows the gap: Meta charges $0.20 per million cached input tokens, against $0.25 for Fable 5.1. If it really performs at Fable’s level, that’s a big saving for teams running agents all day.
If Muse really performs at Fable’s level, that’s a big saving for teams running agents all day.
I tested the standard Muse Wonder against Fable 5.1 head-to-head on three hard agentic and memory tasks to see whether it matches Meta’s claims.
The tests
I ran Muse Wonder through OpenRouter, served by Meta, and Fable 5.1 through Anthropic’s API. Each model ran once per test at its default reasoning setting. Meta’s published comparisons used maximum reasoning effort. A script graded every answer against keys I built and verified before either model saw them. I ran each test once, so results could vary on another run.
- Agentic bug fix – A 27-module Python job-queue library with three interacting bugs and one test that is itself wrong. Each model used tools to read, search, edit, and run tests, with a cap of 25 turns.
- Incident investigation – Logs, metrics, deploy history, and config history for 20 fake services during a cascading outage – The root cause is a config change, hidden behind two decoy deploys and a server whose clock runs 263 seconds slow.
- Long-session memory – A scripted 50-turn chat about a webhook relay service, with 25 project rules, eight of them changed later and three only implied. At the end, each model wrote the config and code, then took an eight-question recall quiz.
Agentic bug fix
Both models traced the first bug to the right file, even though the error message pointed somewhere else. Both fixed the third bug, broke none of 22 regression tests, left the wrong test alone, and explained why it was wrong.
The difference was the second bug. Fable passed all six hidden tests. Muse passed five, because its fix still sent the old attempt count to the job’s failure event.
On price, Muse used about twice as many input tokens, so it cost about twice as much despite the lower price. Both models’ costs include prompt caching discounts.
The final numbers:
- Muse 15 turns, 269,615 in, 4,627 out, $0.75, 55.9 s.
- Fable 14 turns, 138,213 in, 3,132 out, $0.39, 68.5 s.
Incident investigation
Both models scored 10 of 10. Each named config change CFG-4470 as the root cause, ruled out both decoy deploys, caught the slow clock on the checkout service, and listed all nine affected services in the right order.
…Muse cost more because of high token usage, despite the lower cost.
Fable got there in six turns. Muse took 13 and read more data along the way, though it spent less total time waiting on the model. Again, Muse cost more because of high token usage, despite the lower cost.
The final numbers:
- Muse: 13 turns, 327,587 in, 8,811 out, $1.03, 69.1 s.
- Fable 6 turns, 108,128 in, 8,593 out, $0.89, 88.3 s.
Long-session memory
Test three created the biggest difference in model performance. Muse scored 25 of 25 on the final deliverable. It used the latest value for all eight changed rules and got all three implied ones, including writing code that runs on Python 3.8 because the client’s servers do. It also scored 8 of 8 on the quiz and answered “unknown” to all three questions the chat never covered.
Fable scored zero on this test. On turn 5, Anthropic’s API returned a refusal with the category “cyber.” That turn asked the model to read the relay’s target URL from an environment variable. Fable refused 34 of the 50 turns, including the final deliverable and the quiz. The project was an ordinary webhook relay and had nothing to do with cyber security. This was made extra interesting because Anthropic says Claude Code users should see about 60% fewer cyber safeguard interventions per session with Fable 5.1 than with Fable 5. Fable 5 never skipped my testing work for this reason.
I followed Anthropic’s guidance and discarded refused output while keeping my own messages in the chat, so Fable still had every rule. An earlier attempt that kept the refused turns in the history drew 45 refusals, so I reran it. Anthropic suggests setting up a fallback to another Claude model for refused requests. I didn’t, because that would test a different model. Anthropic’s own Fable 5.1 benchmarks handed cyber-flagged tasks to Claude Opus 4.8.
Because Fable refused the work, this test says little about its long-session memory. It does show how each model treats everyday backend code that a cyber filter can mistake for security work. Muse finished the job and scored 25 of 25.
Muse’s numbers:
- 50 turns, 93,977 in, 9,848 out, $0.46, 143.2 s.
Results
| Test | Muse Wonder | Claude Fable 5.1 | 
| Agentic bug fix | 5 of 6 | 6 of 6 | 
| Incident investigation | 10 of 10 | 10 of 10 | 
| Memory deliverable | 25 of 25 | 0 of 25, refused | 
| Memory quiz | 8 of 8 | 0 of 8, refused | 
| Turns | 78 | 70 | 
| Total tokens in / out | 691,179 / 23,286 | 365,528 / 16,456 | 
| Total cost | $2.24 | $1.85 | 
| Total model time | 268.2 s | 256.8 s | 
On agentic work, Muse Wonder performed at Fable 5.1’s level, though Meta’s own benchmark table shows the standard model trailing Fable 5.1 on some agent tests, including OSWorld. It matched Fable on the incident and came within one hidden test on the bug fix.
It did not save money in my tests, though. Muse used more tokens per task, and its total came to $2.25 against Fable’s $1.85. Fable’s total includes $0.57 and 119,187 input tokens from the memory session it refused; on the two tests both models finished, Muse cost $1.78 to Fable’s $1.28.
Fable’s cyber safeguards blocked a routine backend project that Muse completed
In the memory test, Fable’s cyber safeguards blocked a routine backend project that Muse completed, so developers using Fable on similar code may see requests stopped partway through.
What do I think
Muse Wonder came much closer to Fable 5.1’s performance than I expected. That said, for agentic debugging and investigation, I’d still pick Fable 5.1. It was slightly more accurate, used fewer turns, and cost less overall in my tests.
Muse Wonder is an alternative when Fable’s cyber safeguards block work from happening. I just can’t confirm if the rate is reasonable compared to other models since I don’t have any data to compare Meta’s price with.

title: “Developers are paying frontier prices for amnesia”: Uvi wants to stop the agent relearning brain drain
text:
“Developers are paying frontier prices for amnesia”: Uvi wants to stop the agent relearning brain drain
Every time an AI agent has to trawl Slack threads, Jira tickets and old pull requests to piece together something a company already knows, the customer pays for that work again. Uvi, an Israeli startup that emerged from stealth on Wednesday with $7.5 million in seed funding from investors including CT Innovations, Cardumen, Mana VC and 91 Ventures, says this repeated context-gathering is quietly inflating the cost of running agents on frontier models.
The firm says in-house agents built on frontier models, connected directly to six company systems, cost roughly eight times more than they needed in internal testing, mostly because of repeated context gathering rather than actual reasoning.
Developers are paying for amnesia
Uvi co-founder and CEO Gilad Salinger tells The New Stack that models are rented, but context is owned.
“Developers are paying frontier prices for amnesia,” Salinger says. “Every quarter there’s a new model that is faster and cheaper, and every quarter the company’s memory of why it built things the way it did stays exactly where it was: in people’s heads, in old tickets, in Slack threads nobody will read again.”
He explains that Uvi takes that memory out of people and tools and puts it in one place every agent, on every model, can read. If developers need to swap the model tomorrow, they don’t have to relearn anything. Salinger insists that Uvi makes sure that memory information is actually usable.
“Context is unique to every company and demands a deep understanding of how that company defines its work, from what counts as a feature to how two departments communicate.”
Working through “both sides” of agent testing
In terms of core mechanics, Uvi champions a semantic layer, a knowledge graph, and a reasoning layer that sits on top of relevant, permissioned, tightly synchronized live data. The Uvi team tested its platform against more than 900 real employee questions, according to the company, using the same frontier model on “both sides” of the test. The tests are internal and not independently verified.
“Both sides” means two different ways of building an AI agent, using the same frontier model to answer the same questions.
“On one side, we had an agent connected directly to six enterprise systems, including Slack, Jira, and GitHub. Every time someone asked a question, it had to dig through those systems, piece the information together, and figure out how it all connected before it could answer. That took 15 to 35 round trips per question,” clarifies Salinger.
On the other side, he explains that his team used an agent with Uvi, so it used the same model and asked the same questions with the same company information.
“Uvi had already connected the dots between the company’s decisions, conversations, code and processes, so the agent got its context in one step,” Salinger says. “The first agent was doing detective work every time someone asked a question. The second already had the case file. And here’s the ridiculous part: The first approach cost roughly eight times more and took more than twice as long. We weren’t comparing a stupid model against a smart one. We were comparing the same brain with and without an understanding of the business it was supposed to work for.”
How much more expensive is 8x, exactly?
Built the way most enterprises are building today, Uvi claims an answer costs $0.75 to $1.41 and can exceed $2.00. Built on Uvi, the same answer costs $0.10 to $0.16. On open-ended questions where agents got stuck in search loops, Uvi claims to be up to 46 times cheaper.
If Uvi’s claimed results hold water, Salinger thinks the real shame isn’t cost; it’s the lost opportunity to stay at the vanguard of business.
“The real worst case is not waste. It is losing the race,” he says. “Enterprises today compete with other players who can flip an entire market overnight. A software-centric company’s only lasting advantage over AI labs is the information nobody else has. So if it cannot turn that into something agents use quickly, safely, and precisely, the advantage is theoretical. We are at the point where companies understand the cost and energy it takes to build that environment themselves and stay competitive. That is the moment this category exists for.”
Developers floundering in tokenmaxxing context blindness
All of this raises the question: is the AI industry missing a trick, or is there widespread awareness of a predicament that leaves some developers floundering in tokenmaxxing context blindness?
“They [the frontier model companies] know. You do not set up consulting arms for large enterprises unless you understand that context is the whole game,” Salinger says. “Look at the shape of their business: a huge market to serve seamlessly at scale. Context is the opposite. It is unique to every company and demands a deep understanding of how that company defines its work, from what counts as a feature to how two departments communicate. That does not scale the way a model does.”
Salinger explains that Uvi’s approach does two things at once: it works to understand the information and the connections between pieces. This means (for example) that a question about a billing exception pulls the decision, the people, and the dependencies, not every document that mentions billing. Uvi understands each organization and its specific way of working, so the same question gets answered differently inside two different companies.
“The first agent was doing detective work every time someone asked a question. The second already had the case file.”
That combination is what lets this platform hand the agent the “smallest correct slice”, at the speed, security, and precision an enterprise expects. Of course, diminishing returns exist at this level, Salinger agrees, so he notes that Uvi’s job is to find the point of enough, per question, per company.
Additional Uvi integrations are in development
Most of what a company knows was never captured in a single document. A decision may begin in a Slack thread, become a Jira ticket, change in a pull request, and end up behind a feature flag, with no individual system holding the full story. Uvi maps how those pieces connect and reconstructs what was decided, why, what changed, and what happened next.
It then makes that context available to whatever models and agents the company chooses to run. Without that history, an AI agent can confidently recommend the same migration a company rejected three years ago for the same reasons.
“The real worst case is not waste. It is losing the race”
Uvi says that its software runs in production at Lemonade and monday.com, both public companies, and at Melio, now part of Xero. It connects to Slack, codebases, coding sessions, meeting notes, Jira, and Confluence, with additional integrations in development.

title: Scripted tests can't keep up with AI-written code. Datadog is betting agents can.
text:
Scripted tests can’t keep up with AI-written code. Datadog is betting agents can.
Nearly a year into the agentic coding explosion, many teams now use AI to write software as their de facto approach. As a result, Anthropic’s engineers are shipping eight times as much code as before, and some engineers are shipping thousands of PRs per month.
Management teams expecting their engineering capacity to explode will find that AI-written code doesn’t necessarily compress the software development lifecycle (SDLC) on its own.
The critical bottleneck in software creation has shifted from writing code to a later SDLC stage. After coding agents spit out new code, it still needs testing, and traditionally that meant humans writing the tests. That work includes deciding which user flows need testing, scripting tests for them, and rejiggering them when those flows change.
We’ve made it easy to write code and, in the process, increased the burden on humans to test new code. If we want to slash software development timelines, something has to change.
The observability and monitoring giant Datadog bought Propolis earlier this year, adding agent-written, goal- and output-oriented test writing to its platform. The approach lets agents explore applications, follow user flows on their own, and generate tests from plain-language prompts.
Add Datadog’s observability heft, and you get a system that can test code while providing the logs and traces it needs to vet system performance without the fragility hardcoded testing brings.
You have successfully registered for the webinar.
The New Stack will sit down with Ruxanda Lueck and Matthew White of Datadog on Wednesday, November 4, at 9 a.m. Pacific / 12 p.m. Eastern.
Lueck is a group product manager working on goal-based testing of AI features. White co-founded and served as CTO of Propolis. These are precisely the people to help us understand the current state of the art and what comes next.
We’ll ask how much test-writing teams can offload today and whether agentic testing has reached its own Claude Code moment. We’ll also ask whether plain-language testing instructions expand the number of staffers who can help test new code, and how long it will be before agents can read agent-written code and handle testing without humans lifting a finger.
Agent-written code has created tensions across the SDLC that no single tool can settle on its own. If testing can speed up code writing, though, teams clear one more obstacle between an idea and working software in production.
You’ll learn:
- How agents can test user flows that no one thought of
- How to write plain-language testing prompts
- How goal-based testing persists even when user flows change
- How to test AI features that return probabilistic, instead of deterministic, outputs
- Where scripted tests still have their place

title: How to review AI code without reading the code
text:
How to review AI code without reading the code
The argument over whether engineers should stop reading code is over, because we already have.
Faros AI’s new report shows a 76.3% increase in pull requests merged without review since their last report in April. Many companies now run AI reviews on 50% to 80% of their PRs. AI review took over bug-finding. But it didn’t take over the conversation where a team debates what it decided and why, and that is the part I missed too.
The part AI review doesn’t solve
Most teams are stuck in one of two modes. They review every line and become the bottleneck, or they rubber-stamp and lose track of what changed and why. There is no middle ground yet.
“The argument over whether engineers should stop reading code is over, because we already have.”
AI review is good at the mechanical half of the job. It never gets tired, it reads every line, and it holds the same standard on every PR. But it never saw what was decided. It won’t tell you not to build something, and it can’t be accountable for the result. A better model won’t fix that, because the tool reads the wrong artifact at the wrong time.
As I wrote in “Kill the code review theater, keep the review,” code review is how a team builds a mental model of its system. That has been the only scheduled moment for engineers to talk to each other about that system. Teams that hand code reviews to AI tools rarely notice they’ve also given up that moment.
I didn’t notice either. The five layers of trust I proposed in March for replacing code review all checked the code. Four asked, “Is it right?” One asked, “Is that what we meant?” None asked, “Are we building the right thing?”
Debating decisions replaces reading the code
A decision is any point where the change could have gone another way: a token bucket or a sliding window, fail open or fail closed, one limit for every customer or one each. An AI-written PR is full of them, and almost none of them show up in the diff.
My new framework for the review bottleneck also has five layers.
- Challenge. Before the PR exists, a second agent on a different model pushes back on the coding agent’s approach. The output records what was proposed, what was rejected and why, and which agent gave ground. Settled points stay on the record too, because two agents can also agree to look the other way.
- Capture. The intent (why we’re making the change) and the acceptance criteria (how it should behave) get captured from coding with the agent and go onto the PR. You need both: intent without criteria can’t be checked, and criteria without intent can’t be judged.
- Codify. Review comments your team keeps repeating, like “use the Money type, not float,” go into an AI slop registry, and become invariants, standing rules checked on every change.
- Debate. People discuss the decisions the agents surfaced and couldn’t settle, and leave the line-by-line checking to the machines. It’s the only layer that asks whether we’re building the right thing.
- Own. A model has no reputation and can’t be asked why, so a named team owns the invariants and the mental model behind them, and signs off on the change.
The first three are work for machines, and tools for them exist today. Debate and Own are work for people, and Debate is the layer that was missing.
“The principle we designed around is simple: agents verify, people decide.”
The principle we designed around is simple: agents verify, people decide. People are better at judging whether a change is right, weighing trade-offs and risks, and owning the decision. Invariants are rules for agents. Decisions are judgment calls for people, and the calls that keep coming back become rules.
Debate also ends the argument over whether engineers should read AI-generated code.
I recently spoke to Robert ‘Uncle Bob’ Martin, the author of “Clean Code,” who recently said that he doesn’t read the code anymore. But he did say that humans should take responsibility for the systems, just above the code. Decisions sit at that level.
A reviewer who has debated the decisions doesn’t have to read code line by line to explain a change.
Should we just review specs?
The obvious objection is that this just moves the reading somewhere else, and at some point that place was specs. My issue with reviewing specs is that it seems backward. A spec takes time to write, gets written before the work teaches you anything, and drifts the moment implementation starts.
Decisions come out of the work itself. They are generated live, they are short, and each one exists because the change could have gone another way. That is also why Capture pulls the intent and acceptance criteria out of the coding session after the work, instead of asking anyone to write them up front.
How I see decision review working
Here is how I see it working, based on what we’ve been building at Aviator.
Where decisions come from
Most decisions already happen on the author’s machine, and today we throw them away.
- A capture skill pulls intent, acceptance criteria, and decisions out of the coding agent session. Every time the agent stops to ask and the engineer makes a call, it records that call.
- A review skill runs an adversarial review agent that argues with the coding agent before the PR is submitted. It records what they disagreed about and how they settled it. What they couldn’t settle is what the team debates.
What a decision looks like
This example uses a PR that adds a per-installation rate limit to webhook ingest.
The intent is one sentence: throttle webhook bursts per GitHub installation so one noisy customer can’t starve the broker, without dropping events or breaking their order.
The PR carries six decisions. The one still open is a product call, not a code one: the burst limit is one value for every customer. Two are accepted risks: a Redis outage fails open, and deferred events hold their payload in the broker. Exposing limiter metrics on the on-prem Grafana board became a follow-up with a linked ticket. The other two were argued out between the author, the reviewer, and the agents and settled.
Take one of the settled ones, “token bucket, not a sliding window.” The author’s agent explains it in the thread: one Lua call per event instead of a sorted-set scan, chosen after profiling a replay of a webhook storm. A reviewer who disagrees can push back in the same thread or ask the agent directly.
None of that is visible in the diff.
What the reviewer does
The reviewer’s part comes down to three steps:
- Read the intent and what’s changing.
- Go through the decisions and argue where you disagree.
- Check what isn’t passing, then approve.
