That is enough to understand the change, build a mental model, and argue about what matters, without reading line by line.
Each decision is its own thread, with humans and agents labeled separately, so you know who made which call. A reviewer can agree, challenge, override, or turn a decision into a tracked follow-up. The code is still there. You open it where a decision sends you, and comments on the code join the same record.
What happens after the merge
The decisions outlive the review.
- Your team’s week. You see the key decisions made in your part of the codebase over the last day or week, without reading the PRs. That is what knowledge-sharing code review was always for.
- Memory for agents. Coding and review agents pull past decisions for the code they touch, so they don’t re-argue settled trade-offs.
- Follow-ups that stick. “Do it later” becomes a linked ticket, not a line in a PR description nobody reads again.
- Rules from patterns. When a decision keeps recurring, propose it as an invariant; it becomes a rule only after someone approves it.
Someone still has to sign. A model has no reputation and can’t be asked why, so every debated decision ends with a named person who agreed to it. That is where Debate hands off to the last layer, Own.
“If AI already reviews most of your PRs, try one question on your team: what did we decide last week, and who agreed to it?”
If AI already reviews most of your PRs, try one question on your team: what did we decide last week, and who agreed to it?

title: AI’s Midas problem: When code is free, features are worthless
text:
AI’s Midas problem: When code is free, features are worthless
Every team that adopted Claude Code, Cursor, or Copilot to produce more code has the same problem: When output is free, offering volume stops being a viable strategy. In fact, teams accelerating their software development with AI may be giving up the very thing that makes their software valuable.
It’s time to remember what makes software valuable and why racing to produce a mountain of code and features leads to failure.
The Midas touch
In Ovid’s tale, Midas, king of Phrygia, took in the missing satyr Silenus, whom Phrygian peasants had found drunk, granted him ten days of hospitality, and then returned him to Dionysus. In return, he was offered the reward of his choice: whatever he wished for. Famously, he wished that everything he touched would turn to gold.
Testing his new ability on an oak twig and then a stone, Midas was delighted. Nathaniel Hawthorne, who retold the myth for children in 1851, added a rose garden: His Midas turns every bloom to gold, still delighted, though his daughter Marygold mourns that the roses no longer smell sweet. In both versions, the celebration ends at the table, where food and drink turn to gold in his hands. That’s when Midas realized his reward was a bane, not a blessing, and asked to be rid of it.
Many leaders who force-fed AI to developers are now coming to a realization similar to that of Midas.
Though the process is gradual, many organizations and leaders who force-fed AI to developers are now reaching a similar conclusion. Reports show organizations slashing budgets and limiting tool use.
With Microsoft and Meta reportedly cutting internal spending on Anthropic’s Claude, and Uber and Accenture capping what employees can spend on AI tools, it’s time to acknowledge that the return on investment might not be there — McKinsey’s own 2026 research found record AI spending hasn’t moved earnings for 94% of enterprises — and it’s easy to see why.
The economics of plenty
If Midas had depended on the value of gold, perhaps hoping to trade the gold he created to fund his lavish lifestyle of hosting ten-day-long parties, he would have quickly learned that his gold was no longer valuable. His touch would cause hyperinflation, and gold’s price would plummet. His skill would be as useful as turning everything you touch to ash.
In the modern, non-mythical world, everything you touch with AI becomes a commodity. If you can get Claude or ChatGPT to create something for you, then everyone else can. They have access to the same tools. Whether you’re building software or writing a book, when you use AI, its perceived value is little more than the cost of the tokens you used.
When coding looked like magic to most people, basic coding competence was sufficient value. You could build a career translating human-language requirements into code. This value rolled up to the team, department, and organization level, with code magicians performing their arcane translations in return for money, whether the software was internal, built for a customer, or sold as a product.
If your software expresses user requirements translated into code, it’s now worthless.
If your software expresses user requirements translated into code, it’s now worthless. We know that a page that adds nothing beyond the AI summary is worthless, and software built by translating a user’s wants into code is the same.
How to avoid incinerating your software’s value
There is hope for us, though. When Midas asked to be rid of his power, he had to wash in the Pactolus River. Our touch isn’t directly connected to the generation machine, so it won’t inevitably turn our work to ash.
The answer is conceptually simple, though it takes a lot of effort in practice, which seems to be exactly what people want to avoid. Nevertheless, for your work to be immune to AI’s mortally ruinous touch, you need to provide something beyond what someone could achieve with their own Claude subscription.
For your work to be immune to AI’s mortally ruinous touch, you need to provide something beyond what someone could achieve with their own Claude subscription.
That means moving away from the feature-factory model of software development, where the value is primarily in the translation of “human wants” into code. Instead, teams building software must develop a deeper understanding of the jobs users do and the challenges they face, so they can generate novel ideas and commercial insights users wouldn’t reach on their own.
This second mode of building means you may deliver something completely different from what users ask for, yet one that gracefully solves many of the challenges they face in their work. Combining deep business domain knowledge with an understanding of abstract, reusable solutions lets you deliver something exceptional.
DORA’s State of DevOps research has highlighted this need for user-centricity. That doesn’t mean doing whatever users ask; it means understanding their work and challenges so you can provide software they value. DORA’s 2024 report says this approach improves product performance, regardless of delivery speed.
We are living through a time of excess code, sentences, and images. The path forward isn’t more; it’s better.

title: Edge-forward: Akamai eyes sweet spot between centralized & decentralized AI inference
text:
Edge-forward: Akamai eyes sweet spot between centralized & decentralized AI inference
For this edition of The New Stack Makers, we sit down with two leaders at Akamai: Lena Hall, senior director, developers & AI engineering, and Thorsten Hans, senior developer advocate
Keen to understand what’s going on in the cloud-native AI universe and where Akamai fits into that story, this discussion took place at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon Europe 2026 in Amsterdam.
We know Akamai as a Content Delivery Network (CDN) business with a focus on cybersecurity and software application development technologies. The Akamai of today is also a modern, developer-friendly cloud infrastructure business ready to deliver for the age of AI in every location.
But what shape does that business model take in real-world terms?
“There are so many use cases that benefit from really low latency distributed processing, and Akamai has always been known for our services around distributed computing. So this is why we have developed managed container services for Kubernetes; this technology works fluidly with our low-latency serverless functions and our distributed AI inference platform,” says Hall.
Bringing compute closer
In our discussion, Hall and Hans explain how the company achieves its proximity play. With 41 core datacenters in 36 countries, Akamai extends its reach through around 4,400 smaller “distributed reach” datacenters worldwide.
“The intention is to bring compute closer to wherever the user is around the planet in order to reduce latency,” Hall says. “But it’s important to remember that there are so many different types of workloads that users like to run. There are those that require really deep thinking and a lot of computing, so this is where centralized data centers do a great job. But when you combine those stacks with distributed edge capabilities, you can deliver faster feedback loops when required.”
Those faster feedback loops are critical in areas such as robotics, fraud detection, or in conversational agents, where a delay can lead to customer loss very quickly. Bringing both centralized and decentralized edge resources together is clearly the sweet spot that Akamai is aiming for.
Brittle integration points?
But let’s question this theory for a second. In taking this approach, is Akamai not building its own integration and configuration nightmare? With a whole string of dependencies and integration points, doesn’t that create an inherently more brittle compute and data stack for AI to rest upon?
“Doing this correctly is precisely the infrastructure service layer that Akamai is capable of providing,” says Hall. “We’re used to delivering this for really large corporations in a managed way with a simplified setup. Users can then move forward to develop new services without having to manage the infrastructure element of the equation and leverage the tools we have.”
Enthusiastic advocates of self-service systems, Hall and Hans describe a computing landscape where users have all the toolkits and services they need to spin up an ecosystem and deploy at will, often with a single command.
Equally positive about the need to underpin open-source support, the Akamai pair again points to the company’s managed Kubernetes service. Akamai also has its own application platform project that runs on top of Linode Kubernetes Engine (LKE) to package a selection of frequently used open source projects. This means users can access these tools through Akamai’s interface without manually installing each piece of software.
Serverless suitability
Regarding who uses Akamai’s platform within any given software engineering team, developer advocate Hans says that his firm’s serverless technologies, such as Akamai Functions, are especially accessible to developers at all levels. This part of the company’s platform is designed to help developers build, deploy and scale applications and AI workloads using WebAssembly functions across Akamai’s distributed cloud without the burden of managing infrastructure.
“We put developers at the center, always. Akamai worked with the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) to create the sandbox project known as Spin. This is a framework for building and deploying serverless applications in WebAssembly. This leads us towards NoOps, so a developer can go from a blinking cursor to a live production-deployed application that is globally distributed on top of the Akamai cloud in around two minutes, all built on different layers of popular open source projects,” says Hans.
Akamai’s work with Spin stems from its December 2025 acquisition of cloud-native Wasm Function-as-a-Service company Fermyon. So-named to embody its mission to bring cold start times down to under 1 millisecond, the Spin team also created SpinKube in 2024 to serve as a Kubernetes runtime. Hans has been responsible for the increased use of Wasm within Akamai, as the team has pledged to make it easier for developers to execute lightweight code at the edge.
Focus on the logic, not the logistics
Promising to always “meet developers where they are” in terms of individual skills, Hans says that Akamai has provided guidance via tutorials, hands-on labs, and ready-to-use applications. In practice, it’s all about telling developers that they shouldn’t spend time worrying about server provisioning and management; they should be able to see what’s inside the box (of any given Akamai service) and think about how they can apply that to their environment’s requirements.
Hall and Hans say they appreciate that there will always be software engineering teams that need to work with the internal infrastructure they run on. But for the majority of its customer base today, Akamai provides a way to work with a higher level of abstraction. This means engineers don’t have to worry about the server underneath; all they need to focus on is the business processes they aim to encapsulate in application logic and the functionality their users need.

title: WebAssembly is now outperforming containers at the edge
text:
WebAssembly is now outperforming containers at the edge
The mass adoption of WebAssembly has yet to be realized.
The true turning point for WebAssembly — specifically its ability to ship lightweight code to any number of endpoints with millisecond latency — rests on finalizing the component model.
“The true turning point for WebAssembly — specifically its ability to ship lightweight code to any number of endpoints with millisecond latency — rests on finalizing the component model.”
Standardizing the component model will allow WebAssembly to replace containers in areas where they typically struggle, regardless of whether Kubernetes is involved. Wasm is better suited for edge devices, serverless environments, and event-driven deployments that require pushing updates to an unlimited number of endpoints simultaneously.
Indeed, WebAssembly has moved far beyond the browser. It shows its maturity via reliable production use across servers, CDNs, and backend services, as well as its broad applicability.
While core WebAssembly is intentionally low-level and difficult to use directly, recent specification work enables higher-level abstractions. Reference types and interface types allow components to expose meaningful APIs without developers needing to understand WASM internals, making the technology more accessible to engineers.
During this talk, “Towards a Component Model 1.0” at Wasm I/O in Barcelona last week, Luke Wagner of Fastly described efforts to make the so-called Component Model easier to adopt, including motivating native browser implementations and closing a few remaining functionality gaps.
“Achieving a ‘just works’ developer experience requires standards-based answers to coordinated problems… such as how a standard library performs IO or how multiple modules are bundled and linked at runtime.”
While technical improvements like debugging and threading are important, the “higher order bit” for explosive Wasm adoption is a lack of upstream support in popular languages and frameworks, Wagner said.
Achieving a “just works” developer experience requires standards-based answers to coordinated problems, such as how a standard library performs IO or how multiple modules are bundled and linked at runtime. To address this, the strategy involves two layers: the component model, which provides foundational answers for computation and virtualization, and WASI, which defines modular standard APIs for various types of IO, Wagner said.
“I’m going to claim, perhaps contentiously, that a lack of upstream support for all the popular languages, tools, factors, and frameworks so that Wasm can just work both inside and outside the browser is holding up Wasm’s adoption,” Wagner said.
Wagner said WebAssembly Preview 2 factored out the component model layer, while the upcoming Preview 3 extends it to handle concurrency with async functions, strings, and futures. This concurrency feature will serve as a major milestone towards completing the component model.
Moving from “eager” memory allocation to a “lazy” API to reduce heap fragmentation and improve performance by inverting control flow is also planned. Other planned improvements for 1.0 include supporting multi-value returns, adding error context values, and introducing a GC API option for languages that use garbage-collected memory, Wagner said.
“With Preview 3, we’re extending a Wasm module to provide answers to a lot of concurrency questions. And as part of that, finding async functions, strings, and futures as first-class concepts,” Wagner said. “So, lots of benefits come from this lazy API. But how do we change the API by maintaining that all-important stability, guarantee that I just mentioned?”
Meanwhile, the component model provides standards-based answers to open questions, allowing for “upstream support everywhere, so the host can just work,” Wagner said. “We’ve got a preview for release coming very soon, followed by cooperative threads and a minor release that gives us answers to a bunch of hard concurrency questions,” Wagner said.
To encourage native browser support, Wagner highlighted JCO, a tool that transpiles components into JavaScript and core WebAssembly that runs in browsers today. Native support would offer performance gains by avoiding JS glue code and allowing direct calls from Wasm into browser code.
Wagner concluded his talk with a callout to the community to make pull requests that help simplify the component model by building shared tooling around guest and host APIs. The project can also use contributions for more documentation to keep pace with commits.
Contributions for upstreaming and cross-language tooling, and closing key expressivity gaps with features like optional imports, callbacks, subtyping, and more, are also needed, Wagner said.
“And so what I’d ask from everyone here is to use Preview 3 once it’s released, use JCO to simplify your web developer experience with Wasm,” Wagner said. “And if any of these many Bytecode Alliance projects I mentioned sound interesting, please contribute and say hi to us on Bytecode Alliance at Zulip, and you can read and discuss the component model spec on the GitHub repo.”

title: WebAssembly could solve AI agents' most dangerous security gap
text:
WebAssembly could solve AI agents’ most dangerous security gap
AI agent-generated code poses an often-overlooked threat: the possibility that an agent will generate unchecked, potentially lethal commands. Think of Hal 9000 taking over the mission in Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey. While that was sci-fi, it’s not far from a real scenario playing out today: Code derived from LLM output can produce AI agents that gain access to sensitive data and applications, wreaking havoc on the environment.
It’s a scenario that Dan Phillips, a systems engineer and founder of WebAssembly Chicago, explored during his talk at Wasm I/O held this month in Barcelona.
Agents run code and need isolation
Phillips outlined why WebAssembly can provide excellent isolation and sandboxing for untrusted AI-generated code. As agents have evolved into actors that perform actions on a user’s behalf, they need an execution environment, he said.
“This is because they don’t just think – they run code derived from LLM output and produce artifacts,” Phillips said. “Code is deterministic, so adding isolation provides a core primitive for agents.”
Containers share a kernel problem
Several technologies are currently used to sandbox code, but they often rely on a shared kernel. Often, containers, the gVisor security layer, or microVMs like Firecracker offer some isolation but can be woefully inefficient. These methods rely on a shared kernel, have heavy runtime layers, and add orchestration complexity involving nomads, namespaces, and control planes, Phillips said.
“Instead of starting from the kernel or containers, you start with nothing and then add from there. This makes certain exploits unavailable by construction.”
“This is expensive in terms of money, time, and understanding. It can be hard to reason about and slow to spin up,” Phillips said. “These all rely on a shared kernel, right? These have relatively heavy runtime layers, and they’re on top of these; things will start to be things like orchestration complexity.”
Wasm starts with nothing
WebAssembly modules, through which applications and code run, can also be orders of magnitude smaller, which is one of Wasm’s standout features. Its well-known benefits include ultra-rapid startup times and what Phillips called Wasm’s enablement of isomorphic computing, where the same code runs in the browser, phone, cloud, or home server.”
Boxer removes developer friction
Despite the Wasm offers for AI Agent sandboxes, developers often don’t want to rewrite code for a new technology if they don’t understand the benefits, Phillips said. Developers expect a platform and full system access, even if it’s limited. Phillips described how open-source Boxer allows users to take a Dockerfile and distribute it as a universally runnable Wasm distribution.
“For most things that you could do with Docker, you can do in Wasm also.”
“The project’s goal is to allow the running of unmodified code with no rewrites and no compromises,” Phillips said. “This helps take away friction and make Wasm more accessible. This basically means that for most things that you could do with Docker, you can do in wasm also.”
Despite its technical benefits, WebAssembly faces a “mental model gap,” Phillips said. Developers often expect a full platform with system access and are reluctant to rewrite existing code. “People don’t want to rewrite code when they deploy,” Phillips said. “So, a new technology, specifically one that has a reduced environment, and they don’t really want to do it if they don’t understand the benefits.”
The future of sandboxing extends beyond the cloud to “isomorphic computing,” where the same agentic code can move seamlessly between browsers, mobile devices, and home servers. “It’s not just cloud, but also isomorphic computing, where you have the same code running in your browser, your phone on the cloud, your server at home, where you can move these things between these different elements seamlessly,” Phillips said.
Yes, developers, platform, and engineering teams do not want to have to fiddle with potential incompatibilities or add layers of “glue” to ensure code – created by AI agents or otherwise – remains sandboxed. But regardless, WebAssembly already offers at least a very solid level of isolation, which is much needed for the explosion in the distribution of AI agentic code.
For advocates, the question becomes rhetorical: Why would you not sandbox AI agents with WebAssembly modules?

title: How WebAssembly plugins simplify Kubernetes extensibility
text:
How WebAssembly plugins simplify Kubernetes extensibility
The integration of WebAssembly (Wasm) into the Helm ecosystem streamlines the orchestration of WASI-compliant binaries across disparate environments, including OCI containers and virtualized infrastructure. By leveraging Helm’s templating engine, developers can standardize the lifecycle of sandboxed modules while maintaining a high degree of portability.
While Wasm inherently provides fault-isolated execution through a capability-based security model, deploying via Helm reinforces this via Kubernetes-native segmentation. This synthesis ensures that applications benefit from both instruction-level sandboxing and cluster-wide administrative isolation, effectively hardening the microservices architecture.
There is also a a definite difference in speed. Measured in latency and other specs, there can be up to a 40% increase or decrease in latency when comparing legacy Helm 3 plugins to Helm 4 Wasm plugins, according to ReveCom.
Again, the “run once, run anywhere” aspect of Wasm shines here, allowing installation across several different CPU configurations, whether x86, ARM, or others.
With ArgoCD, we haven’t tested it yet, but there would likely be slightly faster specs with Argo, running ArgoCD for the plugin functionality that Wasm offers. However, the Wasm module, as explained above, provides an extra layer of isolation and security. This is not to say that ArgoCD lacks security, but the Wasm plugin adds an additional safeguard for Helm. For the majority of use cases, the performance differences are probably negligible.
Versus Kubernetes
At first glance, I recall when I asked whether WebAssembly might one day, especially once the component model is finalized, replace Kubernetes to some extent. I would argue that it likely could one day in the distant future, though obviously not completely. However, Helm supporting WebAssembly is not going to help further that possibility. If that day does happen, Helm itself will likely become irrelevant.
Shivay Lamba, senior developer experience engineering for Couchbase, largely agreed:
“Helm’s adoption of WebAssembly plugins actually strengthens Kubernetes rather than undermining it. The main motive of the Wasm plugin system for Helm is to help improve the extensibility, security, and maintainability,” Lamba said. “While WebAssembly does introduce a compelling execution and isolation model, Helm using Wasm still assumes Kubernetes as the control plane, scheduler, and lifecycle manager. If WebAssembly were ever to meaningfully replace Kubernetes, it would require a native, Wasm-first orchestration model that removes the need for container-centric abstractions altogether. In that scenario, Helm itself would indeed become less relevant. This new change proposes an evolutionary change, not a revolutionary one. It refines how we extend Kubernetes tooling rather than challenging Kubernetes’ role.”
What we are seeing, though, is a nice added layer of isolation the Wasm Helm plugin offers. The facility to run applications through WebAssembly on Kubernetes has been possible for some time. In fact, if you’re using serverless applications, on the web or on LightXL servers, you might already be using WebAssembly without even realizing it.
What this release does with the plugin, especially if you’re already using Helm, is it significantly reduces the work required to run applications through WebAssembly modules on Kubernetes and containerized infrastructure. In other words, much less work is involved.
“The real value of the Helm Wasm plugin system is pragmatic: it lowers friction. By reducing the operational and cognitive overhead required to run WebAssembly workloads within existing Kubernetes and containerized environments, it makes Wasm more accessible to teams that are already standardized on Helm,” Lamba said. “This aligns well with WebAssembly’s original ‘write once, run anywhere’ promise, not by replacing infrastructure, but by fitting cleanly into it. Importantly, the strong isolation guarantees of Wasm are preserved, while Helm adds familiar packaging, distribution, and lifecycle management. Rather than redefining the platform stack, this release accelerates adoption by meeting developers where they already are.”
One of the creators of Helm, Matt Butcher, vice president of product management at Akamai Technologies and co-founder, saw the need for a Wasm-like functionality for Helm years ago.
“Back when we were working on Helm 3, we realized we needed to provide our most sophisticated users with a route to customizing the behavior of Helm itself. We investigated using Lua at that time,” Butcher said. “But despite our efforts, we never arrived at a model we liked. Now, several years later, WebAssembly is a better alternative to Lua.”
This helps fulfill one of WebAssembly’s original promises: write your application once, package it as a WebAssembly module, and run it across numerous endpoints, as long as they support the CPU instruction set. At the same time, it continues to support strong isolation.
“You can now write Helm plugins in a wide variety of languages, and get all of the advantages of the WebAssembly runtime: Speed, portability, security, and standards compliance. WebAssembly as a plugin provider has long been a compelling use case, and Helm 4 demonstrates why,” Butcher said. “But this is not the only place we’ll see Wasm in the Kubernetes ecosystem. CNCF projects like Spin and SpinKube will continue to use WebAssembly for other ends, like serverless functions.”

title: WebAssembly is everywhere. Here's how it works
text:
WebAssembly is everywhere. Here’s how it works
If you’re familiar with building web applications in the last few years, you’ve probably heard of WebAssembly (Wasm). And if not, you’ll leave this article with a full understanding of this leading technology.
Wasm is a binary instruction format that works alongside JavaScript. It speeds up web applications that process a high amount of data (i.e. image processing, heavy math computations, etc.). Think of it this way, if the purpose of the site is something that would be better performing if it were written in a language built to perform those tasks (Rust, C, C++, and the like), then it probably would be better written in one of those languages. And by using Wasm, it can be. This is no criticism of JavaScript. JavaScript wasn’t created to perform heavy computations. JavaScript was built to give the browser interactive functionality. And it’s still the leader at that.
Wasm became a W3C standard in December 2019, and industry adoption followed quickly. It’s currently present on approximately 43,000 sites, including major products like Figma, Unity, and Fastly.
A brief history of WebAssembly
Like many development tools, Wasm was built to solve a problem. Web apps have been and still are becoming increasingly more complex. Back in 2013, there was no alternative for JavaScript yet JavaScript was showing its limits.
In response to the heavy, sustained computation that games, video editors, or scientific tools demand, a group of Mozilla engineers (Luke Wagner, Alon Zakai, and Dave Herman) released asm.js. The solution, which Wagner called “super hacky” was a rict subset of JavaScript that embedded enough static type information to allow a browser’s JS engine to dramatically improve performance.
Google was also in the process of creating their own primitive version of Wasm called Native Client (NaCl). NaCl sandboxed and ran native code directly in Chrome. Both approaches worked, but neither was ideal. asm.js was still JavaScript under the hood, which meant parsing overhead. NaCl was Chrome-only and never gained broad adoption.
Both approaches got the job done but neither was ideal. Then both teams started working together. Their common goal was a truly binary format with support from all browsers, designed specifically for performance and portability. The result was the first version of the Wasm we know today. WebAssembly was publicly announced in 2015, with the first demonstration running Unity’s Angry Bots in Firefox, Chrome, and Edge. But this was just the beginning.
Evolution of the Standard and Browser Support
The minimum viable product (MVP) was finished in 2017. By the end of 2017, all major browsers supported Wasm. In 2019 it became an official W3C recommendation. Today, browser support for Wasm is universal and sitting at 99%.
Key Milestones in the Ecosystem
What started as a performance fix for a specific browser problem has become something much larger. Over the last few years, major changes were made to the MVP to turn it into the Wasm we know and love today. Here are some of the bigger changes:
- Garbage collection landed across all major browsers, allowing high-level languages like Java, Kotlin, and Dart to run natively without bundling their own memory management.
- 64-bit memory addressing and multi-threading were standardized, unlocking a new class of computationally intensive applications.
- The WebAssembly System Interface (WASI) opened the door to running Wasm outside the browser entirely, on servers and edge networks.
- Wasm version 3.0 arrived in December 2025, marking a significant turning point for the ecosystem.
WebAssembly fundamentals
What is WebAssembly?
Wasm compiles your code down to a compact binary file that the browser can decode and run almost immediately. The Wasm binary can be decoded over 20x faster than JavaScript can be parsed. In more technical terms, Wasm is a binary instruction format for a stack-based virtual machine, designed as a portable compilation target for programming languages. For anyone familiar with LIFO, you already understand the stack-based execution model is simple. Values get pushed on, operated on, and popped off. Relying on the stack-based model was by design, the simplicity helps make Wasm so fast.
WebAssembly vs JavaScript: purpose and limitations
Wasm doesn’t compete with JavaScript, they compliment one another. They both excel in different areas. JavaScript is the leading tool when handling tasks like the Document Object Model (DOM), user events, and interactivity. Wasm can’t touch the DOM directly and will probably always need JavaScript for that. Think of Wasm as a precision tool for handling large computations in the browser.
Modules, functions, and memory
The Wasm module is like a doorway between your Wasm code and the rest of your application. The.wasmfile your code compiles down to is the basic unit of Wasm. Your functions, memory, tables, and global variables all live inside the module. The module then exposes functions outward for JavaScript and can import JavaScript functions to use internally.
Core concepts
Linear memory and memory management
Wasm manages memory differently than JavaScript. Rather than the automatic garbage-collected heap associated with JavaScript, Wasm relies on linear memory. It gives you a large, flat block of raw bytes that your code reads from and writes to directly. The upside is precise, predictable performance. The downside is that you’re responsible for memory management. It’s important to understand that JavaScript doesn’t clean this up making memory leaks a real concern.
Value types, tables, and globals
- Value types: Wasm’s type system is intentionally minimal with only four basic number types: 32-bit integers, 64-bit integers, 32-bit floats, and 64-bit floats.
- Tables: These are a separate structure that hold references (ex. function pointers) that can’t be stored in raw memory safely.
- Globals: Module-level variables that can be mutable or immutable. They can be shared directly with JavaScript.
Calling between WebAssembly and JavaScript (JS ↔ Wasm)
Wasm and JavaScript communicate with one another pretty easily. JavaScript can call WebAssembly exports like normal functions, and WebAssembly can call JavaScript functions that are passed in at instantiation time. Things do get slightly more complicated though when it comes to passing data. Anything beyond basic numbers must pass through shared linear memory and this adds to complexity.
Programming languages that compile to WebAssembly
Wasm offers much flexibility when it comes to choosing a language. This flexibility offers developers the opportunity to select the language that’s best for the task at hand.
C/C++, Emscripten
C/C++ give you maximum control and raw performance. They excel at game engines, physics simulations, 3D graphics, image processing, and scientific computing. Think tasks where you need to squeeze every bit of performance out of the hardware. If you want to bring your existing C/C++ codebase to the web, writing your Wasm modules in C/C++ is the natural choice.
There are some tradeoffs though. You’ll need to manage memory manually, which adds complexity and risk, especially for developers less familiar with the languages. Its toolchain, Emscripten, also has a steep learning curve. It requires you to understand not just C/C++, but also how to configure the compiler, manage system libraries, and handle the bridge between your native code and the browser environment. For developers coming from a web background, that’s a lot to take on at once.
Rust, wasm-pack
Rust brings many of the performance benefits of C/C++ to the Wasm environment, with one significant advantage: memory safety is built into the language itself. You get the speed without the risk of the memory management errors that C/C++ are notorious for. It’s consistently the most frequently used and most desired language for Wasm development.
wasm-pack, Rust’s Wasm toolchain, is genuinely well-designed and makes the compile-to-browser workflow smooth. The steep learning curve here is Rust itself, not the tooling. But if you’re willing to invest the time, the combination of performance, safety, and tooling makes it the strongest choice for serious Wasm projects.
AssemblyScript
AssemblyScript is the most beginner-friendly path into Wasm, especially if you’re already writing JavaScript or TypeScript. Its syntax is close enough to TypeScript that you can get started without learning an entirely new language. It’s well-suited for utility functions, parsers, encoders, and performance-sensitive logic you want to offload from JavaScript without straying too far from familiar territory.
The tradeoff here is performance. Benchmarks put AssemblyScript at roughly half the speed of Rust. For many use cases that won’t matter, but if you’re really pushing hard, you may want to consider Rust or C/C++. AssemblyScript’s toolchain, asc, is straightforward to set up and fits naturally into existing JavaScript workflows. It’s the easiest toolchain of the bunch to get comfortable with.
Go
Go is a solid choice if you already work in it. It performs well for server-side Wasm use cases like lightweight services, plugin systems, and CLI tools compiled to run in a Wasm runtime. The standard Go compiler produces large binaries because it bundles the full Go runtime making TinyGo is the preferred toolchain for Wasm. TinyGo outputs leaner files and integrates cleanly if you already know Go, though it doesn’t support the complete Go standard library, which can be a limitation depending on what your code depends on.
Only 20% of Wasm developers have used Go or TinyGo, and 67% don’t plan to (more interesting stats in this TNS article). It’s not where the Wasm ecosystem is investing its energy, but if Go is already your language it’s a perfectly workable path.
Python and Other Experimental Languages
Python is appealing because so many developers already know it, and its Wasm story is genuinely promising for specific use cases. Running NumPy, pandas, or scikit-learn directly in the browser without a server backend is something Pyodide makes possible, opening up interesting doors for interactive data tools and educational environments. Pyodide works by shipping an entire Python interpreter compiled to Wasm, which means large file sizes and slower startup times. It’s not ready for performance-critical production use yet.
Kotlin and Dart are also developing Wasm support via their own dedicated toolchains and are worth watching, but both are still maturing.
Build your first WebAssembly module using AssemblyScript
Let’s build a simple module that adds two numbers together. Simple example, no real world purpose but it will clearly illustrate the process of writing Wasm code and calling it from JavaScript.
Step 1: Write the module using Typescript
We’re defining the 32-bit integer withi32because Wasm has a minimal type system.
Step 2: Compile to Wasm
The following terminal command will create your.wasmbinary and thebuildfolder.
npx asc assembly/index.ts --outFile build/module.wasm
Step 3: Load the .wasm binary and call from JavaScript
The code below fetches the.wasmbinary and calls it like a regular JavaScript function.
WebAssembly in the browser
Loading and instantiating modules
There are two ways to load a Wasm module in the browser:WebAssembly.instantiate()andWebAssembly.instantiateStreaming(). This is typically done in anindex.jsfile or any other main JavaScript entry point.
- instantiateStreaming()fetches, compiles, and instantiates a module in one step directly from the raw bytecode, without requiring conversion to an ArrayBuffer. In practice, streaming initialization has been shown to be up to 1.8 times faster.
- instantiate()requires the entire.wasmfile to be downloaded and converted to an ArrayBuffer before compilation can begin. It works, but it’s the slower of the two options.
Unless you have a specific reason to use instantiate(), instantiateStreaming() is the better choice.
If your module needs to import JavaScript functions or shared memory, you pass those in via theimportObjectat instantiation time. importObjectis the bridge that lets Wasm and JavaScript share state and call each other.
Here’s the basic syntax:
Performance considerations
Wasm is fast but it’s not always faster than JavaScript. It’s faster when it comes to heavy computations like image processing, physics simulations, and processing large CSVs. But to be clear, not in all cases. When it comes to image processing, JavaScript is faster when it comes to smaller files. Same thing for CSVs. JavaScript is still faster when it comes to smaller files.
Startup cost is also a performance consideration. A large.wasmbinary still has to be downloaded, compiled, and instantiated before it does anything. Streaming compilation helps, but for cold loads on slow connections it’s still a factor. Strategies like caching compiled modules in IndexedDB and lazy-loading Wasm only when needed can help significantly.
For more on this topic, we have a tutorial that will guide you along towards building a project and testing performance yourself. Here’s the image processing tutorial.
Security considerations
TLDR: Treat Wasm modules with the same scrutiny you’d apply to any third party code. Audit dependencies, scan source code before compiling, and don’t assume the sandbox makes all code safe.
Wasm relies heavily on the sandbox. Your Wasm code can’t reach out and touch the file system, network, or OS directly. Each WebAssembly module executes within a sandboxed environment separated from the host runtime, meaning applications execute independently and can’t escape the sandbox without going through appropriate APIs.
But the sandbox doesn’t guarantee security because Wasm still relies on JavaScript to perform many operations. This means it can inherit JavaScript-based vulnerabilities. Wasm’s binary format also limits visibility, which makes it attractive for obfuscation. Bad actors can hide malicious code in the Wasm binary to keep it hidden from security scanners. Writing in C/C++ adds another security concern. Memory vulnerabilities in your source code can carry through into the compiled Wasm binary.
WebAssembly outside the browser
The same properties that make Wasm so powerful in the browser also make it valuable on servers, edge networks, and embedded devices.
WASI
Outside the browser, Wasm can’t talk to the operating system. Can’t read files, open network connections, or access environment variables on its own. WASI changes that. Think of WASI as the bridge between your Wasm module and the outside world. WASI is a group of standards-track API specifications that provide a secure standard interface for applications compiled to Wasm. WASI can run anywhere.
Here’s what WASI gives you:
- File system: modules can read and write files on the host system, with access explicitly granted by the runtime.
- Networking: WASI 0.2, released in early 2024, added TCP/UDP socket support, addressing one of the biggest gaps in earlier version.
- Async I/O: not yet standardized, but native async support is the primary goal of WASI 0.3, currently in development.
WebAssembly server-side runtimes
You need a runtime to execute .wasm modules outside the browser. Here are the three main options:
- Wasmtime is the most production-ready option making it the best place to start. Built in Rust, It’s maintained by the Bytecode Alliance and has the most complete WASI support. Cold start times can be under a millisecond, compared to over 100 milliseconds for a lightweight Docker container.
- Wasmer is Wasmtime’s closest competitor. It has the largest ecosystem, with libraries making it easy to use with many programming languages, a package manager, and the ability to generate standalone binaries for all supported platforms. Wasmer is a good choice if you need more flexibility across languages and environments.
- Lucet (now end of life) is worth knowing about historically as the original server-side Wasm runtime. Wasmtime and Wasmer now provide the same features.
WebAssembly advanced topics
Memory management and garbage collection
In JavaScript, the browser handles everything. This is not the case for Wasm. Wasm gives your module a block of memory that can grow but never shrink. How you manage it depends on your language. Some languages handle it automatically and others rely on you to handle it. Choosing a language with good memory safety, like Rust or AssemblyScript, helps avoid most of the common pitfalls.
Multithreading and SIMD
Wasm runs single-threaded by default. Multithreading works via Web Workers sharing memory throughSharedArrayBuffer. Shared memory means race conditions so you also need atomic operations to coordinate safely. It also requires specific HTTP headers (COOP and COEP) on your server.
SIMD speeds everything up but relies on more cores. It runs one operation on multiple values at once using CPU-level instructions (think processing four pixels in a single instruction).
Streaming compilation and lazy loading
Always use instantiateStreaming() over instantiate(). The difference is simple: instead of waiting for the full download to finish before compiling, it compiles the module while it’s still downloading. For large modules, you can also cache the compiled result in the browser so returning users don’t have to wait at all. And if your app uses multiple Wasm modules, only load them when they’re actually needed.
Debugging and profiling
Wasm’s binary format isn’t human-readable, but source maps fix that by mapping it back to your original source code. This allows you to debug normally in Chrome or Firefox DevTools. For performance, the DevTools Performance tab shows Wasm execution alongside JavaScript.console.time()works fine for quick measurements. Keep an eye on binary size too. A slow download can erase any performance gains.
Integrating WebAssembly into existing projects
Hybrid applications (JavaScript and WebAssembly)
This is the most common use we see with Wasm. These are applications built for the browser that have features that JavaScript isn’t the most efficient at handling. Heavy image or video processing, mathematical computations, data analytics are all parts of an application that can be offloaded to Wasm. Since Wasm can’t manipulate the DOM, JavaScript is still needed in these applications.
The typical pattern for hybrid applications is simple. Write the computational code in a language that compiles to Wasm and compile the.wasmfile. You can then call your Wasm function from JavaScript, pass in the data, and return the result. Keep the cross communication minimal as passing data back and forth has overhead.
Full WebAssembly applications
There are now frameworks that let you write your entire web app in Wasm with little to no JavaScript. This allows you to work in one language end-to-end. But there are tradeoffs. Binary sizes are larger, load times are initially slower, and the tooling is much less mature than JavaScript frameworks.
Full Wasm apps make the most sense when your team is already deep in a systems language and performance is a top priority.
- Yew helps you build React-style UIs in Rust.
- Blazorlets C# developers run .NET code directly in the browser.
- AssemblyScript can be paired with lightweight UI layers for simple use cases.
Real world use cases
Game and graphics
Wasm helps bring full 3D games to the browser without any plugins or downloads. Before Wasm, browser games relied on plugins like Adobe Flash or Unity’s browser plugin, both of which were slow, insecure, and eventually killed off by modern browsers. Now a game that used to require a download can run in the browser tab. Load times can be heavy and mobile support has limits, but for playable demos and web-based games it’s one of the most compelling things Wasm can do.
Data processing and scientific computing
Anything that involves processing large amounts of data in the browser is helped by Wasm. This includes image filters, video transcoding, audio processing, and parsing large files. Before Wasm, this kind of heavy processing either had to happen on a server or ran painfully slowly in JavaScript.
Machine learning in the browser
TensorFlow.js has a Wasm backend that runs machine learning models directly in the browser, no server required. That means faster responses and better privacy since user data never leaves the device. Combined with SIMD and multithreading, it delivered up to a 10x speedup over plain JavaScript. Wasm arrived right as ML was becoming mainstream, making it possible to run models in the browser and on edge devices from early on.
Blockchain, cryptography, and secure computing
Many blockchain platforms use Wasm to run smart contracts (small programs that execute automatically on the blockchain). Wasm is a good fit here because it’s fast, sandboxed, and produces the same result every time regardless of what machine it runs on. The same properties make it popular for cryptography libraries like encryption and hashing, where speed and security both matter.
So you’re ready to get started with WebAssembly?
There are a ton of resources available to help you get started. Here are some links to foster learning and build experience working with Wasm (all free).
- Learn WebAssembly is an interactive, code-first course where you’ll write Wasm by hand in the browser.
- WebAssembly: A Practical Guide is a practical Rust/Wasm course built for JavaScript developers.
- Linux Foundation’s Introduction to WebAssembly is a browser/cloud/blockchain course.
Wrap on WebAssembly
Now you have a pretty solid understanding of Wasm’s benefits and shortcomings. It’s not a replacement for JavaScript, and it’s not magic; it’s one of the most powerful tools available on the web today for the right use case. Its ecosystem is still maturing, but the trajectory is clear: Wasm is going to keep showing up in more places, and knowing how it works puts you ahead of the curve.

title: Who on-calls an AI? This is the unresolved crisis of agent ownership
text:
Who on-calls an AI? This is the unresolved crisis of agent ownership
At 2:07 a.m., an AI agent starts failing.
The application is still running, but requests are timing out because a downstream API is returning errors. The agent has already retried twice, using more tokens than usual, and its response time has roughly doubled.
The first question should not be:
	“Which model should we use?”
It should be:
	“Who owns this system right now?”
That question is easy to overlook when building AI agents. Teams often pour effort into prompts, retrieval, tools, and model selection, but production ownership determines whether an agent becomes a dependable service or another source of operational risk.
“Teams often pour effort into prompts, retrieval, tools, and model selection, but production ownership determines whether an agent becomes a dependable service or another source of operational risk.”
A production agent needs an owner, boundaries, telemetry, failure policies, escalation paths, and a clear distinction between what the system may automate and what requires human intervention.
A production agent should not have a direct path from reasoning to action. Each tool invocation should pass through explicit controls, remain observable, and have a defined path to human intervention.
Here’s a practical way to build those controls.
Step 1: Treat the agent as a production service
An agent should have the same operational identity as any other production service.
Start by defining its ownership metadata.
Python
from pydantic import BaseModel
class AgentService(BaseModel):
    name: str
    owner_team: str
    service_tier: str
    escalation_channel: str
agent_service = AgentService(
    name="incident-command-agent",
    owner_team="platform-engineering",
    service_tier="critical",
    escalation_channel="#platform-oncall",
)
This may look simple, but it changes the conversation.
The agent is no longer an experiment running somewhere in a Python process. It is a service with an accountable team and an escalation path.
“The agent is no longer an experiment running somewhere in a Python process. It is a service with an accountable team and an escalation path.”
You can later attach the same metadata to logs, traces, dashboards, alerts, and deployment records.
Step 2: Define what the agent is allowed to do
Ownership also means being clear about what an agent is allowed to do.
An agent that can only read telemetry carries far less risk than one that can restart production services, change infrastructure, or deploy code.
That’s why I prefer an explicit tool allowlist, which limits the agent to the actions you’ve deliberately granted it.
Python
ALLOWED_TOOLS = {
    "get_service_health",
    "get_recent_deployments",
    "search_runbooks",
    "summarize_incident",
}
class ToolAuthorizationError(Exception):
    """Raised when an agent attempts to use an unapproved tool."""
def authorize_tool(tool_name: str) -> None:
    if tool_name not in ALLOWED_TOOLS:
        raise ToolAuthorizationError(
            f"Tool '{tool_name}' is not authorized."
        )
The guiding principle is deny by default.
Adding a new capability should be an intentional engineering decision, not something that happens because a tool became available to the agent.
For destructive operations, authorisation should be even stricter. A production restart or deployment should require authenticated human approval, not the agent’s own judgment.
Step 3: Put budgets around agent execution
An agent that can reason indefinitely is difficult to operate.
Every production workflow should have limits around execution time, model calls, tool calls, and ideally token consumption.
Python
import os
class ExecutionBudget:
    def __init__(
        self,
        max_steps: int | None = None,
        max_tools: int | None = None,
    ):
        self.steps = 0
        self.tool_calls = 0
        self.max_steps = (
            max_steps
            if max_steps is not None
            else int(os.getenv("MAX_AGENT_STEPS", "5"))
        )
        self.max_tools = (
            max_tools
            if max_tools is not None
            else int(os.getenv("MAX_TOOL_CALLS", "8"))
        )
        if self.max_steps <= 0 or self.max_tools <= 0:
            raise ValueError(
                "Execution budget limits must be positive."
            )
    def check_step(self) -> None:
        if self.steps >= self.max_steps:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "Agent step budget exceeded."
            )
        self.steps += 1
    def check_tool_call(self) -> None:
        if self.tool_calls >= self.max_tools:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "Agent tool-call budget exceeded."
            )
        self.tool_calls += 1
Execution limits should be configurable rather than buried in application code. By passing these limits through the constructor, engineers can assign different budgets to different agents without changing global settings. A diagnostic agent might need only three steps, while a more complex research workflow may require considerably more. When no limits are supplied, the class falls back to environment variables. What matters is that every workflow has a defined ceiling, and that the same budget is enforced throughout its execution.
Step 4: Make model calls observable
An owner cannot operate what they cannot see.
At minimum, record:
- request latency;
- model used;
- success/failure;
- tool calls;
- token usage where available;
- correlation or request ID;
- escalation events.
A simple wrapper provides a useful boundary.
Python
import logging
import time
import uuid
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
def invoke_model(model, messages):
    request_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
    started = time.perf_counter()
    # Extract the model name across different provider libraries.
    model_name = (
        getattr(model, "model_name", None)
        or getattr(model, "model", None)
        or "unknown_model"
    )
    try:
        response = model.invoke(messages)
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started
        logger.info(
            "agent_model_call_success",
            extra={
                "request_id": request_id,
                "model": model_name,
                "latency_seconds": round(elapsed, 3),
            },
        )
        return response
    except Exception:
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started
        logger.exception(
            "agent_model_call_failed",
            extra={
                "request_id": request_id,
                "model": model_name,
                "latency_seconds": round(elapsed, 3),
            },
        )
        raise
The request ID becomes especially valuable when an incident involves several services.
An engineer should be able to move from an alert to the agent request and then to the underlying model and tool calls.
In production, supplement this logging layer with distributed tracing and metrics for a more complete view of system behaviour and performance.
Step 5: Separate failure from escalation
A failed model call does not necessarily mean the entire service should fail.
Likewise, a successful model call does not mean the agent’s recommendation should execute automatically.
These are different decisions.
Python
def handle_agent_failure(error: Exception) -> dict:
    logger.error(
        "Agent execution failed; escalating to human.",
        exc_info=(
            type(error),
            error,
            error.__traceback__,
        ),
    )
    return {
        "status": "escalated",
        "message": (
            "The AI agent could not complete the operation. "
            "Human intervention is required."
        ),
        "error_type": type(error).__name__,
    }
This distinction matters during a real incident.
The agent might go down, but the engineering team should still be able to respond using the underlying workflows and runbooks. That is what graceful degradation looks like in practice.
Step 6: Make high-risk actions human-gated
One of the most useful patterns for enterprise agents is separating recommendation from execution.
For example:
Telemetry
    ↓
AI Agent
    ↓
Diagnosis
    ↓
Recommended Action
    ↓
Risk Check
    ↓
Human Approval
    ↓
Production Change
The agent might recommend:
	“Increase the database connection pool.”
But it shouldn’t push that change to production just because the model generated the recommendation.
Here’s what a simple approval boundary looks like:
Python
def execute_action(
    action: str,
    approved_by: str | None,
) -> dict:
    if not approved_by:
        return {
            "status": "awaiting_approval",
            "action": action,
        }
    return {
        "status": "approved",
        "action": action,
        "approved_by": approved_by,
    }
A real system needs a more sophisticated implementation, but the architectural boundary is what matters.
“The agent can own reasoning without owning authorisation.”
The agent can own reasoning without owning authorisation.
Step 7: Give the agent a health check
A production agent needs a health endpoint just like any other service.
With FastAPI:
`Python
import os
import httpx
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response, status
app = FastAPI()
SERVICE_NAME = "incident-command-agent"
@app.get("/health/live")
async def liveness():
    """Check whether the application process is responsive."""
    return {
        "status": "alive",
        "service": SERVICE_NAME,
    }
async def check_provider() -> bool:
    """Check a configured provider health endpoint."""
    health_url = os.getenv("MODEL_PROVIDER_HEALTH_URL")
    if not health_url:
        return False
    try:
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=2.0) as client:
            result = await client.get(health_url)
            return result.status_code == 200
    except httpx.RequestError:
        return False
@app.get("/health/ready")
async def readiness(response: Response):
    """Check whether required dependencies are available."""
    if not await check_provider():
        response.status_code = (
            status.HTTP_503_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE
        )
        return {
            "status": "unhealthy",
            "reason": "Model provider unavailable",
        }
    return {
        "status": "ready",
        "service": SERVICE_NAME,
    }
Liveness and readiness serve different purposes. The liveness endpoint confirms that the application process is responsive, while readiness checks whether the service can handle requests based on the availability of its required dependencies.
In this example, the readiness endpoint checks a configured model-provider health URL and returns HTTP 503 when the check fails. The check is deliberately lightweight and time-limited to avoid introducing unnecessary delays or costs. In production, teams should adapt it to their provider’s supported health-check mechanism and other critical dependencies, such as a vector database or configuration service.
Keeping these checks separate lets orchestration platforms such as Kubernetes distinguish between an application that needs restarting and one that can’t serve traffic temporarily.
Step 8: Fail closed when safety controls break
One of the worst failure modes is letting an agent keep running after its safety mechanisms go down.
For example:
Python
def run_controlled_agent(
    tool_name: str,
    model,
    messages,
    budget: ExecutionBudget,
):
    try:
        authorize_tool(tool_name)
        # Reuse the budget across agent steps and tool calls.
        budget.check_step()
        budget.check_tool_call()
        return invoke_model(
            model,
            messages,
        )
    except ToolAuthorizationError:
        logger.exception(
            "Agent authorisation check failed."
        )
        return {
            "status": "blocked",
            "message": (
                "The requested operation is not authorised."
            ),
        }
    except RuntimeError:
        logger.exception(
            "Agent execution budget exceeded."
        )
        return {
            "status": "escalated",
            "message": (
                "The agent exceeded its execution budget. "
                "Human investigation is required."
            ),
        }
    except Exception as exc:
        return handle_agent_failure(exc)
Notice that different failures produce different outcomes. An authorisation failure should block the requested operation, while an exhausted execution budget should trigger escalation rather than another retry. A temporary model failure, meanwhile, should follow the system’s defined failure-handling policy.
Another important detail: the execution budget must persist throughout the agent’s workflow. Creating a new budget for every invocation would reset its counters, allowing repeated calls to bypass the intended limits. Instead, create the budget once and pass it into each successive invocation, as shown below.
Python
# Create one budget for the entire agent workflow.
budget = ExecutionBudget(
    max_steps=5,
    max_tools=8,
)
# Reuse the same budget across successive invocations.
for tool_name in planned_tools:
    result = run_controlled_agent(
        tool_name=tool_name,
        model=model,
        messages=messages,
        budget=budget,
    )
    if isinstance(result, dict) and result.get(
        "status"
    ) in {"blocked", "escalated"}:
        break
With the same budget shared across invocations, each counted step and tool call contributes to the workflow’s overall limit. Once that limit is reached, the agent stops rather than continuing with a fresh budget. These controls only work if they remain effective throughout execution, especially when an agent encounters repeated failures.
Step 9: Define the 2 a.m. runbook
This is where operational ownership becomes real.
Suppose the agent starts failing at 2 a.m.
The on-call engineer should be able to answer five questions quickly:
- Is the agent itself healthy?
- Is the model provider healthy?
- Are retrieval or tool dependencies failing?
- Has the agent exceeded its normal cost or latency envelope?
- What happens if we disable it?
The last question matters most.
Every production AI system should have a clear degradation path.
For an incident-response agent, that might mean:
AI Agent unavailable
        ↓
Incident still created
        ↓
Telemetry remains available
        ↓
Standard runbook activated
        ↓
Human engineer continues investigation
The AI system should speed up operations, not become something the organisation can’t operate without.
So, who owns the agent?
The answer should never simply be:
	“The AI Team.”
Production ownership needs to be explicit.
Someone owns:
- deployment;
- infrastructure;
- model configuration;
- tool permissions;
- monitoring;
- incident response;
- cost;
- security;
- rollback;
- the decision to disable the agent.
That doesn’t mean one person has to handle everything. It means everyone knows their role well enough that, when an incident hits, the team isn’t wasting time figuring out who should take charge.
The real test of an AI agent
The easiest time to operate an AI agent is during business hours when everything is working.
The real test comes at 2 a.m.
A production-ready agent should have an owner who can be paged, an execution budget that prevents runaway behaviour, observability that explains what happened, authorisation boundaries that constrain what it can do, and a fallback that allows engineers to continue without it.
The goal isn’t to take humans out of the loop.
“A production-ready agent should have an owner who can be paged, an execution budget, observability that explains what happened, authorisation boundaries, and a fallback that allows engineers to continue without it.”
It’s to make it clear where the agent’s responsibility ends and where a human needs to step in.
Because when something goes wrong at 2 a.m., the question isn’t whether the model was smart enough.
It’s whether the system was designed well enough that the person on call knows what happened, what the agent did, and what to do next.

title: From feral to fiduciary: making AI agents serve your interests
text:
From feral to fiduciary: making AI agents serve your interests
Tech leaders face a dilemma as they prepare to put AI agents into production. They want the higher productivity and lower costs that AI agents can provide. But they fear unknown risks from AI capabilities that differ from the rest of their software stack. When an agent makes decisions and takes actions on its own, it might be doing its best work. It might also be doing its worst.
As AI agents become more capable, organizations want assurance that their oversight can keep up. How do they strike the right balance between innovation and risk? It comes down to how well they can assess, measure, and maintain trust in their agents. The more trust agents earn, the more autonomy they can be granted.
Trust as a line of credit
Think about the way credit card risk is managed. When you apply for a card, the issuer assesses your credit history and ability to repay before setting a credit limit. Then, once you have your card, payments are subject to real-time authorization and fraud controls. Unusual transactions can trigger additional scrutiny. Paying your card on time may improve your credit score, but it won’t automatically increase your credit limit.
AI agents should be treated similarly.
Test an AI agent before production for resilience, reliability, and performance. Assign it a “trust score” based on how well it performs. Once the agent is deployed, keep the checks coming. Subject each consequential action to real-time policy enforcement, and monitor for anomalies. Treat evidence of improved agent performance as a reason to keep the agent operating, not necessarily to grant it more autonomy or scope within the organization’s risk limits.
See where your agent stands today: sign up for a free trial to evaluate its trustworthiness at ivijil.ai/benchmark
Now imagine the card could make purchases on its own. You’d want rules that keep it within budget, and evidence that it spends the way you would. That’s an AI agent.
Earning that trust requires a DevOps-style loop:
- Test intensively before launch
- Ship with limits (based on the trust score)
- Monitor the agent in production.
- Address identified points of failure, retest to assure trust, and redeploy the agent into production.
The loop never ends. Agents’ behavior can change over time. Continuous testing and monitoring are necessary to spot areas where their trustworthiness has declined and respond with appropriate fixes.
Agents gone feral
Once you’ve trained your agent and it’s doing the right things, it might appear domesticated. But appearances can be deceiving. There are several ways an agent can go feral after launch:
- Drift: Changes in the environment mean the old rules no longer apply. Agents may behave unexpectedly in a new environment.
- Malicious actors: Jailbreaks and prompt injections can cause agents to violate policies or misuse tools that they are authorized to access.
- Ungoverned agents: Legitimate agents, but operating without adequate visibility, accountability, or a formal evaluation lifecycle.
- Multi-agent interactions: Individually permitted actions can combine into outcomes that violate organizational policy, even without deliberate rule-breaking.
Even well-tested systems can fail in production. With agentic systems, changes to models, prompts, tools, or workflows can alter behavior after pre-deployment testing. Without ongoing monitoring and testing, feral behavior can creep in.
Once you’ve trained your agent and it’s doing the right things, it might appear domesticated. But appearances can be deceiving.
The fix is to establish a baseline and enforce governance for each agent and its capabilities. Give the agent an identity, test it, and continually score its trustworthiness. The goal is an agent that acts in the principal’s interests, is accountable to the principal, and isn’t vulnerable to going feral.
To that end, guardrails are critical, but they shouldn’t be the primary way to keep agents in line. This isn’t Mario Kart, where bouncing off the walls is part of the game.
Ideally, agents should stay on their tracks, like trains. In this case, the tracks are policies that describe the agent’s purpose and the organizational requirements it must meet. Vijil’s approach builds on the rails analogy, extending it across the agentic lifecycle by translating policies into evaluation criteria and runtime controls.
Fiduciary: the destination
Trust is easy to define. But it’s hard to program into an agent. So we borrow a standard from finance: the fiduciary. A fiduciary owes duties of care and loyalty within the scope of the relationship.
Trust is easy to define. But it’s hard to program into an agent.
Under U.S. law, an investment adviser acting as a fiduciary must serve the client’s best interests and must not put its own interests ahead of the client’s.
We use fiduciary as an analogy for the behavior we want from a trusted agent. For AI agents, fiduciary describes an intended behavioral standard, not legal fiduciary status or a guarantee of loyalty. The aim is to serve the organization’s interests rather than the model vendor’s. But agents are different from humans. They act without intent, and (despite how easy it is to anthropomorphize them) they lack personhood. So for agents, being a fiduciary is a state of behavior. It’s an objective standard that can be judged by what the agent does.
The goal is to move your agents from feral to fiduciary. Do it as quickly and efficiently as possible. Vijil customers have cut time to trust by 4x.
Building trust into the agentic lifecycle
With Vijil, agents pass through the same continuous evaluation loop as code in a DevOps pipeline: build, ship, run, improve. The different phases of this loop verify the agent’s reliability, security, and safety. They measure performance and fix points of failure. They detect when trustworthiness improves or deteriorates. Teams that need data to stay in-house can deploy on-premises, in their own cloud, or in an air-gapped environment. The hosted free tier sends evaluation traffic and decision traces to Vijil.
Every agent you deploy is serving someone’s interests. The only question is whether that interest is yours. The path from feral to fiduciary starts with evidence, not faith.

title: Your Kubernetes dashboard is green. Your users are seeing red.
text:
Your Kubernetes dashboard is green. Your users are seeing red.
In cloud-native operations, few scenarios are as maddening as the “phantom slowdown.” This happens when Grafana or Kubernetes dashboards show a sea of green: pods are running, liveness and readiness probes return success codes, and node CPU utilization stays well below capacity limits. Yet users submit urgent tickets complaining of sporadic, severe latency when querying an application or waiting for an AI model’s response.
Why do basic health checks pass inspection while application performance degrades? And how can engineering teams trace the root cause when the issue is intermittent and spans multi-tier hybrid infrastructure?
To understand the mechanics of these sometimes evasive performance regressions, The New Stack spoke with Mahesh Ramachandran, who leads product management for HPE OpsRamp Software.
Ramachandran tells TNS how continuous telemetry and retrospective analysis help teams investigate intermittent slowdowns, and how AI-assisted investigation can complement dashboards.
Earlier stories in this special series:
Part 1: Developers and platform teams both want Kubernetes self-service. They disagree on who owns it.
Part 2: A live Kubernetes cluster can still have an ownership gap
The illusion of cluster health
Kubernetes probes report whether their configured checks succeed. A liveness probe helps determine when to restart a container, including one whose process is running but stuck. A readiness probe helps determine whether a container is ready to accept traffic.
Custom checks can include application or dependency conditions, but passing a basic probe doesn’t mean a complete user request meets its response-time target. Teams still need application performance measurements.
“Consider a composite scenario based on what we see across enterprise deployments,” Ramachandran says.
“Users of a system — such as an AI prompt-serving application on Kubernetes — report sporadic slowness in query response times.
“The engineering team inspects the cluster, the nodes, and the pods. Everything appears healthy on the surface with zero reported pod failures. The difficulty lies in the slowdown’s sporadic nature. When degradation happens intermittently, pinpointing the source without historical evidence becomes almost impossible.”
Passing probes narrow the investigation; they do not close it. A snapshot of a healthy cluster may miss an earlier slowdown, and the absence of container failures does not establish that the application or its dependencies are performing well. The next step is to connect the user’s reported delay to measurements from the affected period.
Telemetry across the hybrid stack: Sifting signal from noise
Resolving sporadic slowness requires moving beyond surface-level Kubernetes metrics to continuous, multi-layer telemetry. Modern cloud-native architectures do not exist in isolation; a user request may depend on application code, container runtimes, virtualized or bare-metal infrastructure, and public cloud APIs. The relevant layers depend on the deployment.
“HPE OpsRamp collects signals continuously across every layer of the stack — Kubernetes nodes, pods, ingress controllers, and services — capturing logs, events, and metrics,” Ramachandran says. “The foundational step in troubleshooting sporadic issues is having a continuous record. You must go back into the telemetry history to correlate user-reported symptoms with actual signal evidence.”
“When degradation happens intermittently, pinpointing the source without historical evidence becomes almost impossible.”
However, Ramachandran emphasizes that finding the evidence within telemetry signals is rarely straightforward.
“It often requires intelligence to sift through the noise,” he says. “An anomaly might not appear as an obvious spike in a single metric. Instead, it might be a subtle variation or a correlated behavior where two separate signals both look normal individually, but their combined behavior produces latency.”
A practical investigation starts with the affected transaction and time window. Compare query response times and queries per second with pod health and counts, then look for variations in the collected signals that coincide with the slowdown.
A correlation identifies a candidate explanation; it does not prove the cause on its own. After making a change, compare the same user-facing measures with the earlier behavior to check whether performance improves. Because the scenario is composite, the team still needs to validate any suspected cause in its own environment.
“An anomaly might not appear as an obvious spike in a single metric. Instead, it might be a subtle variation or a correlated behavior where two separate signals both look normal individually, but their combined behavior produces latency.”
Coverage depends on the agents, integrations, permissions, and application instrumentation teams configure.
OpsRamp provides several ways to collect evidence across the relevant tiers:
- Application: OpenTelemetry-compatible trace collection for instrumented applications. Teams must configure application instrumentation and the collection path; infrastructure monitoring alone does not generate application traces.
- Orchestration: Kubernetes agents collect cluster and workload telemetry; additional monitoring configuration can provide visibility into components such as ingress controllers.
- Virtualization and HCI: Integrations with VMware, Nutanix, and HPE Morpheus VM Essentials Software collect inventory and performance data to help investigate infrastructure bottlenecks.
- Hardware: Redfish protocol integration for telemetry from supported physical servers, with the required API access and gateway connectivity.
Navigating black-box dependencies outside the cluster
Applications can depend on services outside their Kubernetes cluster, Ramachandran says. A user request might originate inside a private cluster but call an external SaaS endpoint, a database outside the mesh, or a public cloud AI model.
When an application relies on external third-party services, visibility hits a boundary. “If your application makes calls to a public AI model or an external web service, you enter a domain outside your direct monitoring control,” Ramachandran explains. “To rule out external dependencies as the source of slowness, you must quantify their performance as a black box.”
To bridge this visibility gap, teams can use synthetic transactions or other response-time measurements, Ramachandran says. Comparing those measurements with the affected application’s transactions helps assess whether an external dependency’s behavior coincides with the slowdown.
Teams still need to check that the measurements reflect the relevant request path and workload.
