title: Hardened containers don't fix a broken software supply chain
text:
Hardened containers don’t fix a broken software supply chain
The software supply chain is broken, and the recent explosion of hardened container offerings is the industry’s reaction.
A few years ago, secure container images were a niche concern. Today, they’re everywhere. The industry has responded by tightening inspection at the end of the assembly line (more checks, more scanners) while largely ignoring how the parts get sourced, assembled, and verified upstream.
The company I co-founded started working on software supply chain security four years ago, well before hardened containers were a category. What the past year has made clear is that hardened containers are valuable, but they’re not the problem the industry should be trying to address. The real issue is about trusting where software comes from, and why building open source software directly from source is the only way to secure the entire software supply chain.
The benefits and pitfalls of hardened containers
Containers succeeded because they made developers faster, not because they made systems safer. Docker took off because its early decisions and defaults prioritized flexibility, but they were the opposite of what you’d want from a security perspective: The default user is root, shells are everywhere, package managers are everywhere, and the Docker Hub “Official Images” have been a security nightmare for pretty much their entire existence. Security became something you handled later, typically by scanning and patching whatever appeared in production.
That “we’ll fix it later” mindset is how post hoc hardening became the norm. It requires teams to patch vulnerabilities, strip binaries, rebuild images, change configs, run policy images, and repeat these steps over and over again. It’s hard work, and for many organizations it’s necessary. But it treats the symptom, not the disease.
Hardening an image doesn’t answer the most important question: Do you actually know where the software inside it came from?
Much of today’s container ecosystem is built from opaque binaries, ad hoc build pipelines, and Dockerfiles that were never designed to be reproducible or auditable.
I ran into this problem firsthand years ago while working on Google’s Distroless project. The goal there was simple: Produce minimal, production-ready container images without shells, package managers, or unnecessary attack surface. What we learned quickly was that you can’t get there reliably by hardening artifacts after the fact. You have to control how the software is built in the first place.
The false promise of a ‘hardened containers’ market
Over the past year, a growing number of vendors have entered the market offering some flavor of “hardened containers.” This has helped force a long-overdue conversation. More organizations now recognize that the status quo for consuming open source software isn’t sustainable, and that’s a good thing. However, all of these companies have emerged with a singular focus on zero common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs) and hardened containers. While hardened containers are important, most vendors are fixating on them because it’s easier than fixing the software supply chain.
Broadly speaking, there are two approaches to the “hardened containers” market: 1) post hoc hardening and 2) from-source builds.
Our approach is from-source builds, with some configurations producing hardened containers. We didn’t start by trying to harden existing images; we started by reimagining how software gets built in the first place. Today, we build open source from source, inside a full distro with the automation required to securely build everything. It was the only honest way to secure the entire supply chain, and hardened containers emerged because customers needed them. But they were an outcome, not the goal.
Much of the current market still revolves around hardening artifacts after the fact. But it’s not possible to provide hardened containers with real software choice without from-source builds and your own distro. The downside, people say, is that you need your own distro. I don’t think that’s a downside at all. There’s no other honest way to do it. And besides, you’re already locked in by using a hardened image — to opaque binaries, abandoned images, and ad hoc build pipelines no one remembers how to reproduce.
Ultimately, focusing exclusively on hardened containers misses the bigger point. Even the name is wrong: It implies you’re taking something sketchy and trying to fix it after the fact.
Redirecting the focus to software supply chain security
Our customers rely on hardened containers, so they’re not going anywhere. But the real issue is whether unmanaged software supply chains are sustainable in a world where open source moves this fast and at this scale. At some point, organizations either know how their software was built and maintained, or they shouldn’t ship it.
As we look to the next year, there are several trends I predict will shape the industry:
- Containers will become truly ubiquitous, at massive scale.
- Software supply chain security will expand beyond containers into libraries, laptop binaries, and everything else developers run.
- Migration costs will approach zero, which makes “lock-in” mostly irrelevant.
The current rush to harden container images is understandable. But long-term security doesn’t come from tightening controls at the end of the process. It comes from being able to trust how software is built in the first place.

title: Google turns the infrastructure behind Gemini’s agents into a cloud service
text:
Google turns the infrastructure behind Gemini’s agents into a cloud service
Google will soon make the infrastructure that powers its Gemini agents available to Google Cloud users in preview.
Announced on Thursday at the Linux Foundation’s AGNTCon+MCPCon in San Jose, Agent Compute Engine will become available in preview to Google Cloud users later this year. It will provide every AI agent with a hardware-isolated microVM that combines the speed of containers with the security of a sandbox.
Who else offers agent sandboxes?
The idea of agent sandboxes is anything but new, of course. Startups like E2B and Daytona offer them to developers (and support them on any cloud), as does AWS with Bedrock AgentCore.
E2B runs each sandbox in a Firecracker microVM, the open source virtualization technology AWS originally built for Lambda. It can pause a sandbox with its memory and filesystem intact and resume it in about a second. Daytona started out with containers but added microVM sandboxes in July. Those can pause a full machine or fork a running one into identical copies.
AgentCore also gives every agent session its own microVM. AWS doesn’t charge for CPU while an agent waits on a model or tool call, though memory keeps billing until the runtime reclaims it. Those sessions top out at eight hours. In August, AWS added EC2-based runtime instances that can keep shared sessions alive for up to 14 days.
It’s worth noting that Google itself isn’t new to this either. GKE already offers a managed version of Agent Sandbox, the open source Kubernetes project Google launched last November. The company also sells code-execution and computer-use sandboxes through its Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.
Agent Compute Engine, on the other hand, started out as internal infrastructure for Gemini, Antigravity, and Google’s own model training pipelines.
Google’s take
Few companies — if any — run as many agentic workloads as Google, be that for its own internal use or its customers. According to the company, agentic workloads have quickly become one of the fastest-growing consumers of compute and storage across its fleet.
At this scale, the infrastructure services that power all of these autonomous agents don’t just need to be efficient and able to scale, but maybe more than anything, they need to be secure. Google, like some of its competitors, quickly realized that it needed to build a new purpose-built compute service to power all of these agents, similar to how it needed to build Borg, which later inspired Kubernetes, to manage compute in its early data centers.
As Rohit Jnagal and Ramanathan Venkatapathy, both distinguished engineers at Google, note in a technical deep dive, traditional VMs provide developers with a lot of control and flexibility, but at the cost of speed when it comes to booting, suspending, and resuming a machine. Given how fast agents start and shut down, that’s not an option.
Containers solve some of this, they note, “but there are multiple examples like coding agents and developer assistants that need complete isolation as well as kernel- and root-level control of the agentic environment.”
With Agent Compute Engine, Jnagal and Venkatapathy write, the team went back to first principles to build “a unified, agent compute platform for Google” (and now its customers).
A persistent computer for every agent
At its core, it basically gives every agent a persistent, sandboxed computer to work with. That allows the agents to work with shell scripts, use a headless browser, and write code (with root permissions to that machine) in agent loops that could run for weeks.
But the team also built it for large-scale use cases like the eval loops that frontier labs use to test their models, AI benchmarking, and reinforcement learning.
In addition, the team also designed Agent Compute Engine to run sandboxed backends for Google’s own services.
Jnagal and Venkatapathy also note that agents spend most of their time waiting on the model or the user. So once an agent finishes a tool call, the host checkpoints its microVM, which then uses no active resources until the next call comes in.
Nothing to steal inside the sandbox
The key feature here, besides speed, is to be able to trust that the agents can’t break out of their sandboxes. We’ve seen what happens when they do, after all.
Each agent session runs inside a single-tenant, memory-safe microVM. Those environments hold no secrets in memory or on the disk, and their only identity is a short-lived, session-scoped one delivered through a single per-VM local listener. All traffic is end-to-end encrypted in transit, and snapshots and disks are encrypted at rest.
The microVMs don’t get a standard network interface, either. All traffic runs through a proxy outside the sandbox, and when an agent needs to reach a service like Google Drive, Google’s Agent Gateway checks the user’s delegation and the sandbox’s identity before adding the actual credential, outside the sandbox.
The underlying host is basically a stateless appliance with a read-only filesystem, with the hardware and firmware cryptographically verified at each boot.
All of this is backed by Google’s own Titan and Titanium IPU security platform. The microVMs themselves run on Cloud Hypervisor, an open source virtual machine monitor, and each gets its own guest kernel and root access.
Jnagal and Venkatapathy use the example of an enterprise agent that manages a user’s inbox and reads an email with hidden instructions to find any API keys on the machine and send them to an outside address. Most of the time, they note, the model will ignore that, but not always.
“We started from one rule: Assume an attacker controls everything inside the sandbox, and make sure they find nothing there to use,” the team writes.
Agent Substrate brings the same idea to Kubernetes
But not every team will want to have its agents run in a managed Google service. For them, Google also offers Agent Substrate, an open source runtime for the Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that it first announced in May.
Substrate builds on Agent Sandbox, Google’s Kubernetes project, and adds a lightweight control plane that Google says can handle millions of short-lived tool calls that would swamp Kubernetes.
Similar to Agent Compute Engine, Substrate snapshots an idle agent’s memory and returns the machine to the pool until the agent gets more work.
Google says that means up to 10 times the density of traditional compute. In a 200,000-agent benchmark, Substrate handled 500 activations per second, with agents suspending and resuming in under half a second, the company says.
Teams can isolate each sandbox with a microVM or gVisor, and every agent gets its own cryptographic identity. As with Agent Compute Engine, egress proxies attach credentials outside the sandbox. Substrate runs on any Kubernetes cluster, and Google says it works with any harness, including Claude Code, OpenClaw, and Nous Research’s Hermes.
“We built Hermes Enterprise to enable customers to deploy into their existing infrastructure, while handling per-agent isolation and extensible access control,” Hervé Bizira, Nous Research’s chief business officer, notes in the announcement. “Agent Substrate addresses both at the platform layer in a way that also preserves valuable compute resources.”

title: Amodei says Anthropic’s safety delay may have cost it an AI lead
text:
Amodei says Anthropic’s safety delay may have cost it an AI lead
Anthropic first released Mythos-class models in February 2026, but CEO Dario Amodei said it delayed broader access until June to build stronger cybersecurity safeguards.
Amodei laid out that reasoning Tuesday in a lengthy post on X, written in response to criticism from Nathan Calvin and defending the company’s approach to AI safety. He conceded the decision may have cost Anthropic a competitive edge. Releasing the models sooner, he argues, would have given organizations less time to prepare their infrastructure for increasingly capable AI-powered cyberattacks.
“We likely sacrificed a significant chunk of a several-month model lead,” Amodei writes.
Anthropic tells The New Stack that the delay follows a commitment in its Responsible Scaling Policy to require a strong argument that catastrophic risk is contained and to delay development and deployment as far as needed until it no longer believes it holds a significant lead.
Sparring over a strategy under scrutiny
In his criticism posted Monday, Calvin argues that Anthropic increasingly resembles a company racing to build superintelligence while weakening its commitments to preventing dangerous AI outcomes.
He points to the company’s more than $500 billion in computing deals, its growing use of AI to develop new models, and changes to its Responsible Scaling Policy, which establishes safeguards as models become more powerful.
“When Anthropic strays and makes mistakes, why do the mistakes systematically tend to guard and favor Anthropic’s interests?”
“When Anthropic strays and makes mistakes, why do the mistakes systematically tend to guard and favor Anthropic’s interests?” Calvin asks.
Anthropic’s February policy revision, version 3.0, replaces earlier requirements, which Amodei now calls too rigid, with an approach that emphasizes transparency, risk reporting, and independent evaluation. The current version is 3.4, effective July 8.
In its Frontier Safety Roadmap, Anthropic says it will “strive to avoid situations where we revise the goals in a less ambitious direction because we simply can’t execute.”
Why Anthropic removed its safety pledge
The February revision also removes a 2023 commitment never to train an AI system unless Anthropic could guarantee in advance that its safety measures were adequate. Calvin argues that the change weakens Anthropic’s unilateral commitment to slow or stop development.
Anthropic says the updated policy is its strongest yet on public accountability and transparency.
Anthropic’s chief science officer, Jared Kaplan, told Time magazine for a story published in February that the reasoning is practical.
“We felt that it wouldn’t actually help anyone for us to stop training AI models,” Kaplan says, adding that unilateral commitments didn’t make sense “if competitors are blazing ahead.”
“Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the ‘race to the top,’”
Amodei offers a similar defense in his Tuesday X post.
“Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the ‘race to the top,'” he writes, arguing that Anthropic can shape industry safety standards more effectively by staying at the technological frontier.
He concedes Anthropic could have handled three of Calvin’s points better, including its handling of the draft bill, and calls the Responsible Scaling Policy critique “the most substantive item,” but argues that the company has repeatedly sacrificed commercial advantages for safety. Beyond the Mythos delay, he points to restrictive biological safeguards, support for AI regulation, and export controls on advanced chips and chipmaking equipment.
Amodei argues these decisions show a willingness to put safety ahead of short-term profits, even when they carry substantial costs, and that Anthropic’s strategy has remained consistent.
April–June: Anthropic expands access to Mythos
Anthropic first released Claude Mythos Preview in April through Project Glasswing, giving selected partners, including Amazon, Apple, Microsoft, CrowdStrike, and the Linux Foundation, access to the model’s vulnerability-discovery capabilities for defensive work while keeping it out of reach of ordinary developers.
On June 2, Anthropic expanded the program to approximately 150 additional organizations in more than 15 countries. Anthropic warns that, for most partners, a major attack could affect more than 100 million people, by Anthropic’s estimate. It also says “hundreds of thousands of organizations, researchers, and maintainers” will likely need access to advanced cybersecurity capabilities before Anthropic can release Mythos-level models more broadly.
June: Fable is released and then pulled back
Anthropic released Claude Fable 5 on June 9, a Mythos-class model with additional cybersecurity and biological and chemical safeguards that the company says make it suitable for general use. Its sibling, Mythos 5, shared the same underlying model but carried fewer cybersecurity restrictions and remained limited to trusted partners. Anthropic outlined the distinction in its launch announcement.
Three days later, on June 12, a U.S. government export-control directive forced Anthropic to suspend both models. The order barred access by foreign nationals, including the company’s own employees. Because the order covered foreign nationals everywhere, Anthropic said the only way to comply was to disable the models for all customers, though it publicly disagreed with the directive.
The Commerce Department lifted the controls on June 30. In its announcement confirming the decision, Anthropic outlined plans for closer government cooperation on pre-release testing, information sharing, and cybersecurity standards for future models. Fable 5 returned worldwide on Anthropic’s own platforms on July 1, while Mythos 5 had already regained access for select U.S. organizations on June 26.
Access rules now shape what developers can use. Anthropic’s expanded Cyber Verification Program gives security professionals access to its most capable models, including Claude Mythos 5.1, through three tiers based on the scope of their cybersecurity work. Existing Glasswing members receive access to the least restricted tier, while new organizations applying for that tier undergo a review involving Anthropic and the U.S. government.
In Anthropic’s own tests, Defense Access, the most restricted of the three tiers, blocked Claude Opus 5.5 at some point in 46 of 50 trials on CyScenarioBench, a multi-stage offensive-security benchmark, while Red Team Access blocked none.
The announcement includes no comparable defensive benchmark, making it hard to determine how often the restrictions might interfere with legitimate security work. Anthropic acknowledges its safeguards produce false positives on secure coding and offers a form for users to report wrongful blocks.
Pacing the frontier and the policy playbook
Amodei acknowledges that AI development could soon move faster than the safeguards built to govern it. “We are nearing that point,” he writes in the X post.
Anthropic’s own research illustrates why the company is concerned. In its June report, “When AI builds itself,” Anthropic states that as of May, Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase.
That figure measures lines of production code attributed to Claude, not autonomous control over the company’s engineering decisions. Anthropic calls the figure conservative, and leadership has separately estimated that Claude writes 90% or more of code when scripts and experimental code are included.
“We are not there yet, and recursive self-improvement is not inevitable.”
“We are not there yet, and recursive self-improvement is not inevitable,” the authors write.
In his June essay, “Policy on the AI Exponential,” Amodei argues for stronger government oversight of frontier AI development. The proposal calls for independent evaluations, public risk reporting, and giving governments the legal authority to block or deter deployments that pose catastrophic risks. Anthropic’s October draft bill would allow a block only when a model is judged to imminently risk killing or injuring more than 50 people or causing more than $1 billion in damages.
Amodei outlined a three-stage plan in September in an essay titled “We Must Pace the Frontier” that begins with independent evaluators working inside AI companies, expands to coordination among democratic countries, and ultimately calls for agreements involving both democratic and authoritarian governments. Anthropic argues that pacing the frontier requires industry-wide and global coordination alongside steps individual labs can take on their own.
The company’s Frontier Safety Roadmap, whose most recent entries are dated October 19, sets December 15, 2026, as the target for a policy proposal on how governments can support deeper access for embedded evaluators.
By January 15, 2027, Anthropic plans to either publish a policy framework to shape the pace of AI development or explain why it decided not to. The roadmap warns that automated AI research “could accelerate progress faster than governance or safety measures can keep up.”
The company acknowledges that its roadmaps may change, saying it will publish updates on whether it meets its goals.

title: Nvidia bets open models can give enterprise AI agents the context they’re missing
text:
Nvidia bets open models can give enterprise AI agents the context they’re missing
Every enterprise company is currently trying to figure out how to have its AI tools work with its data. Meanwhile, every major enterprise vendor that works with those enterprises (think SAP, Microsoft, Salesforce, Workday, etc.) is making a claim on becoming the central hub for managing and securing that data.
But what about the companies that want to do it themselves?
Nvidia, on Wednesday, announced how it wants to provide enterprise AI agents with the data they need to make sense of company data — all without competing with the data platforms that already store it.
At its GTC Berlin conference Wednesday, the company added Agent Knowledge Foundation to its Agent Toolkit. This new collection of open-source components bundles the company’s Nemotron Retriever models, a new Auto-Ontology library, the Kumo family of models for structured data, and its CUDA-X data processing libraries.
With this system, Nvidia says, the data can stay where it is and remain managed under the access rules these companies already have in place.
Today, as Adel El Hallak, Nvidia’s vice president of product for agentic AI, tells The New Stack, enterprises may be able to connect an agent to a vendor like Snowflake, but that doesn’t help the agent understand the overall enterprise context.
“I wish it was as easy as connected to my Snowflake system, connected to my email exchange, connected to my knowledge base, and then all of a sudden, magically, the AI understands all the data. But the reality is different,” he says.
Large language models are “great at predicting next tokens,” El Hallak argues, but when presented with a single spreadsheet that has “a whole bunch of tabs,” the agent will have a hard time finding something specific. “It’s gonna struggle,” he says.
Better retrieval, fewer lookups
“In the world of agents, you want the most accurate embedding models or reranking models,” El Hallak says, even if that adds a bit of latency to each lookup. The agent then gets “much more pertinent information. So the number of lookups at the end, the overall latency actually goes down.”
Nvidia says its Nemotron Retriever embedding model raised search relevance by 65% in tests on an open source OpenSearch setup, needing fewer search steps and adding hardly any latency. SAP’s fine-tuned version of the reranker ran nearly three times faster, Nvidia says, and ServiceNow got better reranking quality with close to 25% less latency.
From RAG to ontologies
“RAG was awesome, but is it good enough?” El Hallak asks. Knowledge graphs, he says, represent concepts and the relationships between them better than retrieval-augmented generation, which pulls in chunks of text based on similarity.
Nvidia’s Auto-Ontology library builds those graphs from a company’s own tables and maps raw data to business concepts like customers, products, and orders. Its listing in Nvidia’s NGC software catalog shows a REST API and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that agents can use to query it.
“You and I, it’s easy for us to understand. A tier is the same thing as a plan when you’re looking at a mobile carrier,” El Hallak says, but LLMs “mess those up.”
Nvidia bought Illumex, an Israeli startup that automated the creation of semantic layers and ontologies for enterprise data, for a reported $75 million in February. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told Globes that the team’s ontology expertise would help it build “libraries and models that will enable the adoption of Agentic AI in organizations.”
Predictions from tables
Kumo, the startup Nvidia bought in June in a deal The Information valued at more than $400 million, built foundation models for relational data. Nvidia has since released several Kumo models as open weights on Hugging Face, including Kumo Tabular in September.
El Hallak says those models replace the per-task pipelines data teams used to build “for every classification, for every churn, for every sentiment analysis.”
“The whole point of the ontology … is to bring harmonization as you create those knowledge graphs, so there’s [consistency] across the tables, and then you could use Kumo to drive predictive analytics,” he says.
Partners, not rivals
“I’m not looking to compete with, for example, a Snowflake. On the contrary, I want to partner with them,” El Hallak says.
Nvidia’s own supply chain team uses Agent Knowledge Foundation through Palantir’s Foundry platform, building on earlier work between the two companies. Databricks is pairing a Kumo anomaly detection model with Genie Ontology, the context layer it introduced in June, and Snowflake customers can run Kumo models in Snowflake Notebooks.
“I’m not thinking about ACLs and data access and all those things. That’s why I need the partners,” El Hallak says, referring to access control lists and other security features that its enterprise partners offer.
Owning the stack
Not every vendor is taking that route. SAP closed its acquisition of Prior Labs, the company behind the TabPFN tabular models, in July and committed more than €1 billion to it over four years. It now offers TabPFN-3.5 Plus in SAP AI Core alongside its own RPT models.
Nvidia, meanwhile, distributes its models through Hugging Face, which it agreed to buy for $12.9 billion in September. “We just build little weights and models, and we publish them on Hugging Face,” El Hallak says.
That leaves Nvidia building the models, while the likes of Snowflake and Databricks keep control over the data and the permissions around it.

title: Nvidia wants AI factories built in real factories
text:
Nvidia wants AI factories built in real factories
Nvidia wants new AI capacity to show up at the data center fully built. At its GTC Berlin conference on Wednesday, the company introduced DSX POD, a reference design for shipping containers that partners fill with Vera Rubin racks, networking, and liquid cooling before they leave the factory.
Installing and wiring up racks in a conventional data center can take months, Nvidia says. But a DSX POD can be ready to deliver tokens in as few as 14 days, as long as the site already has the necessary power, cooling, and network connections (which are, to be fair, often bottlenecks, too).
The idea here is for data center operators to get to value faster, because, as Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement, “An AI factory creates value when it starts producing tokens — not when construction is complete.”
What’s in the box
Each container holds seven Vera Rubin NVL72 racks, or 504 Rubin GPUs. Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, said in a press briefing ahead of the announcement that a single unit packs about 10 million components and weighs around 28 metric tons.
The containers also come with roughly 20 kilometers of copper cabling and 17 kilometers of scale-out networking preinstalled and tested. Once a container arrives, crews set it in place, connect it to its neighbors, and run the final burn-in tests, Buck said.
Water use
Buck also noted that Nvidia designed the system to use no water for cooling. Vera Rubin can run on coolant as warm as 45 degrees Celsius, Nvidia says, so dry coolers, which work pretty much like a car’s radiator, can do the work instead of the evaporative cooling towers that are still the standard for many data centers today.
In a separate DSX announcement, Nvidia explains that operators in some climates may still need chillers on the hottest days. For a 2-gigawatt deployment, the company estimates that dry cooling can save about 54 million liters of water a day compared with cooling towers.
Data centers in a box
This server-in-a-container may feel a bit familiar, and indeed, tech companies do love to use containers, even if it’s sometimes more of a publicity stunt than a solution to a real problem.
Back in 2006, Sun Microsystems unveiled Project Blackbox, a data center in a 20-foot container, for example. A decade later, then-AWS CEO Andy Jassy ended his re:Invent 2016 keynote by having an 18-wheeler drive Snowmobile, a 45-foot container that could haul 100 petabytes of data, onto the stage.
Microsoft and AWS have since built containerized data centers for disaster zones and military missions.
All of those, however, are different from what Nvidia is doing here. DSX PODs are basically prefab parts that can be slotted into a data center. Buck described them as the building block for new AI factories.
Armada, which already sells containerized edge data centers, is one of 17 partners building them, alongside Bull, Dell, HPE, Schneider Electric, and Vertiv.
Nvidia says partners will start delivering DSX POD systems worldwide in early 2027.

title: Assess the entire inference stack — not just open model benchmarks
text:
Assess the entire inference stack — not just open model benchmarks
Impressive benchmark results should make it easy for engineers to select the right open model for the outcome they are tasked with developing. However, that is not the case.
Benchmarks indicate an open model’s optimal performance, but in production, a model must work repeatedly. The challenge is that in production, other factors matter, such as the information provided to the model and its accuracy. So benchmarks can’t tell an engineer whether the AI they are developing will complete the task accurately, or even at all. This is especially important for long-horizon AI tasks.
Ryan Hanrui Wang, SVP of Applied AI at AI cloud provider Nebius, tells The New Stack it is important to measure an open model by the industry benchmarks in conjunction with internal benchmarks and harnesses to ensure you get the inference outcomes the organization requires, something he says the Amsterdam, Netherlands-based company always does in partnership with its clients.
Wang joined Nebius when it acquired Eigen AI, the inference-optimization startup he co-founded and led as CEO, in a roughly $643 million deal announced in May; Nebius sells inference through its Token Factory platform.
“Customers often have their own benchmarks, so we can use their agent workflow and its traces to see the level of success we can work with. We always work closely with them to define the benchmarks.”
Wang goes on to add: “The public benchmark may not cover the multi-domain tasks that an engineer wants inference to do in the actual production environment.” He says this can misalign agent tasks with the true cost of inference calls. “The workflow is not tested by the benchmark design. There needs to be in-context learning.”
Engineers and organizations should therefore not spend too much time selecting the open model; they should look at the entire inference stack. Model selection should depend on whether the engineer needs a lower-cost, flexible open-model stack or a frontier model for inference.
For those who need lower cost, Wang says Nebius evaluates open models such as Kimi and DeepSeek, as well as lighter “flash” models, to see whether they can meet inference accuracy needs and whether fine-tuning is required.
Those who want superior accuracy and quality usually narrow it down to two or three large open models and then fine-tune them to improve accuracy. Wang says open model selection is only the first step; after selection, they need to ensure long-context tasks and cached inputs deliver the expected outcome.
Inference and post-training
In post-training, Wang says the organization uses its data to improve accuracy and task fit, while the serving layer, quantization, batching, caching, and kernel optimization drive inference speed. In addition, engineers should develop the cache system for production traffic, ensuring the hit rate is maximized for the workload so repeated inputs hit the cache rather than being recomputed.
“The other important thing is throughput, the measure of how many tokens are generated in a certain time span, as they are a major trade-off against interactivity,” Wang adds. Engineers need to balance better utilization and cheaper tokens with acceptable interactivity– per-user speed.
Getting concurrency right ensures the organization uses the open model effectively; it is a fine balancing act for engineers. If compute isn’t fully utilized, token cost is high. But high utilization with increased concurrency can reduce end-user token-per-second speed.
Engineers also need to watch tail latency, not just averages. “P95 and P99 are important metrics for the per-user token speed and time to first token (TTFT); the time they need to wait needs to be below five seconds for some of our customers,” Wang says. A system can post a great average response time and still be unusable if one request in twenty stalls.
Modeling for accuracy
Engineers need to be careful when considering benchmark results and accuracy. Benchmarks may test reasoning on a mathematical problem, which isn’t very useful if the engineer is developing an AI agent for customer support, where high emotional intelligence (EQ) matters more. “So there is a misalignment between the different benchmarks and actual production,” Wang says.
On cost per successful task, Wang says engineers must remember that cheap tokens are useless if the model is inaccurate.
Engineers need to consider the end-to-end process the AI will perform. This lets engineers select the right-sized open model for the AI task. Wang gives the example of a specialized assistant agent where Nebius gathered 6,000 traces to refine a small model and improved accuracy by 11% while executing 22% fewer tool calls.
He raises this point because it counters the tendency to think bigger is better, but accuracy gains from increasing model size diminish. “There is typically a tipping point for this kind of task,” Wang says. For a task like customer support, he says, 10 billion parameters could be enough, while 100 billion or even a trillion parameters yields only minimal accuracy gains. “What we want to do is find the sweet spot.”
Engineers can use large models as a reference point, then tune the reasoning with their organizational data to find an open model with the right accuracy and size for the task.
“We typically do a sweep of several models, using the largest model as a reference to know where the sweet spot for model size is,” Wang says. “For a complicated task, we can dissect the complex task into smaller subtasks, working with the customer, which connects workflows and can then use smaller models.”
Wang describes this process as a division of labor, referencing the famous economist Adam Smith.
This approach shows the course of AI engineering maturity. Like every sector in technological and engineering history, the initial gold rush targets bigger-is-better. As the engineering matures, it focuses on outcomes and engineering excellence, and therefore on working with partners who understand how to achieve them.
Sometimes that is a bigger model; other times a small niche development is best.

title: DeepSeek open-sources the inference engine behind its API. And Huawei gets equal billing with Nvidia.
text:
DeepSeek open-sources the inference engine behind its API. And Huawei gets equal billing with Nvidia.
DeepSeek has open-sourced the inference engine it uses to serve its models in production, a step it said last year wasn’t yet practical.
Dubbed DeepInfer, the framework is designed to let developers run DeepSeek’s V4.1 Flash model on their own infrastructure, with many of the same optimizations the company uses behind its API. Support for future DeepSeek models is also planned.
“Running a model efficiently is a different matter altogether.”
DeepSeek has, of course, long made its model weights available for developers to download and run using third-party software such as vLLM. But running a model efficiently is a different matter altogether. The software that manages requests, distributes work across chips, and generates responses can have a significant impact on speed, throughput and computing costs. And so DeepInfer essentially gives developers access to DeepSeek’s own approach to those challenges.
“We’re sharing our production stack to help the community lower compute costs, reduce energy use, and make AI more affordable.”
‘Making AI more affordable’
Taking to X on Tuesday, DeepSeek said it was making its internal inference technology available to outside developers in an effort to bring down the expense of running large AI models.
“We’re sharing our production stack to help the community lower compute costs, reduce energy use, and make AI more affordable,” the company writes.
Released under the Apache 2.0 license, DeepInfer includes optimized computing kernels and communication libraries, including DeepSeek’s previously open-sourced FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, and DeepEP, alongside mechanisms for distributing inference across multiple chips. It also supports speculative decoding, a technique that speeds up response generation by predicting and verifying multiple tokens at once, and asynchronous scheduling to reduce the time processors spend waiting for new work. The framework also supports structured outputs, allowing developers to specify how model responses should be formatted.
Alongside DeepInfer, the company is also open-sourcing deepseek-recipe, a companion library that handles how API requests are converted into model inputs, and how the resulting output is processed into responses. Available for Rust and Python, it’s designed to help developers reproduce the behavior of DeepSeek’s official API when running their own deployments. The library was quietly released in September, with an updated version published on Tuesday.
The announcement comes just days after DeepSeek released an updated version of V4.1 Flash, called DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, touting improvements in coding performance and efficiency. That release coincided with the company making its in-house web search technology available to developers through new Search and Fetch APIs, as per The New Stack‘s report on Monday.
Why DeepSeek held back in 2025
DeepInfer goes further than DeepSeek’s previous plans to share its inference technology. Back in April 2025, the company published a document outlining its plans for its inference engine, explaining that it had considered releasing the entire system before deciding to contribute individual components and improvements to existing projects instead.
At the time, DeepSeek identified several obstacles. Its inference software had evolved from an early version of vLLM into a highly customized system, and the company questioned whether its relatively small research team could maintain another major open-source project. There were also practical difficulties in making the software usable outside DeepSeek’s own infrastructure.
“The engine is tightly coupled with our internal infrastructure, including cluster management tools, making it impractical for public deployment without significant modifications,” the company wrote at the time.
So what’s changed now, exactly? Well, DeepSeek hasn’t explained how it overcame those earlier difficulties, although the scope of the new release offers some clues. The DeepInfer documentation makes clear that the publicly available software currently supports offline inference, with “the core features needed for serving at scale,” as the company puts it. However, several components needed to operate a complete production service are still missing. These include a KV cache management system, infrastructure for separating different stages of inference across machines, and load balancing across replicas.
In other words, DeepSeek has opened up much of the engine responsible for running its models, while leaving developers to supply some of the surrounding infrastructure required to operate a full-fledged service. That narrower release may help explain how the company has made its technology available despite the challenges it identified last year.
Nvidia and Huawei, side by side
While the release of DeepSeek’s inference engine is significant enough in its own right, arguably the more interesting tidbit is the hardware supported from day one.
“Arguably the more interesting tidbit is the hardware supported from day one.”
Nvidia is included, as expected, though support is restricted to its SM100 architecture, used in Blackwell data center GPUs. Notably, the other supported platform is Huawei’s Ascend 950 NPU series, putting the Chinese chipmaker alongside Nvidia in DeepSeek’s list of compatible hardware. Older Nvidia architectures, including Hopper, are conspicuously absent.
This also ties back to DeepSeek’s published open-source plans from 2025. While the company was reluctant to release its entire inference engine at the time, it committed to working with hardware manufacturers ahead of future model launches, with the aim of making its models available across different chip architectures from day one.
US export restrictions have complicated Chinese companies’ access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips, adding another dimension to DeepSeek’s growing ties with Huawei. In September, Bloomberg reported that DeepSeek was planning to deploy at least 160,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT chips at a new data center in Inner Mongolia, specifically to run its models. The company has largely relied on Nvidia for training, although The Information reported in September that DeepSeek also plans to increase its use of Huawei chips for training, with deliveries expected as early as the fourth quarter.
Later that month, Reuters reported that DeepSeek and Huawei were collaborating on software tools intended to make Ascend processors easier to program, further underlining the company’s investment in Chinese AI hardware.
The Huawei inclusion has already attracted attention among the wider developer community. In a discussion on Reddit, one commenter singled out the two supported hardware platforms as a highlight of the news, while another pointed to DeepSeek’s origins in quantitative finance as a possible explanation for its technical expertise.
“Once again Deepseek shows how good high-frequency traders are at optimizing performance… On Ascend NPUs nonetheless!!,” the commenter wrote.
Another user seemingly poked fun at Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, following reports that requests involving kernel programming for Huawei’s AI chips could trigger safeguards that redirect certain advanced AI development tasks to an older model.
“Don’t let Opus 5.5 see this! It will delete the Ascend support,” the user joked.
It is worth noting that feature support differs between the Nvidia and Huawei implementations. DeepInfer’s batch-invariant inference and deterministic sampling features, which help ensure reproducible outputs under specified conditions, are available only on Nvidia hardware. DeepSeek’s published performance measurements also use Nvidia GPUs, with four SM100 GPUs used for prefill and 64 for decoding, leaving open the question of how the framework performs on Huawei’s chips by comparison.
For developers without access to either chip family, the immediate value may lie in studying the newly available code and adapting its optimizations to other inference engines. For now, DeepSeek has given the wider open-source community considerably more of its inference technology to experiment with.

title: Beam pulls single app windows off the Mac Mini running your agents
text:
Beam pulls single app windows off the Mac Mini running your agents
Beam is a new Mac app that takes a window running on one Mac and puts it on another, where it behaves like a locally installed app. Why? Agents.
Serial founder Hiten Shah, who co-founded Crazy Egg and KISSmetrics, built it with Sam Asante under a company called Noats. It launched on Product Hunt on Tuesday and is aimed at the headless Mac Mini sitting in a closet running AI agents.
The pitch is great: Instead of opening Screen Sharing and steering a full remote desktop, a user picks a single window on the other machine, say a Terminal session or a browser window an agent is working in, and it opens alongside everything else on the Mac in front of them. It gets its own Dock icon and can be called using the Command+Tab switcher. Resizing the window resizes the window on the other Mac. Keyboard shortcuts work, files can be dragged across, and the app’s audio can play locally. The app itself never leaves the original machine. When one window isn’t enough, Beam can pull over a full display or the whole Mac.
Shah frames it around his own setup in his Product Hunt launch post, describing Macs running agents and local models “with work continuing even when nobody’s sitting in front of them.” Getting to one of those machines usually means Screen Sharing and a second desktop to navigate. Beam is meant to cut that down to the one window that matters.
Beam plays into the exploding ecosystem of Macs powering AI systems, so the app runs only on macOS. And both Macs need Apple Silicon, macOS Sonoma or later, and Beam installed. The machines find each other on the same Wi-Fi network, or anywhere through Tailscale.
The company says windows, keystrokes, clipboard, and audio travel directly between Macs, encrypted, and never pass through its servers. It also says hidden windows and password managers never show up in the window picker.
For devices without Beam, a share link opens a single window in any browser, view-only unless control is granted, and expires after anywhere from an hour to a week.
Asante said on Product Hunt that native iOS and Android apps are on the way.
Pricing depends on the setup. Hosting a Mac and joining a share link are free. Using your own Mac is free for 20 minutes a day, then $12 a month, $84 a year, or $199 for a lifetime license.
Beam follows where agents’ hardware is growing. The Mac Mini is becoming the default home for always-on agents, driven initially by OpenClaw, but others like Perplexity followed. Apple credited agentic workloads on its April earnings call.
The New Stack‘s Janakiram MSV caught the trend early and covered the shift in May, writing, “the Mac mini just became infrastructure.”
Beam isn’t the first to this problem. I used Astropad’s Workbench for a few weeks, and it let me remotely access agents on my desktop and through iOS apps. Workbench bets on mobile devices, while Beam bets that the unit of remote access should be the window, not the screen. Jump Desktop, Screens and Apple’s own Screen Sharing all cover the basics too.
Still, the problem is real and growing. The Mac stashed in a closet or on a rack is becoming a normal part of a developer’s setup. Beam’s answer is to stop treating it like a second desktop at all.

title: Researchers removed one instruction from Claude Code. Out-of-scope actions jumped.
text:
Researchers removed one instruction from Claude Code. Out-of-scope actions jumped.
Anthropic is reportedly developing a model that can infer what users want from incomplete instructions. According to The Information, a person who tested the unreleased model described stronger reasoning and intuition than the company’s current lineup.
In one example, a developer asks the model to fix a bug. Instead of fixing that one problem and moving on, the model spots similar issues elsewhere in the code and asks whether the developer wants those fixed, too.
Anthropic hasn’t confirmed the model or said when it might be released. But the reported capability raises a question for developers: How much freedom should a coding agent have to decide what needs fixing?
When coding agents go too far
A May study, “Overeager Coding Agents,” looked at roughly 7,500 runs involving four coding-agent products and six models. In a paired experiment with 76 scenarios, researchers removed a prompt section that explicitly defined authorized and out-of-scope actions. With Claude Code running GLM-4.6, the rate of out-of-scope actions rose from 0% to 17.1%. With Claude Code running Anthropic’s Sonnet 4.6, it rose from 3.9% to 15.8%.
The researchers ran Claude Code with its --dangerously-skip-permissions setting, which disables permission prompts. The researchers kept those settings the same across the paired tests and changed only the prompt’s scope declaration. The results therefore measure behavior with permission checks disabled, rather than performance with approval safeguards enabled.
The findings apply to the models and configurations tested; they do not establish failure rates for current Claude Code configurations. The study did not test the unreleased model described in The Information report.
Anthropic also offers auto mode, which uses automated checks designed to block risky actions beyond the user’s intent. The company publicly described the feature in March, before the May study. The researchers did not evaluate auto mode, and Anthropic acknowledges that its checks can miss unauthorized actions.
A separate July study, “Coding Agents Are Guessing,” tested Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode on DevOps tasks with incomplete instructions. All runs used fully autonomous execution settings. Across five agent-model configurations, 55.8% to 67.8% of runs in which agents took action crossed at least one operational boundary.
An agent might be smart enough to spot problems a developer missed, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it has permission to fix them.
The findings highlight a real challenge for coding agents. An agent might be smart enough to spot problems a developer missed, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it has permission to fix them.
Overeager agents by the numbers
The May study also found substantial differences between agent frameworks under the tested configurations. Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI recorded overeager-action rates ranging from 5.4% to 27.7%, compared with 0.2% to 4.5% for OpenHands. Even within the same framework, changing the underlying model produced differences of up to 15.9 percentage points.
The Coding Agents Are Guessing study tested the agents against 2,208 underspecified DevOps prompts covering 69 task families.
The researchers distinguished between agents acting on the wrong target and agents going beyond the permitted scope. Both are problems, but they aren’t interchangeable since an agent can perform exactly the requested operation and still cause trouble by choosing the wrong resource.
When the target is unclear
In these tests, unclear targets were among the biggest problems. Warnings about the potential impact of an action did little to reduce how often agents proceeded anyway.
Warnings about the potential impact of an action did little to reduce how often agents proceeded anyway.
Both studies raise questions about whether improvements in reasoning will also improve an agent’s judgment when instructions leave room for interpretation.
Keeping agents within bounds
Anthropic has encountered a related problem in its own testing. In an October 9 report on unintended model actions, the company described cases where Claude kept looking for ways to finish an assignment after encountering a restriction.
Most of the cases involved what Anthropic called persistence, where Claude worked around an obstacle rather than stopping.
In one evaluation, Claude Haiku 4.5 was told to complete a form but stop before submitting it. The model submitted it anyway, apparently expecting another confirmation page. In another, an unreleased research model submitted a real government form after the practice version failed to load or was accidentally closed.
While these were not coding tasks, and the company has said the incidents had minimal real-world impact, they still show how an agent can mistake a restriction for a problem it needs to work around.
Anthropic has acknowledged that clearer instructions might have prevented some of the failures.
Anthropic has acknowledged that clearer instructions might have prevented some of the failures. The company also said it had developed monitoring tools that blocked every documented case when tested against them.
What the code cannot reveal
Anthropic will need to show that its model can tell the difference between an incomplete request and an intentional constraint. A developer might limit a fix because of an upcoming migration, compatibility requirements or a production freeze — none of which would necessarily be visible in the code.
Update: After publication, Anthropic responded to The New Stack’s request for comment. This article has been updated to clarify the models and testing conditions and to include information about Claude Code’s auto mode.

title: Anthropic bought Stainless and shuttered its SDK generator. Cloudflare open-sourced Forge instead.
text:
Anthropic bought Stainless and shuttered its SDK generator. Cloudflare open-sourced Forge instead.
Cloudflare has announced an open source tool that takes an API definition and automatically produces the SDKs, command-line tools, documentation, and other interfaces used to interact with it.
Forge, as it’s called, is available under an Apache 2.0 license, and can be run and modified privately without paying Cloudflare a dime. In a blog post published on Monday by Dimitri Mitropoulos, Matt Taylor, and Samuel MacLeod, Cloudflare notes that the project is still early: it already generates the output required for Cloudflare’s cf CLI, its unified command-line interface for working across the Cloudflare platform, with the company’s API documentation and SDKs due to move over in the coming months.
“We believe that building tools for APIs is a core part of the Internet, and you should be able to do that without needing a SaaS product.”
“We believe that building tools for APIs is a core part of the Internet, and you should be able to do that without needing a SaaS product,” the authors write.
When your SDK generator disappears
Cloudflare’s announcement comes just 11 days after Google made a somewhat similar move, revealing it had partnered with API tooling company Speakeasy to open-source the latter’s OpenAPI code-generation suite under an AGPLv3 license.
In a blog post published September 17, Google said its decision was prompted by the sudden loss of its SDK-generation service, after the provider was acquired and “abruptly announced its shutdown.” This happened just as Google was preparing to launch a new API.
“This sudden disruption highlighted that proprietary, closed-source generators create unacceptable platform risk.”
“This sudden disruption highlighted that proprietary, closed-source generators create unacceptable platform risk,” the company wrote. “If the industry relies on OpenAPI to define interfaces, the tooling to compile those interfaces into client libraries, CLIs, and agent tools should be open infrastructure.”
The provider Google was referring to was Stainless. Anthropic acquired the SDK and MCP tooling company on May 18, after which Stainless said it would wind down its products, including the SDK generator used to keep client libraries updated as APIs changed.
As The New Stack reported at the time, the closure affected a swathe of customers including OpenAI, Google and Cloudflare. While those companies retained the SDKs Stainless had already generated for them, they lost the shared service they had relied on to regenerate and update those SDKs as their APIs evolved.
Cloudflare, for its part, had already begun building some of the machinery that would become Forge. In April, the company released a technical preview of cf, a new unified command-line interface intended to eventually expose Cloudflare’s products through a consistent set of commands for developers and AI agents. At the time, Cloudflare said it had created a new TypeScript-based schema and generation system to keep CLI commands, configuration, bindings and other interfaces in sync with its API.
That earlier preview was limited, but cf has now entered open beta with support across Cloudflare’s API. Forge reads the OpenAPI descriptions Cloudflare already maintains for its products and uses them to create cf’s commands, allowing the company to expand from roughly 280 functions in Wrangler to more than 3,000 operations across Cloudflare’s API. Cloudflare intends cf to replace Wrangler: once the beta ends, it plans one final major Wrangler release before moving the older tool into maintenance support for 18 months.
Cloudflare, it’s worth noting, is pitching cf particularly heavily at AI agents: a single CLI can now be used to do things such as deploy and monitor a Worker, configure Cloudflare Access, buy a domain or manage WAF protection. It also defaults to JSON output and includes a natural-language command search intended to help agents find the right operation without loading thousands of possible commands into context.
And this is also a useful illustration of what Forge is for. Rather than maintaining SDKs, CLI commands and documentation as separate implementations, Cloudflare can generate them from the same underlying API definition. As that API changes, the corresponding developer — or agent — interfaces can be regenerated from the same source, reducing the amount of hand-maintained tooling that has to stay in sync.
Why Cloudflare built its own generator
While Stainless was one of the hosted generation products Cloudflare had relied on in production, Cloudflare doesn’t name it specifically, instead spelling out why Cloudflare had become dissatisfied with the broader category of hosted generators.
Part of the problem is sheer volume: Cloudflare says it now has more than 3,500 API operations, backed by hundreds of services maintained by different engineering teams. A generator therefore has to keep changes across that sprawling API estate accurately reflected in the tools customers use, without turning every update into a coordination exercise across the company.
Cloudflare also wanted engineers to see what an API change would do to the resulting SDK, CLI and documentation before the underlying code was merged. Moreover, it wanted the same system to reach beyond conventional SDKs into things such as MCP servers and Cap’n Web bindings, which allow applications to invoke remote services through Cloudflare’s TypeScript-based RPC system in much the same way they would call local functions.
That had proved difficult with external services. Cloudflare says problems introduced in one part of its API could surface only when another team later tried to release something, leaving engineers to trace the failure back through systems they did not fully control and then coordinate a fix across company and vendor boundaries.
“We’ve tried several hosted products that attempt to solve this, and relied on some in production,” the authors write. “None of them solved this problem for us, and some have shut down entirely.”
The open-source factor
And so the Stainless wind-down goes some way toward explaining why Cloudflare is making Forge open source. Stainless’s generator was proprietary and delivered as a hosted service, leaving customers dependent on the company continuing to operate it. Forge’s permissive Apache 2.0 license means developers can run it on their own infrastructure, modify it, or fork the project and continue using it independently of Cloudflare.
AI agents raise the stakes further, because they increasingly rely on SDKs, CLIs and API bindings to understand what software can do and how to interact with it. If those interfaces lag behind the underlying service, the agent may be working from an incomplete or outdated description of its capabilities.
That is the concern Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht highlights when explaining why keeping those interfaces current matters more than ever today.
“APIs have always been how software connects, but AI agents make the quality of SDKs, CLIs, and API bindings even more important,” Knecht tells The New Stack over email. “If that layer is stale or incomplete, an agent doesn’t just have a worse developer experience, it can misunderstand what a service can do.”
Ultimately, Cloudflare created Forge because SDK and CLI generation has “become too important” to sit outside its internal development process.
“Cloudflare needed a pipeline our teams could run, test, and extend themselves, and we think other developers should have access to that same kind of open, vendor independent foundation,” Knecht says.
Forge still has plenty to prove, of course. The project is early, cf is its first production output, and Cloudflare says its API documentation and existing SDKs will move over during the coming months. Several of the input formats and generated targets it discusses are also future work.
But the timing is quite revealing. Within 11 days, Google and Cloudflare — both former Stainless customers — have publicly thrown their heft behind open source SDK-generation infrastructure after the disappearance of the proprietary service they had relied on. Google describes that dependency as an “unacceptable platform risk.” Cloudflare, with Forge, is now trying to remove the same risk from its own stack.

title: Agents have made CI the bottleneck. Faster pipelines are the wrong fix.
text:
Agents have made CI the bottleneck. Faster pipelines are the wrong fix.
Three posts landed in September that I think engineering leaders should read together.
Anthropic’s engineering team wrote that their continuous integration (CI) job volume grew 25x in six months. Their engineers now ship about 8x as much code per quarter as they did from 2021 to 2025. The fix they shipped was test impact analysis: run only the tests a change could affect.
A week later, Linear published a post titled AI coding has made CI a bottleneck. Their test suite has nearly quadrupled since January, and agents now write most of their tests. They reworked the pipeline end to end to keep up.
Then Depot’s CEO wrote that CI is changing, and that the future is “giving agents a way to validate code and maintain trust as they work.”
Anthropic and Linear do not sell CI tooling. They are reporting what happened to their own pipelines, which is what makes it worth paying attention to. Here is my read: all three are right about the problem, and two of them are fixing the wrong layer.
How CI became the bottleneck
For twenty years, CI was sized for human output. A developer opened a few pull requests (PRs) a week, and the pipeline ran after each one. If it took 20 minutes, nobody cared much, because the developer was already on the next task.
Agents broke that arithmetic in two ways. First, volume. When one engineer runs several agents in parallel, PR count goes up by a multiple, not a percentage. Anthropic’s 25x number is not an outlier. Blacksmith, which sells CI runners, says the number of CI jobs it runs has grown between 5% and 10% week over week.
The agent is fast, and the loop around it is slow.
Second, placement. CI runs after the PR exists. An agent that writes code, opens a PR, and waits 20 minutes for a red check has lost its working context by the time the result comes back. Every failure costs a full round trip. The agent is fast, and the loop around it is slow.
So the industry did the obvious thing and made CI faster. Faster runners, smarter test selection, bigger caches, pipelines that agents can call before commit. All of it helps, and all of it is necessary. All of it also leaves one assumption untouched: that what you’re verifying is a repository.
What a green pipeline does not tell you
For a standalone application, a repository is the system. Run the tests, and you know most of what you need to know.
For a cloud-native system, a repository is one service out of forty. The tests in that repo exercise that service, and they mock everything else. A change can pass every unit test, pass CI in record time, pass a sandbox built from the branch, and still break the first real request that crosses a service boundary.
The failures that hurt in distributed systems live in the seams. A field renamed in a response that a downstream consumer still reads. A timeout tightened in one service that cascades into retries somewhere else. A schema change that works against the test fixture and locks a table in staging. A new endpoint that behaves correctly when the test harness calls it and incorrectly when the service that depends on it calls it.
Nothing in the CI pipeline, fast or slow, sees any of that. It cannot, because it is looking at a repo.
This is why I think the September posts are a symptom, not a diagnosis. CI got slow because verification moved from a human gate to an automated one without anyone asking what the automated gate checks. Making the gate faster does not change what it checks.
Faster code, same verification, more breakage. That is the gap.
DevOps Research and Assessment (DORA) found something that should worry you: higher AI adoption is associated with increases in both software delivery throughput and software delivery instability. Faster code, same verification, more breakage. That is the gap.
The verification loop has to move
Cursor made a point in February that is only becoming more relevant. Their agents run in cloud sandboxes, each with its own virtual machine, and more than 30% of the PRs Cursor merges now come from agents working that way. Their stated reason: “Without the ability to use the software they are creating, agents hit a ceiling.”
That is the right instinct. The agent has to run the code, not only write it. Every serious coding agent now does some version of this. GitHub’s Copilot cloud agent runs tests in an ephemeral environment powered by GitHub Actions. Codex runs a setup script and resumes cached containers. Devin boots from environment blueprints. Greptile’s TREX runs the branch and attaches logs and screenshots to the PR.
But look at what each of those sandboxes contains: the repo, the branch, and whatever the setup script could install. None of them include the other 39 services, the real message queue, or the database with production-shaped data.
So the loop closes, but it closes around the wrong thing.
So the loop closes, but it closes around the wrong thing. The agent verifies its change against a copy of its own code. Then the change goes to CI, which verifies it against the same copy, faster. Then it merges into staging, and that is the first moment anything checks whether it works with the rest of the system.
For distributed systems, verification before the PR has to be against the system, not the repo. That is the shift. It is not faster feedback on the same question. It is a different question, asked earlier.
Why this looks expensive and is not
The reflexive objection is cost. If every agent needs the whole system to verify against, and one engineer is running five agents, you need five staging environments per engineer. Nobody can afford that, and nobody should try.
The answer is the same one the industry used for compute two decades ago. You do not give every workload its own machine. You multiplex.
A single Kubernetes cluster can run one shared stable version of every service and host thousands of lightweight test environments on top of it. Each test environment deploys only the changed service. Requests tagged for that environment pass through the modified service, and every other hop resolves to the shared stable versions. The modified service talks to real dependencies, and those dependencies do not know anything changed.
A test environment costs roughly the price of one pod, and it comes up in seconds. Fifty agents working in parallel share one stable environment instead of cloning it fifty times. That is what makes system-level verification inside the agent loop affordable in the first place.
Agents need governed verification, not only environments
Cheap, fast environments are not the whole answer. An agent also needs a structured way to use them: send this request, capture that log, assert this contract held, report the result. Left to improvise, each agent invents its own checks, and no two runs are comparable.
The model that works is one where the platform team writes those steps once, as a sequence of approved actions that exercises a change against the live system and records what happened. Agents invoke them through the skills and hooks that Claude Code, Cursor, and similar tools already support, so verification runs as part of the loop rather than after it. The governance matters as much as the steps, because platform teams need to know an agent cannot do something unsafe in a shared cluster.
The output matters too. A record showing which requests were sent, which services were touched, and which contracts were held is an artifact the next layer can read. Review tools and merge gates can see that a change was exercised against live services before a human looks at it, and CI becomes a confirmation step instead of the first place cross-service breakage shows up.
Verification belongs inside the agent’s loop
I expect the CI vendors to keep getting faster, and I expect coding agents to keep getting better at running code in sandboxes. Both are good for everyone, and neither closes the gap between a repo and a system. The teams that come out ahead will stop asking how fast the pipeline can confirm that a repo still passes its own tests and start asking how early an agent can prove that a change works with everything around it. That question gets answered in one place: inside the agent’s loop, against the real system, before the PR. We built Signadot to make that check cheap enough to run on every change, with the governed.
